Unit 1 — Biblical Foundations — Sickness, Healing, and the Ministry of Jesus

The Old Testament: Sickness, Sin, and Protest

The Old Testament holds two convictions in unresolved tension, and both survive into Christian theology.

The retribution principle. Sickness is widely presented as connected to sin — Deuteronomy 28's blessings and curses, Psalm 38 ("there is no health in my bones because of my sin"), Miriam's leprosy (Num 12). This is the intuitive theology every pastor still meets: what did I do to deserve this?

The protest against it. Job is the sustained, canonical refutation. Job's friends argue the retribution principle with increasing severity; God's verdict is that they "have not spoken of me what is right" (Job 42:7). The book does not explain suffering — it forbids the easy explanation.

Three further texts matter:

  • Isaiah 53:4-5 — "surely he has borne our griefs (ḥŏlāyēnû, literally our sicknesses) and carried our sorrows... by his stripes we are healed." Matthew 8:17 applies this verse directly to Jesus's healing ministry, which makes it the bridge text between the Suffering Servant and the theology of Christ bearing our infirmity.
  • Sirach 38:1-15 — a remarkably balanced text: "Honour the physician... for the Lord created him," while also urging prayer and repentance. Medicine and prayer are not rivals. This is the scriptural warrant for the Church's consistent refusal to set the sacrament against medical treatment.
  • Psalm 41:3 — "The LORD sustains him on his sickbed; in his illness you restore him to full health" — the prayer of the sick person that the later rite takes up.

Jesus's Healing Ministry

Healing is not incidental to the Gospels but structurally central: roughly a third of Mark concerns healings and exorcisms. Three features shape the later sacrament:

  1. Healing is a sign of the Kingdom's arrival, not a display of power. When John's disciples ask if he is the one to come, Jesus answers by listing healings (Mt 11:4-5, echoing Isa 35).
  2. Jesus touches. He touches the leper (Mk 1:41) — a man whom the Law made untouchable. The physicality of the encounter is theologically deliberate and is why the sacrament is an anointing, a bodily act, rather than a prayer alone.
  3. Forgiveness and healing are linked but not equated. In Mark 2 the paralytic is forgiven and healed. But in John 9:2-3 the disciples ask "who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" and Jesus answers "neither" — decisively breaking the automatic link. Both texts must be held: sin and sickness belong to the same disordered world, but this illness is not that person's punishment.

Mark 6:13 — The Sending of the Twelve

"And they cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many that were sick and healed them."

This is the only Gospel text describing the disciples anointing the sick with oil, and it is the passage Trent would cite as the sacrament being "insinuated" (insinuatum) by Christ — hinted at and prepared — before being promulgated by James. Note the careful conciliar verb: Trent does not claim Mark 6:13 is the institution, only its intimation.

Illustration. Notice that the Twelve are given no explanation of why oil. Oil in the ancient Mediterranean was simply what you used on a body — for wounds, for athletes, for the dead, for kings. It was food, medicine, fuel, and cosmetic at once. The sacrament takes the most ordinary substance in the household and makes it the vehicle of the Spirit's strengthening — which is precisely the sacramental logic in miniature.

Unit 10 — Contemporary Debates

1. Where is the threshold? SC 73 and c. 1004 set it at the beginning of danger from sickness or old age, and CCC 1515 explicitly includes before surgery. But how serious is "serious"? Practice varies from the very restrictive (near-death only, in effect reverting to the medieval position) to the very broad (any illness, any distress). The genuine risk at the broad end is that the sacrament becomes a general blessing and loses its specific character; at the restrictive end, that the reform is quietly nullified.

2. Communal anointing services. Now common, and a genuine expression of the ecclesial dimension (LG 11). The disputed question is whether the requirement of serious illness is being observed, or whether such services in practice anoint whole congregations regardless of condition — which would make the sacrament something other than what the rite says it is.

3. Who may anoint? CIC c. 1003 restricts valid administration to priests. The historical argument for extending it — at least to deacons, or in mission territories to lay ministers — appeals directly to Innocent I (Unit 3), who permitted all Christians to use the blessed oil. The counter-argument is that the sacrament's forgiveness-of-sins effect ties it to the priestly power of absolution, and that the discipline is settled. Note that c. 999 already permits a priest to bless the oil in a case of necessity, a modest decentralisation of what was once strictly episcopal.

4. Mental illness, addiction, dementia. Whether and how the sacrament applies where the "illness" is psychiatric rather than somatic. Most pastoral guidance now answers yes for serious cases, but the question of the recipient's use of reason (c. 1004 §1, c. 1005) and of implicit request (c. 1006) requires care.

5. The unconscious and the recently dead. c. 1005's rule — in doubt, administer — governs. Where death is certain, the sacrament is not conferred, but the boundary is medically uncertain and the Church's instruction is to err toward conferral, conditionally.

6. Anointing and the healing ministry. The relation between the sacrament and charismatic healing prayer is theologically underdeveloped and pastorally live, particularly in Africa, Latin America, and Asia, where independent healing ministries are a major force. The sacrament is not a healing service, but the modern rite prays genuinely for recovery, and pretending otherwise concedes the ground.

7. Ecumenical dimension. The Orthodox euchelaion — ideally seven priests, seven epistles, seven gospels, seven anointings — retained the healing orientation throughout, never developing an "extreme unction," and is administered widely, including to the healthy in Holy Week in some traditions. Anglicanism recovered anointing in the twentieth century. The Catholic reform of 1972 substantially narrowed the historic gap with both.

Unit 13 — Examination Preparation

Likely Essay Questions

  1. "The history of this sacrament is a case study in how liturgical accident generates theology." Discuss with reference to the Carolingian reform and the scholastic doctrine of the reliquiae peccati.
  2. Give a detailed exegesis of James 5:14-15 and assess how far it supports the Tridentine doctrine of Extreme Unction.
  3. "Vatican II did not contradict Trent on this sacrament; it exploited a deliberate reticence in Trent's wording." Evaluate, with attention to the word praesertim.
  4. Assess the significance of Innocent I's Letter to Decentius for the contemporary debate over who may administer the sacrament.
  5. Why did Cardinal Cajetan's exegesis of James 5 not lead to a Catholic reform in the sixteenth century, and what changed by 1972?
  6. "The claim that the sick person contributes to the good of the Church is either the sacrament's deepest insight or its cruellest evasion." Discuss with reference to LG 11 and Colossians 1:24.
  7. Compare the Latin sacrament with the Orthodox euchelaion and account for their divergence.
  8. Assess the pastoral relationship between the sacrament of anointing and popular healing devotion in the Indian context.

Ten-Second Recall Anchors

  • "Mark 6:13 insinuates, James 5 promulgates" — Trent's own verbs.
  • "Innocent I, 416: omnibus christianis" — all Christians may use the blessed oil.
  • "Carolingians clericalised it; the Lombard renamed it" — unctio extrema.
  • Reliquiae peccati — Aquinas's proper effect: the remnants of sin.
  • "Praesertim — 'especially,' not 'only'" — the word that left Trent's door open.
  • "SC 73: aptius — 'more fittingly' called Anointing of the Sick."
  • "Forehead and hands" — the essential rite since 1972.
  • "Save and raise up" — the 1972 form tracking James 5:15.
  • "Viaticum outranks anointing for the dying."
  • "Seven priests, seven gospels" — the Orthodox euchelaion.

Comparative Analysis Exercises

  • Tabulate the sacrament across the five eras (Unit 12's master schema) and identify at each stage what changed and what caused the change.
  • Compare Florence's "nisi infirmo, de cuius morte timetur" (1439) with SC 73 and state precisely what was reversed.
  • Compare the medieval anointing of the five senses with the 1972 anointing of forehead and hands, and account for the reduction.
  • Set Innocent I's letter beside CIC c. 1003 and construct the strongest historical case for and against extending the ministry.

Unit 2 — James 5:14-15 — The Locus Classicus

Everything in the Catholic theology of this sacrament turns on one passage, so it must be known in detail.

"Is any among you sick? Let him call for the presbyters of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven." (James 5:14-15)

Element-by-Element Exegesis

Element Greek Observations
"Is any sick" asthenei "To be weak, without strength" — general debility, not necessarily terminal
"Let him call for" proskalesasthō The sick person takes the initiative — the sacrament is requested, not imposed
"the presbyters of the church" presbyterous tēs ekklēsias Plural, and an office — not simply "older men," which is the exegetical point Trent defends in canon 4
"let them pray over him" proseuxasthōsan ep' auton The preposition suggests hands extended over the sick person
"anointing him with oil" aleipsantes elaiō Note aleiphō (ordinary/medicinal anointing), not chriō (ritual/messianic anointing) — a genuine exegetical difficulty for those who want a purely ritual reading
"in the name of the Lord" en tō onomati tou Kyriou The act is done in Christ's authority, distinguishing it from folk medicine
"will save" sōsei Bears both "heal" and "save" — the ambiguity is theologically fertile, not a defect
"will raise him up" egerei Likewise both "raise from the sickbed" and the resurrection verb
"if he has committed sins" kan hamartias ē pepoiēkōs The conditional is important: sin is not assumed to be the cause of the illness

The Central Interpretive Question

Does James describe bodily healing or spiritual salvation? The honest answer is that the vocabulary deliberately holds both, and the history of the sacrament is largely the history of the balance tipping — first toward healing (patristic), then decisively toward preparation for death (medieval), then back toward a unified view (modern).

A crucial historical note for essays. The objection that James 5 concerns bodily healing rather than a sacrament for the dying was not first raised by the Reformers. Cardinal Cajetan, Thomas de Vio — Luther's own opponent at Augsburg and a thoroughly Catholic authority — argued in his commentary that James refers to anointing for recovery, not to extreme unction. That a cardinal made the exegetical point independently is a useful corrective to treating it as a merely polemical Protestant claim, and it partly anticipates the twentieth-century recovery.

Trent's Use of the Text

Trent (Session XIV) reads James 5 as the promulgation of a sacrament insinuated in Mark 6:13, and draws from it: the matter (oil), the minister (presbyters, i.e. priests), the effects (grace, strengthening, forgiveness of sins, and sometimes bodily health). Canon 4 specifically anathematises the reading that "presbyters" means merely elders by age rather than ordained priests.

Unit 11 — Practical and Pastoral Application

Common Pastoral Scenarios

Scenario Response
Family asks for "last rites" Establish what is needed: absolution, viaticum, anointing — and in what order the person's condition permits. Viaticum has priority for the dying
Person is unconscious Confer conditionally (c. 1005); presume implicit request if they were a practising Catholic (c. 1006)
Priest arrives after death The sacrament is not conferred on the dead; but where death is recent and uncertain, conditional anointing is permitted. Then pray the Prayers for the Dead with the family
Person recovers and later falls ill again Repeat it (c. 1004 §2) — this is a positive norm, not a mere permission
Scheduled major surgery Anointing is appropriate (CCC 1515)
Elderly person, no acute illness but notable frailty Appropriate — SC 73 names old age explicitly, independent of illness
A person in manifest grave sin, unrepentant c. 1007: not to be conferred — but note that this concerns obstinate persistence, and any sign of repentance changes the case
No olive oil available Another plant oil may be used (Sacram Unctionem Infirmorum); a priest may bless it in necessity (c. 999)
Non-Catholic Christian requests it Governed by c. 844; permitted for Eastern Orthodox, and for others in danger of death under the conditions there specified

The Indian Context — Healing Devotion and the Sacrament

This is where the sacrament meets one of the most vigorous realities of Indian Catholic life, and the vault's material on Velankanni — the Basilica of Our Lady of Good Health, the "Lourdes of the East" — is directly relevant.

What devotees do. Pilgrims deposit wax and metal ex-votos — replicas of limbs, organs, infants, houses, boats, agricultural tools — offered ex voto suscepto, "from a vow undertaken." Vows follow the Tamil nadai pattern: a conditional covenant pledging a specific offering contingent on divine intervention, whose non-fulfilment after healing carries real moral weight. Fulfilment is embodied — tonsure, sea-bathing, prostrate advance and anga pradakshinam (rolling the body along the path).

What they seek. Not chiefly moksha but concrete deliverance: healing from paralysis and disease, children, success in examinations, security of livelihood. As Vasudha Narayanan observes, Hindus come to such shrines for "time-sensitive reasons" rather than for ultimate liberation.

Why non-Christians come. Narayanan's analysis is that pilgrims seek localised divine power — shakti, barakat — and are drawn to sites established as repositories of it; theological pluralism means that petitioning at a Christian shrine is no betrayal of their own faith. Selva J. Raj described the shared ritual space as "a form of ongoing, authentic interreligious dialogue, arising organically from lived experiences rather than abstracted theologies." Susan Bayly's sharper historical judgement is that at these healing shrines "the would-be converters were themselves 'converted'; they were made over into tutelaries and cult saints so as to fit in with south India's existing forms of worship."

The theological question this poses for the sacrament. Susan Visvanathan notes that Indian Catholics move comfortably between two parallel ritual spaces — "canonical" rituals (the official sacraments, performed by the priest inside the church) and "domestic" or vernacular rituals (tonsure, sea-bathing, nadai vows, managed by family or catechist). The pastoral risk is that the sacrament of anointing is experienced as belonging wholly to the first sphere — clerical, Latin-derived, associated with dying — while the actual religious energy around healing lives entirely in the second.

The opportunity. The 1972 reform's recovery of the sacrament as a prayer for healing and strengthening, addressed to Christus medicus, is precisely the bridge. Two further connections are available and underused: - The patristic pattern (Unit 3) of blessed oil taken home and used by the household is strikingly close in structure to the domestic sphere Visvanathan describes — a genuine precedent, not an accommodation. - Caesarius of Arles's pastoral instinct (Unit 3) — offering the Church's blessed oil as the true alternative to charms and sorcerers — is the same pastoral situation, thirteen centuries earlier.

The caution. Michael Amaladoss's methodological rule applies with full force: inculturation must begin from actual living symbols — and here the living symbols of healing devotion are abundantly documented. What it must not become is either a dismissal of popular practice as superstition or an uncritical absorption of transactional religiosity into the sacrament.

Unit 4 — The Carolingian Shift — From Healing to Dying

The most consequential transformation in the history of this sacrament, and — as with penance — it happened through reform legislation rather than doctrinal decision.

What the Carolingian Reformers Did

The ninth-century reform, seeking uniformity and the suppression of superstition, made the anointing of the sick an exclusively clerical act. Bishops' capitularies (Theodulf of Orleans and others) instruct priests to perform the anointing themselves; the practice of lay and self-anointing is progressively suppressed.

Simultaneously, the anointing was incorporated into the deathbed ordo, the sequence of rites for the dying: penance → anointing → viaticum. Because canonical penance still carried lifelong disabilities (Penance course, Unit 3), being enrolled among the penitents was something one did at the very end — and the anointing, now bound to that sequence, migrated with it.

The Name Changes

By the twelfth century the sacrament is being called unctio extrema — "extreme (that is, last) unction." Peter Lombard uses the term in the Sentences, and it becomes standard. The name both records and reinforces the shift: it is now explicitly the final anointing.

The Consequences — A Chain of Pastoral Disasters

Consequence Effect
Fear of the sacrament To send for the priest was to declare the patient dying; families delayed
The penitential disabilities attached A popular and sometimes canonical belief held that one who recovered after anointing must live as though dead — abstaining from meat, from marital relations, sometimes from legal acts and bearing arms
Deferral to the last possible moment The sacrament was often administered to the unconscious or the barely-living
Loss of the healing dimension Recovery came to be seen almost as an anomaly rather than as something the rite prayed for

Illustration. Consider the trap this created. The sacrament exists to strengthen the sick — but calling for it announces that you are dying, and surviving it may impose the obligations of a penitent for life. So you wait. And because you wait, the sacrament is only ever seen at deathbeds, which confirms everyone's belief that it is for the dying, which makes the next person wait longer. A self-reinforcing pastoral trap, generated not by doctrine but by the accidental bundling of rites. Untangling precisely this knot is what Sacrosanctum Concilium 73 sets out to do.

Unit 3 — The Patristic Era — Blessed Oil and Lay Anointing

The patristic evidence is genuinely surprising to students formed on the modern rite, and it is the strongest historical argument for the twentieth-century reform.

The Focus Was the Blessing of the Oil, Not the Anointing

Early liturgical books contain prayers for blessing oil rather than rites of anointing. The Apostolic Tradition (§5) provides a blessing of oil immediately after the Eucharistic Prayer, asking that it give strength to all who taste it and health to all who use it. The Euchologion of Serapion of Thmuis (4th c., Egypt) contains several such prayers, one asking that the oil become "a means of removing every disease and every sickness."

The key point: the blessing was the reserved, hierarchical act; the application was not.

Innocent I's Letter to Decentius of Gubbio (416)

This is the single most important patristic text on the sacrament, and it should be quoted in any historical essay.

Answering a bishop's query, Pope Innocent I explains that the oil of James 5 is blessed by the bishop, and then states that it may be used not only by priests but by all Christians — "omnibus christianis" — in their own need and in the need of their households. He adds one restriction: it is not to be given to penitents, since they are excluded from all the sacraments while under canonical penance (see the Penance course, Unit 3).

Three consequences follow, all of them significant:

  1. Self-anointing and lay anointing were normal and legitimate for centuries. The oil was taken home; the sick anointed themselves, or family members anointed them. It was also drunk.
  2. The reservation of the sacrament to priests is a later development, not an apostolic given.
  3. The restriction of the oil from penitents is the first hint of the fateful link between anointing and penitential status which would later drive the sacrament to the deathbed (Unit 4).

Other Patristic Witnesses

  • Caesarius of Arles (6th c.) urges the sick to go to the church for anointing with blessed oil rather than to amulets, charms, and sorcerers — an early instance of the Church offering a sacramental alternative to folk healing practice, a pastoral dynamic still entirely live in many cultures (Unit 12).
  • Bede (8th c.), commenting on Mark 6:13 and James 5, is the first major Latin writer to treat the two texts together as describing a single ecclesial practice.

Teaching point. For roughly the first eight centuries the sacrament was: oil blessed by the bishop, applied by anyone, for the recovery of the sick. Every element of that description would be reversed by the Carolingian reform — which is why Sacrosanctum Concilium 73 can present the modern change as a restoration rather than an innovation.

Unit 6 — The Reformation and Trent

The Reformers

Luther (The Babylonian Captivity, 1520) rejects it forcefully on three grounds: James is not of apostolic authority (Luther's low estimate of the epistle is well known); there is no dominical institution; and the promise James attaches — "the Lord will raise him up" — manifestly does not happen, since those anointed die. His sharpest point is the mismatch: the Church promises what James promises but administers it precisely to those it expects not to recover. He adds, characteristically, that he would not object to prayer and anointing as James describes, provided no one calls it a sacrament.

Calvin (Institutes IV.19.18-21) makes the cessationist argument: the healing described in James and Mark was a temporary charismatic gift given to authenticate the apostolic preaching, which ceased with the apostolic age. To continue the outward sign after the gift has been withdrawn is, in his phrase, a "hypocritical stage-play." Calvin's argument is important because it is the one that most directly severs the sacrament from its scriptural warrant.

Cardinal Cajetan — worth restating here — had already argued on purely exegetical grounds that James concerns anointing for recovery, not extreme unction. His view was not condemned, and it stands as evidence that the exegetical question was live within Catholic theology before and during the Reformation.

Anglican practice is instructive: the 1549 Book of Common Prayer retained an anointing in the Order for the Visitation of the Sick; the 1552 revision removed it. It was recovered in the twentieth century through the Anglican and Catholic liturgical movements alike.

Trent, Session XIV (25 November 1551)

Trent treats Extreme Unction alongside Penance, in three chapters and four canons.

Teaching Content
Institution Insinuated by Christ in Mark 6:13, promulgated by James 5:14-15
Matter and form Oil blessed by a bishop; the prayer of the priest
Effects The grace of the Holy Spirit, "wiping away sins if any remain to be expiated, and the remnants of sin"; "alleviating and strengthening the soul of the sick person"; and "sometimes restores bodily health, when expedient for the salvation of the soul"
Minister Priests — canon 4 anathematises the view that "presbyters" in James means elders by age rather than ordained ministers
Recipients "Especially for those who lie so dangerously ill as to seem near to death" (praesertim)

The most important word in the decree is praesertim — "especially." Trent says the sacrament is especially for those near death; it does not define that it is only for them. This single adverb is what leaves the door legally open for Sacrosanctum Concilium 73's reform four centuries later. A strong exam answer notes that Vatican II did not contradict Trent here but exploited a deliberate reticence in its wording — exactly parallel to how Trent's aptissime on transubstantiation left room for later re-expression.

Unit 5 — The Scholastic Synthesis

Fixing It Among the Seven

Peter Lombard's Sentences IV, d. 23 lists unctio extrema among the seven sacraments, and the septenary is then confirmed at Lyons II (1274) and Florence (1439).

Florence's Decree for the Armenians (1439) gives the standard late-medieval definition, and its restrictiveness should be noted precisely: the sacrament is "not to be given except to a sick person of whose death there is fear" (nisi infirmo, de cuius morte timetur). Matter: olive oil blessed by a bishop. Anointings: the five senses, plus loins and feet, with the deprecatory form "Per istam sanctam unctionem..." Effect: healing of the mind and, so far as expedient, of the body.

Aquinas (ST Suppl. qq. 29-33)

Category Content
Matter Olive oil blessed by a bishop
Form The deprecatory prayer, "Per istam unctionem..." — note that unlike penance, the form here is a prayer, not an indicative declaration
Minister Priests
Principal effect The remission of the reliquiae peccati — the "remnants of sin": the weakness, spiritual debility, and residual disorder left by sin even after its guilt is forgiven
Bodily healing An effect per accidens — granted when it is conducive to the person's salvation, not otherwise
Character None; the sacrament is repeatable in a new illness

The reliquiae peccati is the concept to master here. Aquinas needed to identify an effect proper* to this sacrament and not already covered by penance (which forgives guilt) or the Eucharist (which nourishes). His answer: penance heals the wound, but the patient remains weakened; anointing addresses that remaining debility, preparing the soul for its final passage. This is a genuinely elegant solution, and it explains why the sacrament came to be called the sacramentum exeuntium, the "*sacrament of those departing."

The problem with it. The account is coherent but it presupposes and reinforces the deathbed setting. If the proper effect is the removal of the remnants of sin in preparation for glory, the sacrament's natural moment is indeed the end. The scholastic synthesis is thus a brilliant systematisation of a practice that had itself arisen by historical accident — a pattern we have now seen in confirmation, penance, and anointing alike.

Other Scholastic Positions

Bonaventure and Duns Scotus broadly concur on the deathbed orientation, though with differences over whether the sacrament requires actual proximity to death or merely dangerous illness. Scotus, characteristically, is the more restrictive: he holds it should be deferred until death is genuinely imminent, so that the grace conferred is not subsequently lost through further sin.

Unit 9 — Theological Significance

1. Christological — Christ the Physician. The Fathers' favourite title, Christus medicus, is the sacrament's governing image. Christ does not explain suffering; he enters it and touches the sufferer. The anointing extends that touch.

2. Paschal — configuration to the passion. LG 11 asks the sick to "contribute to the good of the People of God by freely uniting themselves to the passion and death of Christ," and CCC 1521 speaks of the sick person receiving "the strength and the gift of uniting himself more closely to Christ's Passion." The theological background is Colossians 1:24 — "in my flesh I complete what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the Church." Nothing is lacking in Christ's redemptive work; what is "lacking" is the members' participation in it.

This is the sacrament's most distinctive and most difficult claim: that the sick person is not merely a passive object of the Church's care but an agent whose suffering, united to Christ's, is fruitful for the whole body. Handled badly it becomes a cruel spiritualisation of pain that tells sufferers to be grateful. Handled well it is the one thing that answers the sick person's deepest fear — that they have become useless.

3. Pneumatological. The form asks explicitly for "the grace of the Holy Spirit." The proper effect is a gift, not merely a consolation.

4. Ecclesial. "The whole Church commends those who are ill" — the sacrament is an act of the entire body, which is why communal celebration (Unit 11) is not a concession but an expression of what the sacrament is.

5. Eschatological. Anointing completes the anointings of Christian life. Baptism anoints for incorporation, Confirmation for mission, and the Anointing of the Sick fortifies for the final struggle and passage — "a solid anointing to fortify the end of our earthly life like a strong rampart for the final struggles before entering the Father's house" (CCC 1523).

The Effects, per CCC 1520-1523

  1. A particular gift of the Holy Spirit — strengthening, peace, courage against discouragement and anguish.
  2. Union with the passion of Christ, giving the suffering a share in his saving work.
  3. An ecclesial grace — the sick contribute to the sanctification of the Church.
  4. Forgiveness of sins, if the person was unable to obtain it through penance.
  5. Restoration of health, if it is conducive to the salvation of the soul.
  6. Preparation for the final journey.

Note the ordering: healing appears fifth, not first, and is conditional — but it genuinely appears, which the medieval practice had all but forgotten.

Unit 7 — Vatican II and the 1972 Reform

Sacrosanctum Concilium 73 — The Decisive Text

"'Extreme unction,' which may also and more fittingly be called 'Anointing of the Sick,' is not a sacrament for those only who are at the point of death. Hence, as soon as any one of the faithful begins to be in danger of death from sickness or old age, the fitting time for him to receive this sacrament has certainly already arrived."

Three moves in two sentences:

  1. The name changes — and the Council says the new name is more fitting (aptius), a quiet judgement that the medieval name had distorted the theology.
  2. The negative correction — "not for those only who are at the point of death."
  3. The threshold is set at the beginning of danger, from sickness or old age — the latter being an important extension, since old age is not an illness.

SC 74 orders a continuous rite in which anointing is conferred after confession and before viaticum. SC 75 directs that the number of anointings be adapted and the prayers revised to fit the varied conditions of the sick.

LG 11 supplies the ecclesial theology: "By the sacred anointing of the sick and the prayer of her priests, the whole Church commends those who are ill to the suffering and glorified Lord, that he may raise them up and save them. And indeed she exhorts them to contribute to the good of the People of God by freely uniting themselves to the passion and death of Christ." Note the two directions — the Church acts for the sick, and the sick contribute to the Church. The sick person is an agent, not merely a recipient.

Sacram Unctionem Infirmorum (Paul VI, 30 November 1972)

The Apostolic Constitution promulgating the reform. Its decisions:

  • The essential rite is reduced to anointing the forehead and the hands (from the medieval anointing of the five senses, loins, and feet). In case of necessity, a single anointing on the forehead — or any suitable part of the body — suffices.
  • The matter is olive oil or, where necessary, another plant oil — a significant practical concession for regions where olive oil is unavailable.
  • The new form, replacing the medieval formula:

"Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Amen. May the Lord who frees you from sin save you and raise you up. Amen."

Observe how closely the second sentence tracks James 5:15 (sōsei... egerei — save and raise up). The reform's method was, once again, ressourcement: go behind the medieval development to the scriptural text.

The Rite (Ordo Unctionis Infirmorum, 1972)

The English-language edition is titled Pastoral Care of the Sick: Rites of Anointing and Viaticum, and the title itself signals the reform's intent — the sacrament sits within an ongoing pastoral care, not a single emergency intervention. The book provides for visits to the sick, communion of the sick, anointing (within or outside Mass, individually or communally), viaticum, and the commendation of the dying.

Canonical Norms (CIC 1983, cc. 998-1007)

Canon Provision
c. 998 Definition: for the faithful who are dangerously ill from sickness or old age
c. 1003 Every priest, and only a priest, validly administers it
c. 1004 §1 May be given to one who, having reached the use of reason, begins to be in danger from sickness or old age
c. 1004 §2 May be repeated if the person recovers and again falls ill, or if the danger becomes graver
c. 1005 In doubt whether the person is ill enough, has died, or has the use of reason — administer it
c. 1006 To be given to those who requested it at least implicitly when they were in control of their faculties
c. 1007 Not to be conferred on those who obstinately persist in manifest grave sin

CCC 1499-1532 gives the systematic treatment, and CCC 1514-1515 repeat the pastoral broadening: before surgery, in serious illness, in the frailty of old age, and repeatedly through a long illness.

Unit 8 — Viaticum and the Order of the Last Rites

A source of persistent confusion among students and among the faithful, and worth stating precisely.

"Last Rites" Is Not a Sacrament

The phrase names a sequence, not a single rite, and the sequence has a proper order:

Order Rite Note
1 Penance (or, if impossible, at least the sacrament's absolution) Reconciliation first
2 Anointing of the Sick The strengthening of the sick person
3 Viaticum The Eucharist as food for the journey

Where time is short, the order of priority differs from the order of celebration: the most important sacrament for a dying person is Viaticum, not anointing. The tradition is emphatic on this and modern pastoral practice often gets it backwards.

Viaticum — from via, "way" — is literally "provision for the journey." Its priority follows from the whole logic of the Eucharist: it is Christ himself, and the pignus futurae gloriae, the pledge of the glory the dying person is about to enter. The proper form adds the words "May the Lord Jesus Christ protect you and lead you to eternal life."

Note that c. 921 obliges the dying to receive Viaticum, and permits it even to those who have already received communion that day — an unusual dispensation that measures its importance.

The Apostolic Pardon

A plenary indulgence at the hour of death, granted in the rite, remitting the temporal punishment due to sin (see the Penance course, Unit 7). Where no priest is available, the Church supplies it to anyone who has habitually prayed during life.

Commendation of the Dying

Prayers, litanies, and brief scriptural verses to be said with and for the dying, and — importantly — the Prayers for the Dead immediately afterward. The rite provides for the family and the community to pray, not only the priest, which recovers something of the patristic pattern in which anointing and prayer for the sick were not exclusively clerical acts.

Teaching point for pastoral practice. When called to a dying person with limited time, the priest's order of operations is: absolution → viaticum if the person can still swallow → anointing. If the person is already unconscious, absolution is given conditionally and anointing conferred; viaticum is impossible. Knowing this sequence, and why viaticum outranks anointing, is a standard pastoral examination question.

1. Changing Ecclesiology in a changing church.pdf

TITLE: A Changing Ecclesiology in a Changing Church: A Symposium on Development in the Ecclesiology of Karl Rahner. Edited by Leo J. O'Donovan, S.J. (Weston School of Theology), with contributions by J. Peter Schineller, S.J. (Jesuit School of Theology in Chicago), John P. Galvin (St. John's Seminary, Brighton, Massachusetts), and Michael A. Fahey (Concordia University, Montreal) [1-3]. Published in Theological Studies, Vol. 38, 1977, pages 736–762 [4-7].

MAIN SUBJECT: The historical development, core themes, and major shifts in the ecclesiology of Karl Rahner across three distinct chronological periods: his post-WWII early foundations (1946–1959), his conciliar contributions around Vatican II (1960–1965), and his post-conciliar focus on structural changes and the concrete church (1966–1976) [3].

KEY TOPICS Covered: * The relationship between individual freedom, personal responsibility, and hierarchical authority in the Church [8, 9]. * The Church as the "protosacrament" or prime sacrament of God’s grace in the world [10, 11]. * The theological synthesis of Church membership, baptism of desire, and salvation outside the visible Church [12, 13]. * The holiness and inherent sinfulness of the Church ("Church of sinners") [14, 15]. * Office in the Church, focusing on episcopal collegiality, the relationship between the Pope and the college of bishops, and the restoration of the permanent diaconate [16, 17]. * "Anonymous Christianity" as a speculative framework for the salvation of non-Christians [18, 19]. * The transition from a cultural "Volkskirche" to a "little flock" in a diaspora situation [20, 21]. * Structural transformations, basic Christian communities (Basisgemeinden), and the task of declericalization [22-24]. * The mission of the Church in humanizing the world versus the dangers of clericalism and "horizontalism" [25, 26].

CONCEPTS EXPLAINED: 1. Dual Notion of the Church: Rahner distinguishes between the Church as the community of the redeemed (the place of inner grace) and the Church as an organized, visible, and juridical society with rules [9]. Tension arises because the organized society must safeguard the ultimately private, spiritual sphere of the unique individual before God [9]. 2. Protosacrament (Prime Sacrament): The understanding that the Church, in her visible, concrete, and juridically verifiable appearance, is the real, permanent sign and physical embodiment of God's salvific will and the grace of Christ in the world [10]. 3. Anonymous Christianity: The theological theory rooted in Rahner's transcendental anthropology asserting that because God's salvific will is universal, those who accept the grace offered to them but have no explicit contact with the Christian message are "anonymous Christians" whose salvation is still ontologically bound to Jesus Christ [54, 175–177]. 4. Ecclesiological Monophysitism: The critical error where the Church conceives of itself purely in terms of its idealized, divine nature, thereby hiding and concealing its actual, historically tarnished concrete reality [27]. 5. Incomplete Identification (Partial Identification): The sociological and psychological phenomenon where modern believers, experiencing various tensions and burdens toward the concrete Church, give only a "partial" or incomplete "yes" to the institutional Church rather than identifying with it unconditionally [28, 29].

ISSUES ADDRESSED: 1. Safeguarding Individual Charism Against Collectivism: Balancing the visible authority of the hierarchy with the freedom and initiative of the individual, ensuring the Church does not slide into an "ecclesiastical totalitarianism" or "religious dictatorship" [9, 30]. 2. Reconciling Ecumenical Salvation with Church Necessity: Explaining how the necessity of the Church as a means of salvation can coexist with the true possibility of salvation for non-Christians and nonbelievers [12, 13]. 3. The Limits and Scope of Church Office: Defining how structured church office relates to nonofficial charisms, asserting that office is deeply dependent on these charisms for its effective and fruitful exercise [31, 32]. 4. Structural Rigidity in a Diaspora Era: Tackling the institutional "ineptitude" and spiritual "bankruptcy" of the larger Church, and proposing that the Church must restructure itself from below through basic communities to remain viable as a minority in a highly secularized world [21, 23, 24].

IMPORTANT QUOTES: * "the Church is for persons, persons are not for the Church." (Page 741 / Passage 17) - Context: Setting down the basic principle to protect the rights, duties, and initiative of the individual believer against ecclesiastical collectivity. * "she is, in her whole concrete, visible and juridically verifiable appearance, a real sign and embodiment of the salvific will of God and of the grace of Christ." (Page 742 / Passage 22) - Context: Explaining the early foundations of Rahner's sacramental ecclesiology where the Church is viewed as the "protosacrament." * "The Church is the salvific society of this final, eschatological stage of salvation history," (Page 747 / Passage 37) - Context: Grounding the permanent, indefectible existence of the Church in the definitive victory of God's self-communication in Christ. * "the word 'Church' should be used without qualification only where Church-distinctive elements are found, not wherever Church-constitutive elements are present." (Page 751 / Passage 54) - Context: Setting terminological limits to prevent conceptual confusion when using the "anonymous Christian" theory. * "The Church of the future, writes Rahner, will be an open Church, ecumenical from its very roots, democratized, and especially declerical-ized." (Page 761 / Passage 86) - Context: Outlining the necessary structural modifications the Roman Catholic Church must undergo to face the modern world.

SUMMARY: The symposium traces the systematic development of Karl Rahner's ecclesiology, demonstrating how his focus shifted from early postwar defenses of individual freedom, ecumenism, and the "Church of sinners" [8, 12, 14] to a conciliar defense of episcopal collegiality and "anonymous Christianity" [16, 18], and finally to a post-conciliar demand for concrete structural change [23, 24]. Facing a secularized "diaspora" world, Rahner argues that the Church must transition from a state-supported "Volkskirche" to an open, democratized, and declericalized community built from below by spontaneous "basic Christian communities" (Basisgemeinden) [21, 23, 24]. Ultimately, the contributors show that Rahner's speculative, transcendental theology served as an essential vehicle for moving Catholic thought from rigid Neo-Scholasticism into active, situational engagement with the modern world [33, 34].

2. Basic communities.pdf

TITLE: Basic Ecclesial Communities: A Meeting Point of Ecclesiologies. By Marcello de C. Azevedo, S.J. (Gregorian University, Rome, and Centro João XXIII, Rio de Janeiro). Published in Theological Studies, Vol. 46, 1985, pages 601–620 [35, 36].

MAIN SUBJECT: An analysis of Latin American Basic Ecclesial Communities (BECs), using Brazil as a primary case study, to show how these communities represent a concrete "way of being Church" that can be read, interpreted, and enriched by several major Western/Northern ecclesiologies [37-39].

KEY TOPICS Covered: * The defining sociological and theological characteristics of BECs in Brazil [37, 40]. * The dimensions of communion and participation as a contrast to Western individualism [40]. * The double meaning of being "at the base" of both the Church and society [41]. * The relationship of BECs to Avery Dulles’s five models of the Church (Institution, Sacrament, Herald, Servant, Communion) [42, 43]. * The chronic shortage of priests and the rise of lay ministers [44, 45]. * The non-naive, relational reading of Scripture in light of daily life (Carlos Mesters) [46]. * The "soteriological component" of BECs and the three levels of salvation/liberation [47, 48].

CONCEPTS EXPLAINED: 1. Basic Ecclesial Communities (BECs / CEBs): Small, flexible grassroots groups (typically gathering 20 to 50 people) that seek to live a pattern of Christian life marked by deep interpersonal communion, shared faith, and active social/political participation [37, 40, 49]. 2. The Base (de base): A term with a double meaning. Ecclesiastically, it refers to the active lay people situated at the bottom of the clerical hierarchy [41]. Sociologically, in developing nations like Brazil, it refers to the structurally poor and marginalized who feel a stronger need for mutual support and societal transformation [41, 49]. 3. Sacrament of Christ's Kenosis: The visible sign of Christ's self-emptying (Philippians 2) lived out by the poor and lay members of the BECs, which serves as a powerful means of grace and renewal for the institutional Church and its pastors [50]. 4. Desobriga: A traditional Brazilian pastoral paradigm of "sacramentalization" where an overworked, scarce priest would travel to rural areas to rapidly "discharge obligations" (baptisms, marriages, confessions) in a brief period, leaving the faithful with a passive, individualized understanding of faith [51, 52]. 5. Praxis: A concrete form of historical commitment and daily involvement in making history, stemming from conscious choices of faith to live out the demands of justice, service, and liberation in time [53, 54].

ISSUES ADDRESSED: 1. The Scarcity of Ordained Priests: Managing the daily life of communities in the chronic absence of priests, which has forced a decentralization of church ministries to the laity without breaking communion with the parish or diocese [44]. 2. The Structural Eucharist Paradox: The critical problem where active, highly cohesive, word-centered BECs are intensely aware of the central structural role of the Eucharist but find it impossible to celebrate it regularly because of strict clerical celibacy and holy orders regulations [12, 55]. 3. Subjectivistic and Ideological Bible Readings: Preventing lay-led Scripture circles from falling into naive, selective, or highly subjective interpretations that strip the biblical text of its historical and material reality [46]. 4. Combatting Individualistic Western Culture: Offering a collective, sharing-centered "gift-economy" of salvation to counter the highly competitive, self-interested, and privatized approach of modern Western culture [40, 41].

IMPORTANT QUOTES: * "the BECs are not simply a movement or association in the Church but rather a way of being Church." (Page 604 / Passage 103) - Context: Establishing the foundational theological premise of Latin American BEC ecclesiology. * "Faith is not locked in the mind and even less within the private, individual horizon. Faith is a dynamic factor of personal conversion and societal transformation." (Page 603 / Passage 100) - Context: Describing how BEC members at the sociological base link gospel demands to daily life. * "The ordained minister takes his place once again within a community growing increasingly aware of its diverse vocations and functions" (Page 609 / Passage 118) - Context: Describing how lay ministerial expansion repositions the priest within a collaborative church model. * "In the living Church embodied by BECs we see, first and foremost, a keen awareness of the structural significance of the Eucharist... but also of the actual impossibility of their having the Eucharist with its full meaning and reality." (Page 610 / Passage 121) - Context: Highlighting the major sacramental crisis confronting multiplying, priestless grassroots communities. * "The little patch of the People of God that is living in each BEC, an 'initial cell' as Medellin puts it, is a sign and sacrament of the People of God" (Page 618 / Passage 148) - Context: Demonstrating how the local "Church of the poor" serves as a microcosm of the universal Church envisioned by Vatican II.

SUMMARY: Azevedo argues that Basic Ecclesial Communities (BECs) in Brazil represent an authentic and transformative "way of being Church" that transcends a mere parish association [38]. By testing BECs against Avery Dulles’s five models of the Church, he demonstrates that these communities enrich and embody the institutional, sacramental, kerygmatic, diaconal, and communitarian dimensions of Catholic ecclesiology at the grassroots level [43, 50, 56-58]. They systematically dismantle the passive, clericalized "sacramentalization" of the old desobriga model by promoting shared lay leadership, prophetic solidarity with the poor, and a communal reading of Scripture in light of real-life struggles [45, 51, 59]. Azevedo concludes that BECs offer a vital, liberating model of "Christian praxis" that can renew global theology by showing how a structurally poor community can live as a true sacrament of the People of God [54, 60, 61].

TITLE: The Church: Its Role In God's Plan Of Salvation. By Fr. Dr. P. N. Wachege (Senior Lecturer, Department of Religious Studies, University of Nairobi, Kenya) [62]. Published in African Ecclesial Review (AFER), Vol. 39, No. 1, February 1997, pages 28–50 [63, 64].

KEY TOPICS Covered: * The Church as the Sacrament of Salvation (Kung, Schillebeeckx, de Lubac, Dulles) [62, 64]. * Small Christian Communities (SCCs) as the basic pastoral priority in Eastern Africa (AMECEA) [65, 67]. * The model of the Church as the "Family of God" endorsed by the 1994 African Synod [65, 66, 68]. * The prominent, salvific position of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Catholic tradition [69]. * The historical and dogmatic evaluation of the exclusive axiom "Outside the Church, No Salvation" (Extra Ecclesiam Nulla Salus) [70, 71]. * The debate surrounding Karl Rahner’s "Anonymous Christianity" and its critics (Küng, Boublik) [72, 73]. * Jacques Dupuis's four progressive historical stages of Church attitudes toward other religions [74, 75]. * The objectives and theological instructions of the 1994 African Synod [67, 76].

CONCEPTS EXPLAINED: 1. Family of God: The central ecclesiological model proposed by the 1994 African Synod, emphasizing solidarity, communal care, warm interpersonal relationships, and an understanding of salvation as a shared, collective journey rather than an individualistic concern [65, 66, 68, 77]. 2. Extra Ecclesiam Nulla Salus: The traditional, exclusive theological axiom ("Outside the Church, No Salvation") championed by St. Cyprian and Fulgentius which historically condemned all those outside the visible Catholic fold to "eternal fire" [70, 78]. 3. Anonymous Christianity: Karl Rahner's pastoral theory asserting that because God's salvific will is universal, individuals who respond to God's grace in their conscience are saved in Christ "anonymously" without needing explicit Christian symbols, although explicit Christianity remains the most direct path of revelation [176–178, 181]. 4. Anonymous Catechumenate: A concept proposed by theologian V. Boublik as an alternative to Rahner's theory, describing the lifelong desire of adherents of other religions to encounter the Savior, which critics find less presumptuous [73]. 5. Synodos: A Greek-derived word meaning "journeying together" (from syn and hodos), used to challenge the African Church to walk collaboratively toward redemption as a family [67, 79].

ISSUES ADDRESSED: 1. The Ruthlessness of Exclusive Dogmas: Overcoming the historical harm caused by exclusive dogmas like Extra Ecclesiam Nulla Salus to foster healthy ecumenical and interreligious dialogue [70, 74]. 2. The Presumption of "Anonymous" Labeling: Addressing Hans Küng's sharp critique that labeling a sincere Muslim, Jew, or atheist an "anonymous Christian" is a presumptuous, imperialistic "theological sleight of hand" that shuts down genuine interreligious dialogue [183–185]. 3. The Historical Condemnation of African Culture: Overcoming the colonial legacy where missionaries condemned African religions, cultures, and ancestral philosophies as "savage" or "primitive" without critically examining their positive salvific elements [80, 81]. 4. The Pitfall of Family Paternalism: Preventing the "Family of God" model from devolving into excessive paternalism or maternalism, which can cause members to remain spiritually immature, irresponsible, and overly dependent on the collective [82].

IMPORTANT QUOTES: * "The Church is the community of those who have committed themselves to the Person and cause of Jesus Christ and who bear witness to it as hope for all men and women." (Page 28 / Passage 159) - Context: Citing Hans Küng's definition of the Church. * "Within this Family framework, therefore, one may not just talk of 'my Saviour', 'my salvation', 'I-myself-am saved'. Instead, one should talk of 'our Saviour', 'our Salvation', 'we-ourselves-are saved'." (Page 30 / Passage 165) - Context: Urging a transition from individualistic Western views of salvation to a communal, family-centered African theology. * "The axiom, 'Outside the Church, No Salvation' no longer applies. Christianity and other religions have salvific elements which... do convey Salvation." (Page 39 / Passage 189) - Context: Explaining the drastic shift in Catholic dogmatic theology toward general revelation. * "To bring the partner to the discussion into our own circle in this way closes the dialogue before it has even begun." (Page 38 / Passage 185) - Context: Quoting Hans Küng's objection to Karl Rahner's "Anonymous Christian" terminology as patronizing to non-Christians. * "Our communion in the Church, our walking together, is not our initiative or our doing. We are people called together by our Father" (Page 45-46 / Passage 203) - Context: Quoting Cecil McGarry on the synodal, Trinitarian roots of the Church's nature.

SUMMARY: Wachege analyzes the Church’s essential role as the primary agent of salvation in a world characterized by changing generations and religious pluralism [63, 65]. He outlines a massive theological shift within Catholicism from the exclusive, historical condemnation of non-Catholics under the Extra Ecclesiam Nulla Salus axiom to a highly optimistic, positive attitude toward other religions [70, 75]. While presenting Karl Rahner’s "Anonymous Christianity" as an important, comfort-giving pastoral theory, he highlights Hans Küng's strong warnings against its potential theological imperialism [72, 83, 84]. Grounding his vision in the 1994 African Synod, Wachege champions the "Family of God" model and Small Christian Communities (SCCs) as the most effective, culturally authentic vehicles for African inculturation, evangelization, and liberating dialogue [65, 67, 68].

TITLE: The Church's Religious Identity and Its Social and Political Mission. By Francis Schüssler Fiorenza (The Catholic University of America). Published in Theological Studies, Vol. 43, 1982, pages 197–225 [85, 86].

MAIN SUBJECT: An exploration of how the Church’s political and social mission relates to its unique religious identity, proposing a hermeneutical, Christological, and historical framework to show that a commitment to social justice is constitutive of—rather than accidental to—Gospel proclamation [85-87].

KEY TOPICS Covered: * Critical analysis of four traditional models of social mission: Improper, Substitutive, Unofficial, and Partial [88-91]. * Hermeneutical evaluation of post-Vatican II magisterial statements (e.g., Justice in the World, Evangelii Nuntiandi, and John Paul II's encyclicals) [92-95]. * Methodological critique of defining the Church’s mission through "specific difference" [96-98]. * Wittgenstein’s "family resemblance" (game analogy) and the phenomenological category of "appresentation" applied to religious acts [99-101]. * The historical connection between the belief in a transcendent God and the emergence of human personhood [102, 103]. * Wisdom Christology (Sophia / Logos) as the theological bridge between creation and redemption [301–303]. * The historical intertwinement of the Church’s diaconal care for the poor and secular political structures (Constantine, Middle Ages, and the industrial revolution) [104-106].

CONCEPTS EXPLAINED: 1. Specific Difference: A traditional logical method of defining a reality's essence by isolating its unique, distinct traits from everything else, which Fiorenza argues leads to a distorted, dualistic separation of the religious from the ethical, social, and political [97, 98]. 2. Family Resemblance: Ludwig Wittgenstein's linguistic concept showing that complex realities (like games or religion) cannot be reduced to a single common denominator, but are instead defined by a complicated, overlapping network of similarities and crisscrossings [99, 100]. 3. Appresentation: A phenomenological concept (adapted from Husserl) describing how the full, unseen meaning of an action (such as its religious dimension) is indirectly but concordantly grasped as being "co-present" with the visible, physical action itself [101, 107, 108]. 4. Wisdom Christology: A post-biblical trajectory that identifies Jesus with the divine order, power, and wisdom through which the universe was created, thereby bridging the theology of creation with the theology of redemption and justifying a concrete social ministry [301–303]. 5. Constitutive Dimension: The theological assertion (proclaimed by the 1971 Synod of Bishops) that action on behalf of justice and world transformation is an integral, non-accidental part of preaching the Gospel [93, 109].

ISSUES ADDRESSED: 1. The Threat of Secularization and Loss of Identity: Addressing critics who claim that focus on social/political advocacy causes churches to lose their religious message and turn into mere secular lobbying or social welfare groups [85, 110, 111]. 2. The Inadequacy of the "Substitutive" Model: Countering the view that the Church should run schools or hospitals only as temporary substitutes until secular state agencies can take them over, which splits the religious from the secular [112-114]. 3. The Split Between "Official" and "Lay" Missions: Rejecting Karl Rahner’s model that restricts the official hierarchy strictly to religious duties while relegating the social mission entirely to "unofficial" lay action [115, 116]. 4. The Tension Between "Conversion of Heart" and "Systemic Change": Comparing Pope Paul VI's structural emphasis on combatting political systems of injustice with Pope John Paul II's personalist emphasis on the conversion of individual conscience within state-communist or Latin American contexts [117].

IMPORTANT QUOTES: * "Action on behalf of justice and participation in the transformation of the world appear to us as a constitutive dimension of the preaching of the gospel..." (Page 205 / Passage 256) - Context: Quoting the ground-breaking statement from the 1971 Synod document Justice in the World. * "a church that is nothing more than a benevolent socially useful group can be replaced by other groups not claiming to be churches: such a church has no justification for its existence." (Page 210 / Passage 274) - Context: Citing Paul Tillich's warning on the necessity of maintaining a distinctive religious identity. * "the religious is distorted... if it is defined precisely in its specific difference from the ethical, social, or political... As human nature is not a pure but an incarnate rationality, so religiosity manifests itself within the ethical, social, and political." (Page 211-212 / Passage 280) - Context: Critiquing the theological dualism that separates religion from life. * "The more the social or political ministry of the Church is related to Christianity's interpretative function as a religion to exhibit and to proclaim Jesus as the Power and Wisdom of the universe, the more constitutive, essential, and distinctive this ministry is." (Page 219 / Passage 308) - Context: Formulating the article's core "rule of praxis" for integrating social ministry with religious identity. * "Its obligation to speak out on social and political issues does not stem from a 'better knowledge' of economic problems... but from its option for those in misfortune." (Page 224 / Passage 326) - Context: Clarifying that the Church's political authority is grounded in solidarity with the marginalized rather than technical expertise.

SUMMARY: Fiorenza addresses the critical theological challenge of how the Church can engage in robust social and political advocacy on behalf of justice without losing its distinctive, supernatural religious identity [85, 86]. Rejecting dualistic models that isolate the "proper" religious sphere from the "improper" political sphere, he uses Wittgenstein's "family resemblance" and Husserl's "appresentation" to argue that the religious dimension naturally crisscrosses and manifests itself within social realities [97-99, 101]. Grounded in a Wisdom Christology that links creation with redemption, and drawing upon a long historical tradition of episcopal oversight of social legislation, Fiorenza proposes a core guideline: the Church’s social and political ministries are intrinsically proper and constitutive to its mission to the exact degree that they are integrated with its central proclamation of Jesus as the Power and Wisdom of the universe [87, 105, 118, 119].

TITLE: Church as Structure and Communitas: Victor Turner and Ecclesiology. By Carl F. Starkloff, S.J. (Professor of Theology, Regis College, Toronto School of Theology) [120]. Published in Theological Studies, Vol. 58, 1997, pages 643–668 [121, 122].

MAIN SUBJECT: The application of anthropologist Victor Turner’s concepts of "structure" and "communitas" to Christian ecclesiology, examining how the dynamic tension between stable institutional order and marginalized, liminal religious experiences can foster ecclesial reform, inculturation, and a deeper communion (koinonia) [121, 123, 124].

KEY TOPICS Covered: * The dialogue between the social sciences and theology (Möhler, Dulles, Boff, Geertz) [336–338, 340, 342]. * Victor Turner's ethnographic fieldwork on Ndembu rituals (rites of passage, circumcision/Mukanda, and women's fertility/Isoma and Wubwang'a) [125-127]. * The fundamental categories of Structure, Communitas, Anti-Structure, and Liminality [355–360]. * The tripartite division of Communitas: Spontaneous (existential), Normative, and Ideological [128, 129]. * Historical applications to religious orders, specifically the Franciscan movement [370–372]. * The anthropological and spiritual analysis of pilgrimages (Our Lady of Guadalupe, Lough Derg) [130-132]. * Contemporary liminal groups: New Tribal Religious Movements, Basic Ecclesial Communities, and "Women-Church" [133]. * Jean-Marie Tillard’s "Ecclesiology of Communion" and a "Church of Churches" [134].

CONCEPTS EXPLAINED: 1. Structure: The patterned arrangements of roles, status sequences, consciously recognized status sets, and legal-practical norms regularly operative in a given society, representing stability and social order [135]. 2. Communitas: A relational quality of spontaneous, full, and unmediated communication (or communion) between definite and determinate identities, serving as the source (fons et origo) and critical corrector of all social structures [136]. 3. Liminality: The middle, transition state in a "rite of passage" characterized by secular powerlessness and sacred power, representing a realm of pure possibility, primitive hypothesis, and symbolic creativity [137, 138]. 4. Liminoid: A voluntary, individual form of liminality occurring in historical or salvation religions (such as pilgrimages) where individuals seek release from the sins of the structural world, as opposed to mandatory, group-focused tribal rites of passage [130]. 5. Flow: A state of total involvement (borrowed from Csikszentmihalyi) where participants lose their focus on the ego, lose track of time, and experience a deep sense of wholeness and unmediated communion [139].

ISSUES ADDRESSED: 1. The Risk of the Church Freezing into Static Structures: Preventing institutional rigidification and spiritual "ossification" by remaining open to dynamic, creative corrections from the margins [122, 140]. 2. The Historical Tension Between Charismatic Origins and Institutional Organization: Analyzing how the spontaneous, radical poverty of St. Francis of Assisi's early circle was forced to transition into a "normative communitas" under Brother Elias to survive historically [141, 142]. 3. The Problem of "Theological Messiness" in Inculturation: Managing the tension when marginalized tribal or feminist groups incorporate native or non-traditional symbols into Christian worship, which mainstream structures often label as "syncretism" or "heterodoxy" [143-145]. 4. The Loss of Meaningful Rites of Passage in Modern, Secular Society: Addressing how modern churches struggle to practice effective, spiritually transforming life-crisis and initiation rituals because of a fragmented sense of community [146, 147].

IMPORTANT QUOTES: * "society is always a dynamic process, consisting of two mutually interdependent and interactive poles that he came to call 'structure' and 'communitas.'" (Page 645 / Passage 342) - Context: Outlining Victor Turner's central anthropological insight. * "Liminality may perhaps be regarded as the way to all positive structural assertions, but as in some sense the source of them all, and more than that, as a realm of pure possibility..." (Page 652 / Passage 366) - Context: Quoting Turner on the creative necessity of the liminal transition state. * "Structureless communitas can bind and bond people together only momentarily." (Page 654 / Passage 373) - Context: Highlighting the inevitable historical necessity for organization and structure. * "The ever-pressing question to be put to Christians, especially Catholics with their highly structured system, would be: What does the Spirit wish to achieve through this tensive unity between communitas and structure?" (Page 658 / Passage 387) - Context: Framing the core theological question of the essay. * "As communitas goes, so goes the Church." (Page 657 / Passage 383) - Context: Rephrasing the traditional Catholic maxim "As Mary goes, so goes the Church" to emphasize the vital role of the margins.

SUMMARY: Starkloff argues that Victor Turner’s anthropological concepts of structure, communitas, and liminality provide an invaluable interpretive lens for contemporary ecclesiology, particularly in balancing institutional continuity with dynamic, creative change [121, 123, 124]. Exploring the history of the Franciscan movement, the phenomenon of pilgrimages, and modern marginalized movements (such as African Independent Churches, Latin American basic communities, and Women-Church), he demonstrates that a healthy Church must exist as a constant, tensive dialectic between structure and communitas [130, 133, 141, 148]. While structure provides the necessary historical organization to prevent sectarian dissolution, spontaneous liminal experiences on the margins serve as the vital source of spiritual renewal, liturgical creativity, and authentic inculturation [149, 150]. Starkloff concludes that by embracing these "processual dynamics," the Church can realize Jean-Marie Tillard’s vision of a "Church of churches" and deepen its overall koinonia [134, 151].

TITLE: "Journet, Congar, and the Roots of Communion Ecclesiology." By Dennis M. Doyle (Ph.D., Catholic University of America; Associate Professor at the University of Dayton). Published in Theological Studies, Vol. 58, 1997, pages 461–479.

MAIN SUBJECT: A comparative analysis of two preconciliar theologians, Charles Journet and Yves Congar, tracing how their respective metaphysical/mystical and historical/ecumenical approaches formed the foundational roots of modern "communion ecclesiology" at the Second Vatican Council.

KEY TOPICS: * The definition of communion ecclesiology as a relationship-centered approach to the Church. * The historical significance of Johann Adam Möhler’s seminal 1825 work Unity in the Church. * Charles Journet's three-volume systematic treatise L'Église du Verbe incarné (1941–1969). * The application of Aristotelian causality (formal, material, efficient, final causes) to ecclesiology. * The structural distinction and unity between the "juridical Church" and the "Church of charity." * Yves Congar's ecumenical and historical starting point in Chrétiens désunis (1939). * Congar’s theological exploration of lay participation, charisms, and structural reform. * The dogmatic dispute concerning the "sinlessness" vs. the "purification" of the Church. * The distinct pneumatological contributions of both theologians to the "formal cause" of the Church.

CONCEPTS EXPLAINED: 1. Communion Ecclesiology: A theological approach that begins with the concept of "communion" (koinonia) among God and human beings, applying this analogously to sacraments, ministry, ecumenism, and the relationship between the Church and the world (Page 461). 2. Aristotelian Causality of the Church: A systematic framework used by Journet and preconciliar manuals to describe the Church's dimensions: its formal cause (Holy Spirit/hierarchy), material cause (laity), remote efficient cause (Trinity), immediate efficient cause (Christ), and final cause (beatific vision) (Page 465–466). 3. The Church of Charity: A concept distinguishing the spiritual community of grace and love from the legal, outer administration, asserting that while both form one interlocked reality, the juridical structures are strictly subordinated to the service of charity (Page 466–467). 4. Creeping Infallibility: A warning conceptualized by Congar regarding the growing preconciliar tendency to treat the ordinary, day-to-day teaching of the hierarchy as absolute and unchangeable, thereby suppressing authentic dialogue and historical development (Page 472). 5. Quasi-Formal Cause: Congar's definition of the Holy Spirit's role in the Church, where the Spirit acts as an internal, dynamic principle that indwells and shapes the Church without composing its essence in a way that ignores human agency or historical limits (Page 473).

ISSUES ADDRESSED: 1. The Overcoming of Preconciliar Juridicism: Overthrowing dry, mechanical manualist apologists who presented the Church solely as an unequal, hierarchically organized juridical society (Page 464–465). 2. Balancing Transcendent Ideals with Concrete History: Bridging the tension between an abstract, "sinless" ideal of the Church's inner mystery and the messy, historically conditioned realities of its daily operations (Page 462). 3. The Debate on the Church's Sinfulness: Resolving whether the Church as such can be said to sin (Journet’s view that only its members sin, leaving the Church's essence untouched, vs. Congar's view that the Church is in constant need of historical purification and repentance) (Page 477–478). 4. Clerical Hierarchy vs. Active Lay Agency: Confronting the passive status of laypeople in traditional manuals, resulting in Congar's retrieval of the priesthood of all believers and the structural necessity of lay-led ministries (Page 471–472).

IMPORTANT QUOTES: * "Congar's emphasis on historical development is complemented by Journet's focus on the mystical and essential." (Page 461 / Editor's Note) - Context: Setting up the comparative framework of the two theological tracks. * "In him [Möhler] I found a source, the source, which I needed." (Page 463 / Footnote 9, quoting Congar) - Context: Describing the profound ecumenical and historical influence of Johann Adam Möhler's early romantic ecclesiology on Congar's career. * "The formal cause of the Church is the Holy Spirit. To the hierarchy he assigned the role of immediate efficient cause." (Page 466) - Context: Outlining how Journet modified Neo-Scholastic Aristotelian categories to center the Church on the Spirit. * "The hierarchy, for Journet, is fundamentally a service to help promote the mystical communion." (Page 467) - Context: Explaining that Journet sought to subordinate legal power to the theological life of grace. * "Present structural arrangements were not to be taken as absolutes." (Page 472) - Context: Describing Congar's radical insistence on the historical conditioning and mutability of church offices. * "The Mystical Body is realized once our life belongs to Christ." (Page 474, quoting Congar) - Context: Illustrating how Congar connected systematic ecclesiology directly with concrete, lived spirituality.

SUMMARY: Dennis M. Doyle compares the preconciliar ecclesiologies of Charles Journet and Yves Congar to prove that the "communion ecclesiology" of Vatican II emerged from two distinct but complementary lines of reform. Journet worked within a speculative, Neo-Scholastic Thomistic framework, using the philosophy of causality to redefine the formal cause of the Church as the Holy Spirit, thereby shifting theological focus from rigid juridical manualism to an interior, mystical communion. Congar, by contrast, pursued a historically conscious, ecumenical methodology, integrating a dynamic Pneumatology that viewed the Church as an unfinished historical pilgrim in need of structural reform, lay activation, and purification. Doyle concludes that while Journet provided the necessary metaphysical defense of the Church's transcendent holiness, Congar provided the historical realism needed to engage the modern world, making both thinkers essential for a holistic, non-reductive Catholic spirituality.
