Unit 6 — Models of the Church: Avery Dulles

Why Models? Why More Than One?

For Dulles, the Church is a mystery: no single concept can fully capture it. Theologians must therefore work with multiple, complementary models simultaneously — "a kind of mental juggling act... no supermodel does full justice to all aspects of the Church." Dulles proposes three criteria any model must satisfy: (1) basis in Scripture, (2) basis in Christian tradition, and (3) the capacity to give members a genuine sense of corporate identity and mission.

The Five Models

Institution — the Church as visible structure and juridical authority of offices (Bellarmine's societas perfecta, "perfect society"). Strength: strong recent magisterial endorsement and a strong sense of corporate identity. Weakness: weak scriptural and patristic basis; prone to exactly the clericalism, juridicism, and triumphalism named in Unit 5; an obstacle to ecumenism.

Mystical Communion — the Church as interior, Spirit-given koinonia (Pauline Body of Christ, People of God). Strength: strong biblical foundation; ecumenically fruitful. Weakness: can leave unclear why anyone must remain loyal to visible, institutional structures at all.

Sacrament — the Church as a visible sign that truly embodies and transmits the invisible grace it signifies (cf. LG 1). Strength: synthesizes institution and communion, securing loyalty while remaining open to reform ("the Church is continually called to become a better sign of Christ than it has been"). Weakness: can appear complacent, insufficiently prophetic against structural sin.

Herald — the Church as kerygmatic community gathered by the proclaimed Word (the OT prophetic tradition; Barth and Bultmann's dialectical theology). Strength: strong biblical foundation, a clear missionary identity, a rich theology of the Word as living address. Weakness: weak on the incarnational and sacramental dimensions; can reduce to bare verbal proclamation.

Servant — the Church as diaconal community modelled on the Suffering Servant, working for justice and healing in solidarity with the world. Strength: deeply relevant to contemporary struggles, bridging Church and world. Weakness: risks secularizing into a mere social agency, losing its supernatural, Christocentric core.

The Integrating Model: Community of Disciples

In a later essay, Dulles proposed "community of disciples" as a way to harmonize the other five: the Church as a visible, structured fellowship of intentional followers gathered around Jesus as Lord and Teacher, under the Spirit's ongoing guidance. Strength: broadly inclusive, building bridges to all five other models and preventing "communion" from collapsing into mere mutual gratification. Weakness: it too is only one more perspective, not a supermodel exhausting the Church's mystery.

Illustration

Dulles's models work like different camera lenses on the same landscape: a wide-angle lens (institution) shows the boundaries and paths clearly but flattens the depth; a macro lens (communion) shows the intimate texture but loses the wider shape. No single photograph does justice to the whole terrain; a competent theologian needs the whole camera bag.

Indian Context

In the Indian pastoral situation — a small, often vulnerable minority alongside vast religious plurality — the servant and herald models often carry special weight (the Church as a visible sign of justice for Dalits and Adivasis, and as witness amid religious pluralism), while the institutional model's triumphalist overtones sit especially awkwardly in a minority context.

Unit 7 — Ecumenical Councils, Conciliarism, and the Convocation of Vatican II

The Theology of a Council

An ecumenical council gathers the world's bishops, in union with the pope, exercising the Church's highest teaching and legislative authority — grounded theologically in the college of bishops as successors of the apostolic college gathered around Peter (cf. Acts 15, the "Council of Jerusalem," as prototype). Both Küng and Rahner stressed, from different angles, that a council is not a mere administrative assembly but a privileged event of the whole Church's self-reflection under the Spirit. The Catholic Church recognizes twenty-one ecumenical councils, from Nicaea I (325) to Vatican II (1962-65).

Conciliarism and Its Condemnation

Conciliarism, prominent in the fifteenth century, held that supreme authority in the Church resides in an ecumenical council rather than in the pope alone. The Council of Constance's decree Haec Sancta (1415) asserted a general council's authority even over the pope in matters of faith, schism, and reform; Frequens (1417) mandated regular future councils. Conciliarism developed partly in response to the Western Schism (1378-1417), when rival papal claimants divided Latin Christendom. It was effectively repudiated at Vatican I, which located supreme, ordinary, immediate jurisdiction in the pope, independent of the college's consent.

Vatican II's Convocation

Announced unexpectedly by John XXIII in 1959 and guided through its four sessions (1962-65) first by him and, after his death in 1963, by Paul VI, Vatican II was animated by aggiornamento — "bringing up to date": not doctrinal change but a fresh, pastoral re-presentation of the faith to the modern world. It was genuinely a "world Church" council in ways earlier councils were not: bishops attended from every continent, not overwhelmingly from Europe as at Vatican I; non-Catholic observers were formally invited; and lay auditors, including women for the first time, participated in the sessions.

Illustration

Vatican I met like a household drawing up a single, urgent legal document under threat from outside (the loss of the Papal States); Vatican II met more like an extended family reunion taking stock of who it now is across the whole world — less a legal act, more a communal self-examination.

Claims

  • Conciliarism located supreme authority in the council; Vatican I decisively rejected this in favour of ordinary papal jurisdiction
  • Vatican II was the first genuinely world Church council in its composition and outlook

Unit 8 — Reception of Vatican II: Paradigm Shifts and Critiques

The Nine Paradigm Shifts

Vatican II re-categorized the Church's self-understanding across nine axes, each a move from a pre-conciliar to a post-conciliar category: (1) Institutional Church → Mystery dimension (LG 1-8). (2) Hierarchy (a pyramid of pope-cardinals-bishops-priests-deacons-passive flock) → People of God (LG 9-17), a baptismal, pilgrim people. (3) Papal Monarchy → Episcopal Collegiality (LG 18-24), a synodal, collaborative exercise of authority. (4) Universal/Roman Church dominating local jurisdictions → Local Church/World Church (Rahner's "communion of local churches"). (5) Roman Catholicism, exclusively identified with Christ's Church → Christian Church (Unitatis Redintegratio's subsistit in, real if imperfect presence in other communities). (6) Christianity as the one true religion, holding an exclusive monopoly on truth → Many religions (Nostra Aetate: "rays of that Truth which enlightens all"). (7) Church-centred/teaching Church (ecclesia docens) → Listening/learning Church (ecclesia discens), engaging the human and empirical sciences and lived experience. (8) Static, "perfect society" isolated from history → Dynamic, evolving pilgrim Church, embedded in history. (9) Church-centred mission (recruiting members; salvation confined to the Roman Catholic Church) → Kingdom-centred mission (the Church as visible, provisional sacrament of the Kingdom of God).

Reception Critiques

"Sedevacantism" — the fringe position that the papal see has been effectively vacant since Vatican II, judging the Council a rupture with tradition — and the Coetus Internationalis Patrum, a minority bloc of conservative council fathers who resisted many reforms from within, are the precursors of later traditionalist resistance (e.g. Archbishop Lefebvre's Society of St Pius X).

From the opposite direction, Hans Küng and Peter Phan argue the Council's own paradigm shifts have been only partially and unevenly implemented in practice — a "restorationist" tendency in the decades since has pulled some dials back toward pre-conciliar categories, especially regarding the real authority of episcopal conferences, and on questions the Council itself left officially unresolved: the precise scope of infallibility, mandatory priestly celibacy, and the ordination of women (flagged by the 1976 CDF declaration Inter Insigniores and reaffirmed by John Paul II's 1994 Ordinatio Sacerdotalis).

Illustration

The nine shifts can be pictured as nine dial settings on a control panel, each moved from one position to another at the Council — but a dial that has been turned does not stay turned by itself. Sedevacantists want to turn all nine back; critics like Küng and Phan argue that, in practice, several dials have quietly drifted back toward their old settings even though official teaching says they were moved.

Unit 9 — Lumen Gentium I: Mystery, Sacrament, People of God

Lumen Gentium as Magna Charta

The Dogmatic Constitution on the Church (promulgated 21 November 1964) is rightly called Vatican II's "Magna Charta": nearly every other conciliar document presupposes its ecclesiology.

Church as Mystery

LG 1-8 traces the Church's origin through the Trinity itself: theocentric (the Father's eternal plan, LG 2), Christocentric (the Church instituted through Christ's mission and paschal mystery, LG 3), pneumatological (sanctified and guided by the Spirit poured out at Pentecost, LG 4). The Church is thus not first a human organization that later acquired a religious purpose, but a mystery rooted in the Trinity's own inner life, unfolding in history.

Church as Sacrament

LG 1 describes the Church as "sign and instrument both of a very closely knit union with God and of the unity of the whole human race." The Church does not merely point beyond itself to salvation (a bare sign); it actively mediates it (an instrument) — while remaining subordinate to, and provisional in relation to, the Kingdom of God it serves and anticipates but does not exhaust.

Church as People of God

The Council deliberately placed this chapter (LG, ch. 2, esp. 9-17) before the chapter on the hierarchy (ch. 3) — a structural decision asserting that all the baptized share a common, prior dignity and equal call to holiness before any distinction of office is introduced. The People of God is a pilgrim people journeying through history toward the eschaton, always reformable (ecclesia semper reformanda), and marked by equal discipleship by baptism.

LG 14-16 describes three concentric circles of belonging. LG 14: the Catholic faithful, fully incorporated through the threefold bond of professed faith, sacraments, and communion with the pope and bishops. LG 15: other baptized Christians, joined to the Church though not entirely, in an "imperfect communion," yet possessing real elements of sanctification and truth. LG 16: non-Christians related to the People of God in different ways — Jews as the people of the first Covenant, Muslims who profess the faith of Abraham, and others who without their own fault do not know the Gospel yet sincerely seek God, including atheists of upright life.

Illustration

LG's decision to place "People of God" (ch. 2) before "Hierarchy" (ch. 3) is itself a small illustration of a large claim — as if a family portrait were re-taken so that every family member appears in the same photograph before the parents are pictured separately giving instructions. Everyone belongs to the family first; distinctions of role come second.

Indian Context

The three concentric circles matter pastorally in India, where Catholics live daily alongside Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, and other believers who are, per LG 16, "related" to the People of God — a theological basis for respectful relationship rather than simple exclusion.

  • The Church, for LG, is sacrament, not simply the Kingdom of God itself

CHAPTER I — WHAT IS THEOLOGY?

Literature note. "What the authors say." Claims extracted → <em>Theology MOC</em>.

Permanent notes created from this chapter are listed at the foot of the file.

Detailed BTh Class Notes

Course: Introduction to Theology (BTh) Source: An Introduction to Theology, Indian Theological Series — Rev. Fr. Kuncheria Pathil CMI & Rev. Fr. Dominic Veliath SDB

Detailed notes on Chapter I. Exact phrases from the book are given in "quotation marks." Indian and technical terms are explained from scratch in simple English, with examples.

CHAPTER OVERVIEW (The Big Picture)

Chapter I answers one basic question: What is theology?

It moves through a clear logic:

  1. Start with the God-Question — why humans naturally talk about God at all.
  2. Ask how finite humans can even know or speak of an infinite God.
  3. Collect the many definitions of theology across history.
  4. Notice the built-in tensions (polarities) every theologian must balance.
  5. Relate theology to the other sciences.
  6. State the goals theology serves.

Keep this map in mind — every section below is one stop on this journey.

A. THE GOD-QUESTION

1. What "the God-Question" Means

Simple meaning: Before theology can say anything about God, it must face the fact that humans are always asking about God. The human being is, by nature, a questioner who reaches for ultimate meaning.

Exact phrase: - Theology is "the discourse on God or God-talk."

The human as a questioner: Humans do not only ask "What is for dinner?" They also ask: Why do I exist? What happens at death? Is there an ultimate meaning? These are ultimate questions. The presence of these questions in every culture shows the human being is oriented beyond the visible world.

Example: A child at a funeral asks, "Where did grandmother go?" That is not a science question — it is a God-Question. It reaches for what lies beyond the physical.

2. Theism and the Idea of God

What is Theism? Theism = belief in God / an Ultimate Reality.

The book notes God is conceived differently across religions and philosophies: - Personal God (Christianity, Judaism, Islam): God is a personal being, "the origin and destiny of the universe and of humankind." - Impersonal Absolute (some systems): God as "an Absolute Power, a Supreme Mind or Will or Spirit, a Pure Act (Actus purus), the Divine, the Sacred, a Higher Power."

Despite differences, God is understood as: - "the Ultimate Reality," - "the Ultimate Ground of Being," - "the Ultimate Horizon of Meaning."

Key insight (quoted): Even if old terms for God must change, "an ultimate point of reference for grasping and interpreting human life and the world will always be needed" (Gordon D. Kaufman).

3. Can We Know God by Reason?

The book's position: Yes — in principle, reason can reach God.

Church teaching (Vatican I, Dei Filius), quoted: - "God, the first principle and last end of all things, can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason."

Thomas Aquinas's Five Proofs: - These are cosmological arguments — meaning arguments that move from the world (cosmos) back to its cause. - Logic: from effects we trace back to the cause, arriving finally at the "Ultimate Cause and the Prime Mover." - Prime Mover = the first source of all motion/change; the one that moves everything else but is not itself moved.

Honest limitation (Cardinal Newman), quoted: - These proofs are "abstract and philosophical," and can only provide a "convergence of diverse probabilities." - Simple meaning: The proofs help someone who already believes; they rarely force a non-believer to believe. They stack up probabilities pointing toward God rather than delivering a knock-down proof.

Example: Seeing a watch, you infer a watchmaker. That is cosmological reasoning: effect (watch) → cause (maker). Convincing to some, not airtight to all.

4. Why Our God-Language Is Limited: ANALOGICAL Knowledge

This is a crucial concept. Explained from scratch:

Three ways words can apply to God:

Way Meaning Problem
Univocal Same meaning as when applied to creatures Would make God just a bigger creature
Equivocal Totally different meaning Would mean we say nothing real about God
Analogical Similar-but-different meaning The correct middle path

Analogical knowledge (simple meaning): When we call God "good" or "father," the word is neither exactly the same as human goodness/fatherhood (univocal) nor completely unrelated (equivocal). It is analogical — truly pointing to God, but always falling short.

Exact phrases: - "Our human words always fall short of the mystery of God." - We must "continually purify our language" so we never confuse our human pictures with the incomprehensible God.

Example: Calling God "Father" tells you something true (loving source, protector) — but God is not male, not biological, not limited like a human father. The word points; it does not capture.

5. Religious Experience and Symbol

Why symbols? Humans are embodied (we live through bodies and senses), so our experience of God comes through concrete things — words, images, rituals.

Religious experience defined (quoted): - "that intimate and immediate awareness of being touched or grasped by the Divine."

Because this experience is mediated through the body, it is expressed in symbolic language.

What is a symbol (simple)? A symbol is a visible/concrete thing that carries and communicates a deeper invisible reality. Water in Baptism is not just water — it symbolizes cleansing and new life.

Human openness to God (quoted): - Christian theology deals with the human being's "fundamental openness to God."

Example: A believer feels overwhelmed by peace during prayer ("touched by the Divine") and later describes it using symbols — "light," "warmth," "a father's embrace" — because there are no literal words for the infinite.

B. VARIOUS DEFINITIONS OF CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY

Theology has been defined differently in each era. Learn these as a historical series.

1. Etymology (Word-Origin)

From Greek: - Theos = God - Logos = word, discourse, science / reason

Literal meaning (quoted): - "discourse on God," "science of God," "God-talk."

2. Greek and Patristic Era

  • Greek philosophers (Plato, Aristotle): used "theology" for metaphysics (study of ultimate reality) and even to critique the poets' myths.
  • Church Fathers (Clement of Alexandria, Origen): used it for "Trinitarian and Christological discussions" and the "interpretation of the Sacred Scriptures."

Christological = about the person and work of Christ. Trinitarian = about God as Father, Son, Spirit.

3. Medieval / Scholastic Era — Anselm's Classic Definition

The most famous definition of all: - fides quaerens intellectum = "faith seeking understanding." - Anselm's motto: "I believe in order to understand" (credo ut intelligam).

Simple meaning: Faith comes first and drives the search for understanding. You do not understand and then believe; you believe, and belief makes you want to understand.

4. The Eastern Approach — Prayer and Belief Together

Latin dictum (quoted): - Lex orandi, lex credendi = "the law of praying is the law of believing."

Simple meaning: How the Church prays shapes and reveals what the Church believes. Worship and doctrine are inseparable. To know Eastern theology, watch its liturgy.

5. Modern and Contemporary Definitions

a) Theological Anthropology — Karl Rahner - "God and humanity are correlative terms." - Theology studies not God in isolation, but the human being and "the mystery of God's plan for human salvation." - Correlative = they belong together; explain one and you are already explaining the other.

b) Critical Reflection on Praxis — Gustavo Gutierrez - Theology is "a critical reflection on Christian praxis in the light of the Word." - Shifts focus from orthodoxy (right thinking) to orthopraxis (right action) and the transformation of the world. - Praxis = committed, practical action — not just theory.

c) Hermeneutics (Interpretation) - Theology is "the interpretation of Christian faith in the context of contemporary existential realities and the interpretation of contemporary realities in the light of the Word of God." - Hermeneutics = the art/science of interpretation. It is a two-way street: read today's life through the Gospel, and read the Gospel afresh through today's life.

d) Interpretation of the Christian Story (Mythos) - Theology reflects on the Christian "mythos" — the "set of symbols, rituals, narratives and beliefs" through which a community encounters the Divine. - Mythos here does NOT mean "false story." It means the deep foundational story a community lives by.

6. The Book's Own Working Definition (Learn This Well)

The authors synthesize everything into one full definition (quoted):

"Christian theology is a systematic and critical interpretation on the meaning of human life and reality in general from the perspective of the Revelation in Jesus Christ on the one hand, and a reinterpretation of Christian Faith on the other, in the light of the new experience and context of the changing realities of the world, in and by the believing community."

Unpacking this definition (simple):

Part of the definition What it means
"systematic and critical interpretation" Ordered + questioning, not random opinion
"meaning of human life and reality" Theology explains all of life, not just "church topics"
"perspective of the Revelation in Jesus Christ" Christ is the lens
"reinterpretation of Christian Faith" Faith must be re-expressed for each new age
"changing realities of the world" Theology answers today's real situations
"in and by the believing community" It is the Church's work, not a lone individual's

C. CREATIVE POLARITIES IN THEOLOGIZING

A polarity = two opposite pulls that must be held together in tension. Drop either side and theology goes wrong. The book lists seven.

1. Mystery and Intelligibility

  • Between the errors of Fideism and Rationalism.
  • Fideism = faith only, reason has no role.
  • Rationalism = reason only, no room for mystery.
  • Reason understands faith to a limited extent, but "faith alone makes it possible to penetrate the mystery in a way that allows us to understand it coherently."
  • The tension stays because "what we know and speak about is not the whole truth; there is an underlying deeper mystery to which we can only point."

Example: We can explain much about the Trinity, yet never exhaust it. We understand and stand before mystery.

2. Identity and Change

  • Theology's fixed identity rests on the "Christ-event, its confession, proclamation and witness."
  • But since the Church lives in history, its formulas need continuous reform.
  • Result: "Christian theology thus involves a creative tension between continuity and change."

Example: The truth "Jesus is Lord" never changes; how we explain it to a 21st-century Indian differs from a 5th-century Greek.

3. Committed and Critical

  • Committed: "theologizing cannot be done without the living experience and practice of faith."
  • Critical: theology must "seriously examine all Christian beliefs... with a critical mind."
  • A true theologian both loves the tradition and questions it.

Example: A son who loves his father can still respectfully question his father's decisions. That double stance is theology.

4. Community and Individual Theologian

  • The "Christian community is the real locus theologicus" — the true "place of theology" where faith is guarded and handed on.
  • Locus theologicus (Latin) = a "source-place" of theology.
  • Yet "every reform and renewal is initiated by the inspiration and creativity of individuals who have a prophetic call or gift."

Example: The community carries the faith; but a prophet (an Aquinas, a Rahner) sparks renewal from within it.

5. One and Many (Transcendental and Historical)

  • The "Christ-event" grounds a "common... universal Christian theology."
  • Yet "pluralism in Christian theology and Catholic theology is both theoretically and practically accepted."
  • Theology forever moves between "the one and the many, the universal and the particular."

Example: One Gospel; many valid theologies (African, Asian, Latin American) — like one melody sung in many languages.

6. Universal and Contextual

  • "All theologies... are historically, socially and culturally situated."
  • The strong claim: "no theology is, in fact, perennial. All theologies are contextual."
  • This gave rise to Liberation, Feminist, and Dalit theologies.
  • Dalit theology = theology from the perspective of the oppressed "Dalit" communities of India, formerly called "untouchables."

Example: A theology written for wealthy Europe cannot simply be copied for poor, caste-divided India; it must be re-rooted in the Indian context.

7. Orthodoxy and Heterodoxy

  • "Fidelity to the original and authentic Christian faith or orthodoxy has been always a perennial concern."
  • Orthodoxy = right/accepted belief.
  • Heterodoxy = belief that departs from the accepted teaching.
  • Yet heterodoxy, though condemned, "may contain new insights for doctrinal and theological developments."

Example: Some ideas once judged "heterodox" later pushed the Church to clarify and deepen doctrine. History is a tension between guarding truth and testing new insight.

D. THEOLOGY AND THE OTHER SCIENCES

Is theology a science? Yes — it is the "systematic study of Christian faith" with its own proper method.

Why theology can dialogue with all sciences (quoted): - Because "all truth and reality come from God." - And: "methodological research in all branches of knowledge... can never conflict with the faith, because the things of the world and the things of faith derive from the same God."

Theology and Philosophy

  • Philosophy was traditionally called the "handmaid of theology" (ancilla theologiae).
  • Handmaid = servant/helper. Philosophy serves theology by supplying tools of reasoning.
  • Difference: philosophy uses reason alone; theology is "guided by the revealed Word of God and faith."
  • Theologians borrow philosophical categories — Greek logos, Indian Vedanta — to express faith in each culture.

Theology and the Social Sciences

  • Contextual and Liberation theologies use sociology, economics, politics.
  • Goal is not only to "understand reality" but to "transform reality" by exposing the root causes of oppression.

Theology and the Religious Sciences

  • Theology draws on the psychology, sociology, and phenomenology of religion to analyze its data.

Example: To preach effectively against caste injustice, a theologian may use sociology (to see the problem clearly) and Scripture (to judge and transform it).

E. THE GOALS / FUNCTIONS OF THEOLOGY

The book lists complementary goals — theology is not for its own sake but serves faith and the world.

  1. Awakening Faith — to "awaken, strengthen and communicate the faith-experience" of the community.
  2. Assimilation — to explain and systematize faith for a "better understanding of faith-experience" in an "ongoing and continuous process."
  3. Biblical Discovery — to "sift the human words in the Bible and to discover within them and beyond them the real Word of God."
  4. Relevance — an "interpretative and prophetic role" to "make the faith relevant and meaningful for today."
  5. Systematic Exposition — to show the "unity and the interconnectedness" of doctrines, all rooted in the mystery of Christ.
  6. Pastoral Empowerment — a "pastoral role of strengthening the faith and empowering Christian life."
  7. Missionary Witness — to "witness to Christ, to proclaim the Gospel and thus to continue Jesus' mission."
  8. World Transformation — to promote the "transformation of the whole world into the Kingdom of God" through justice, equality, and harmony.

Example: Good theology should end not merely in a clever idea but in a stronger believer, a more faithful Church, and a more just world.

CHAPTER I — SUMMARY AT A GLANCE

Section Core point Remember this phrase
A. God-Question Humans naturally reach for God "discourse on God / God-talk"
Analogical knowledge God-words point but fall short "purify our language"
Religious experience God met through symbol "touched or grasped by the Divine"
B. Definitions Many, across history "faith seeking understanding"
Book's definition Christ-lens + re-read for today "systematic and critical interpretation"

STUDY & EXAM POINTERS

Define / Explain: - Etymology of "theology" (theos + logos) - Anselm's fides quaerens intellectum - Analogical knowledge (univocal / equivocal / analogical) - Lex orandi, lex credendi - The book's full working definition of theology - All seven creative polarities (with one line each)

Short notes: - Aquinas's Five Proofs and Newman's "convergence of probabilities" - Rahner: "God and humanity are correlative terms" - Gutierrez: orthodoxy vs orthopraxis - Philosophy as "handmaid of theology"

Reflect: - Which polarity do you find hardest to keep in balance, and why? - Give one Indian example for the "Universal and Contextual" polarity. - Which of the eight goals of theology matters most for the Church in India today?

CHAPTER II — THE SOURCES OF THEOLOGY

Literature note. "What the authors say." Claims extracted → <em>Theology MOC</em>.

Detailed BTh Class Notes

Course: Introduction to Theology (BTh) Source: An Introduction to Theology, Indian Theological Series — Rev. Fr. Kuncheria Pathil CMI & Rev. Fr. Dominic Veliath SDB

Detailed notes on Chapter II. Exact phrases from the book are given in "quotation marks." Technical, Latin, and Indian terms are explained from scratch in simple English, with examples. Church-document citations use standard abbreviations (DV = Dei Verbum; GS = Gaudium et Spes; NA = Nostra Aetate).

CHAPTER OVERVIEW (The Big Picture)

Chapter I asked what theology is. Chapter II asks: Where does theology get its material? What does the theologian build upon?

The logic of the chapter:

  1. Foundations — theology stands on Faith and Revelation (the ground floor).
  2. Three Primary Sources — Scripture, Tradition, Magisterium (the load-bearing pillars).
  3. Their mutual relationship — the three are bound together; none stands alone (DV 10).
  4. Additional Resources — God still speaks through people, cultures, other religions, the poor, and the "signs of the times."

A helpful image: Revelation is the spring of water; Faith is the cup that receives it; Scripture-Tradition-Magisterium are the three channels that carry it to us; and the wider resources (culture, experience, the poor) are the many streams where the same water still flows.

A. FOUNDATIONS OF THEOLOGY: FAITH AND REVELATION

Key statement (quoted): "The foundations of Christian theology are Faith and Revelation."

1. Faith and Revelation Are Two Sides of One Event

  • They are "distinct and distinguishable" yet "inseparably united."
  • Revelation = God's side (God reaches out).
  • Faith = the human side (the person responds).

Exact phrase: - "Revelation is God's self-communication... and faith is the response on the human side."

Simple meaning: Think of a conversation. One person speaks (revelation); the other listens and answers (faith). No speaking-without-hearing makes a real conversation. Revelation without faith is a message no one receives.

Example: God "speaks" through the beauty of creation and through Christ. The believer who says "Yes, I trust this" completes the circuit — that "yes" is faith.

2. What Revelation Means

Full definition (quoted):

"God's gracious self-disclosure reaching out to humans as an invitation, as well as promise, to participate in God's own life of unfathomable love, mediated to us through persons, nature, history, everyday experience, and, in an ultimate way, in and through God's very Word, Jesus Christ."

Unpacking it (simple):

Phrase Meaning
"gracious self-disclosure" God freely unveils Himself — it is a free gift (grace), not owed to us
"invitation... and promise" Revelation calls us in and pledges a future
"participate in God's own life" The goal is not just information but sharing God's life
"unfathomable love" Love too deep to fully measure
"mediated... through persons, nature, history" God reaches us through concrete channels
"ultimate way... Jesus Christ" Christ is the fullness of revelation

Gratuitous = freely given, unearned. Revelation is a gift, not a wage.

3. Four Models (Dimensions) of Revelation

Revelation is "a very complex reality." The book gives four models — different emphases, all true together:

  1. Revelation as Doctrine
  2. The "cognitive contents of revelation as propositions or deposit of truth."
  3. Simple: Revelation as truths/teachings to be believed (held in Scripture and taught by the Magisterium).

  4. Example: "God is Trinity" — a revealed truth.

  5. Revelation as Presence (Personal Encounter)

  6. "a personal encounter with God," not mere knowledge, but "the presence of the living and life-giving God."
  7. Simple: Revelation as meeting a Person, not reading a fact.

  8. Example: A believer in deep prayer senses God's living presence.

  9. Revelation as Experience

  10. An "existential experience, which is universal and possible for all human persons."
  11. Existential = touching real, lived existence.

  12. Simple: God can be encountered in the depths of ordinary human experience — open to everyone.

  13. Revelation as History

  14. A "universal and public historical event that can be historically established."
  15. Simple: God acts in real historical events (Exodus, the life of Jesus) — not only in private feelings.

Why four models? Each corrects the others. Doctrine alone becomes dry; experience alone becomes vague; history alone becomes mere facts. Together they give the full picture.

B. THE THREE PRIMARY SOURCES OF THEOLOGY

1. SACRED SCRIPTURE (The Written Word of God)

a) Inspiration and Inerrancy

  • The biblical books were written by human authors under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so God can be called their author too.
  • Inspiration = the Holy Spirit guiding human writers so their words carry God's message, while remaining fully human writing.

Exact phrase (DV 11):

"the books of Scripture must be acknowledged as teaching firmly, faithfully, and without error that truth which God wanted to put into the sacred writings for the sake of our salvation."

Note carefully: Inerrancy ("without error") is tied to saving truth — "for the sake of our salvation." Scripture teaches reliably what we need for salvation; it is not a textbook of science or exact history.

Example: Genesis teaches that God creates and creation is good (saving truth) — it is not giving a geology lecture on the age of rocks.

b) Need for Interpretation

  • Because "God's word is contained in human words," Scripture "needs to be interpreted" — studying its language, literary forms, and its "basic content and unity as understood by 'the living tradition of the whole Church.'"
  • Final authority for interpretation: "the judgment of the Church" (DV 12).

Literary form = the type of writing — poetry, parable, history, law. You read a poem differently from a legal code.

c) The Canon

  • Canon = the official list of inspired books accepted by the Church.
  • The Church used Apostolic Tradition to recognize which books were genuine.

Exact phrase:

"In fixing the Canon, the Church did no more than recognize certain writings as apostolic, and by the same token, recognize them as regulating her life and faith."

Key insight: The Church did not create the truth of these books; it recognized books that were already apostolic. This shows Scripture and Tradition working together.

d) Scripture as Primary Foundation

Exact phrase (Vatican II):

"sacred theology rests on the written word of God, together with sacred tradition, as its primary and perpetual foundation."

2. SACRED TRADITION (The Living Handing-On)

a) What Tradition Is

  • "The living transmission accomplished in the Holy Spirit is called Tradition."
  • Simple: Tradition is the living process of handing on the whole Gospel — not just old documents, but the living faith carried by the community.

How it is handed down: through liturgy (worship), creeds (professions of faith), and the teachings of the Fathers of the Church.

Careful distinction: - Tradition (capital T) = the living transmission of the apostolic faith. - traditions (small t) = particular customs and practices that carry it.

Example: The words of the Creed at Mass are "small-t" traditions that carry the "big-T" Tradition of apostolic faith.

b) Apostolic Tradition

  • This is the complete Gospel and the foundational experience of the early Church — what the Apostles received from Christ and the Spirit and handed on.

c) Development of Doctrine

  • The deposit of faith is not frozen; guided by the Holy Spirit, implicit truths become explicit over time.
  • Deposit of faith = the whole treasure of revealed truth entrusted to the Church.

Exact phrase: developments are "only explicitations and new understandings of the deposit of faith, never entirely new additions."

Simple meaning: Nothing brand-new is invented. What was implicit (folded up) becomes explicit (unfolded). Like a seed becoming a tree — same life, fuller form.

Example: The full doctrine of the Trinity took centuries to state clearly, but it was already contained, implicitly, in the New Testament.

3. THE MAGISTERIUM (The Teaching Office of the Church)

a) Its Role — Servant, Not Master

Exact phrase (DV 10):

"The task of authentically interpreting the word of God, whether written or handed down, has been entrusted exclusively to the living teaching office of the Church."

Crucial balance:

"This teaching office is not above the word of God, but serves it" — "listening to it devoutly, guarding it scrupulously, and explaining it faithfully."

Simple meaning: The Magisterium is not the boss of God's word; it is its guardian and servant. It hands on only what has been received.

Magisterium = the official teaching authority: the Pope and bishops in communion with him.

b) Collegiality of the Bishops

Exact phrase:

"The Collegiality of the Bishops implies that all the bishops in the Catholic Church together constitute a single body or collegium... upon which is vested the supreme teaching authority of the Church."

Simple meaning: The bishops are not lone rulers of separate territories; together (a collegium = a college/body), united with the Pope, they hold supreme teaching authority — as seen in an Ecumenical Council.

c) Papal Magisterium

  • The Pope is head of the Universal Church and of the college of bishops.
  • He can teach infallibly when speaking ex cathedra (Latin: "from the chair" of Peter — a solemn, definitive pronouncement on faith or morals).
  • To his ordinary teaching, believers owe "religious assent of will and intellect."

Two levels, simply: - Ex cathedra / infallible = rare, solemn, definitive. (Highest.) - Ordinary magisterium = regular teaching (encyclicals, etc.) — requires religious submission of mind and will, though not "infallible" in the strict sense.

d) Sensus Fidei / Sensus Fidelium

  • Sensus fidei = "sense of the faith" — a supernatural instinct for the truth of faith, given by the Holy Spirit to every believer.
  • Sensus fidelium = "sense of the faithful" — that same instinct in the whole body of believers together.

Exact phrase:

"The body of the faithful as a whole, anointed as they are by the Holy One, cannot err in matters of belief."

Simple meaning: The whole People of God, taken together and guided by the Spirit, has a reliable "nose" for the truth of the faith. This is not majority-opinion polling; it is the Spirit-given instinct of the faithful as a body.

Example: Long before some doctrines were formally defined, the ordinary faithful already believed and lived them — the sensus fidelium at work.

C. THE MUTUAL RELATIONSHIP: HOW THE THREE ARE BOUND TOGETHER

This is a key exam point. Scripture, Tradition, and Magisterium are not three rival authorities — they form one interlocking reality.

  • They flow from "the same divine wellspring," and "in a certain way merge into a certain unity and tend toward the same end."
  • "Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture form one sacred deposit of the word of God which is committed to the Church" (DV 6–9).

The famous summary (DV 10), quoted in full:

"It is clear, therefore, that Sacred Tradition, Sacred Scripture and the teaching authority of the Church, in accord with God's most wise design, are so linked and joined together that one cannot stand without the others, and all together and each in its own way, under the action of the Holy Spirit, contribute effectively to the salvation of souls."

Simple meaning — "one cannot stand without the others":

Source Its job Without the others...
Scripture The written Word ...becomes a book open to endless private readings
Tradition The living handing-on ...loses its written anchor
Magisterium The authentic interpreter ...has nothing to guard if it stands alone

Image: Like a tripod — three legs holding one camera steady. Remove any leg and the whole thing falls.

D. ADDITIONAL RESOURCES OF THEOLOGY

Beyond the three primary sources, the book insists God is continually present and active in the world and human history. So there are further resources theology must listen to.

1. People and Their Experience

  • "Human experience is the meeting-point between God's self-gift and the human response to it."
  • "The people themselves are thus the resources of revelation, and it is through the people that God speaks to us."

Simple meaning: Because revelation reaches us through our humanity, the lived experience of real people becomes a place where God still speaks.

2. Cultural Resources

  • God "speaks to humans according to their culture of different ages" (GS 58); therefore "human cultures are clearly resources of theology."

The Indian contribution — Cosmotheandric vision: - India offers a rich "cosmotheandric understanding of reality." - Cosmotheandric breaks into three Greek roots: cosmos (world) + theos (God) + andros (human). It means a vision where world, God, and humanity are held together as one interconnected whole — not separated into "sacred vs secular."

Example: An Indian sees the divine, the human, and nature as deeply woven together (in a sacred river, a sacred tree). Theology can draw on this holistic vision rather than splitting matter from spirit.

3. Diverse Religious Traditions

  • Recognizing other religions as theological resources is "perhaps, the greatest challenge facing our time."
  • Other religions "reflect a ray of that truth which enlightens all" (NA 2).
  • "The sacred Scriptures of all religions are the heritage of the entire humanity" and can be powerful sources of spiritual experience and liberation.

Balance to remember: The book affirms other religions as genuine resources while still affirming that Jesus is the source of salvation for all. Openness, not relativism.

4. Peoples' Movements and the Marginalized

  • "God's word resounds in a special way in the voice of the marginalized."
  • Theology must attend to human rights, peasant, Dalit, tribal, and women's movements that stand for freedom and justice.
  • Dalit = communities formerly branded "untouchable" under the caste system; Dalit theology reads the Gospel from their struggle for dignity.

5. The Cry of the Poor

  • Liberation theologians speak of the "epistemological privilege of the poor."
  • Epistemological = about knowing/knowledge. The phrase means the poor have a privileged "way of knowing" God's truth — they see the Gospel from an angle the comfortable often miss.
  • "God speaks today in a very special way through the cry of the poor, their struggles, aspirations, visions and hopes."

Example: A slum community's cry for justice is not "outside" theology — it is a place where God's word is heard afresh.

Chapter III — Development and Pluralism in Theology

Literature note. Full detail also in the combined file *BTh_Chapters_2_and_3*. Claims extracted → <em>Theology MOC</em>.

Master thesis

Theology keeps a "delicate balance between maintaining the single focus — Christ, and allowing a legitimate pluralism of expression." Uniqueness of Christ + multiplicity of expression = the two facets of Christian faith. Pluralism is present from the very beginning — inside the Bible itself.

A. Biblical theologies

The Bible is "a library, a collection of books and consequently of theologies." - OT: Yahwist, Elohist, Priestly, Deuteronomic, Wisdom theologies → Old Testament Theologies - NT: Matthean, Marcan, Lucan, Johannine; Paul's ascending/descending/cosmic Christologies → New Testament Theologies and Paul's Three Christologies - Gospels are "anecdotal rather than biographical"; "history interpreted through faith."

B. Patristic period (→ mid-8th c.)

Deaths marking the close: John Damascene (749), Gregory the Great (604), Isidore of Seville (639). - Apostolic Fathers (Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Polycarp) — "pastoral, didactic and exhortatory." - Apologists (Justin, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria). - Alexandrian vs Antiochene schools → Alexandrian and Antiochene Schools - Latin Fathers (Tertullian, Ambrose, Augustine).

C. The Aristotelian turn

Theology shifts "from the plane of action to the plane of being"; need for "second order" reflection.

D. Scholasticism (c. 800–1500)

Pre / Early / High / Late. University "lectures and disputations." Anselm (1033–1109), Aquinas (1225–1274), Bonaventure (1221–1274), Duns Scotus (1266–1308), Ockham (1285–1347).

E. Post-Scholastic

Reformation (Luther, Calvin, Sola Scriptura); Council of Trent; Neo-Scholasticism (Aeterni Patris, 1879).

F. Modern & contextual

Vatican II (1962–65) → "World Church." Contextual theologies → Contextual Theologies (Modern).

Literature note. "What the author says." Synthesized from NotebookLM queries against the four primary-source volumes (2026-07-20; full Vol 2 added and re-extracted same day). Author: <em>George Soares-Prabhu</em>.

Grounded in the Collected Writings, Vols 1–4 (NotebookLM: "George Soares Prabhu A Biblical Theology for India")

1. The Corpus

Vol Title Focus
1 Biblical Themes for a Contextual Theology Today Context & Mission — mission, inculturation, liberation, dialogue
2 A Biblical Theology for India (full, 332pp, 16 chapters) Methodology, OT, portraits of Jesus, Indian readings
3 Biblical Spirituality of Liberative Action Spirituality — Abba experience, dharma of Jesus, religious life
4 Theology of Liberation: An Indian Biblical Perspective Liberation — structural action, human rights, Kingdom as new society

The arc is thematic, not chronological: context → method → interiority → structural action.

Three constants across all volumes: 1. The foundational Abba-experience of Jesus. 2. Unwavering commitment to the concrete Indian reality: massive poverty, the caste system, pluriform religiosity. 3. The preferential option for the poor.

2. Volume 1 — Biblical Themes for a Contextual Theology Today

Thesis: Indian Christian theology must break free of Western colonial frameworks and address poverty, caste, and religious pluralism.

Part I: Mission

  • Ch 1 — Expanding the Horizon of Christian Mission: mission ≠ church growth; building God's Kingdom through solidarity, poverty, powerlessness.
  • Ch 2 — The Church as Mission: mission is theocentric (glory to God); witness of the whole community over individual proclamation.
  • Ch 3 — Following Jesus in Mission: the Great Commission = radical detachment, "missionary discipleship" vs colonial conquest.

Part II: Inculturation, Liberation, Dialogue

  • Ch 4 — Inculturation–Liberation–Dialogue: Asian theology must stop imitating Western academia; address Asia's poverty + profound religiosity.
  • Ch 5 — From Alienation to Inculturation: the Indian Church is alienated by colonial roots; must integrate into Indian culture.
  • Ch 6 — The NT as a Model of Inculturation: the early Church constantly adapted its message to new cultures — the blueprint.
  • Ch 7 — The Liberative Pedagogy of Jesus: teaching non-elitist, praxis-oriented; framework for Indian liberation theology.
  • Ch 8 — The Indian Church Challenged by Poverty and Caste: "Christian dalits" = contradiction of Jesus's inclusive Kingdom.
  • Ch 9 — Challenged by Pluralism and Dialogue: abandon exclusivism; other religions are valid ways of salvation.
  • Ch 10 — Religion and Communalism: overcome intolerance via Jesus's radical anti-communal love and open boundaries.
  • Ch 11 — Jesus Christ amid the Religions and Ideologies of India Today: Jesus bridges the spiritual focus of Indian religions and the material concern of secular ideologies → holistic liberation.

Part III: Contextual Interpretation of the Bible

  • Ch 12 — Towards an Indian Interpretation of the Bible: dual approach — "religious reading" (Indian methods, dhvani) + "social reading" (liberation).
  • Ch 13 — The Table Fellowship of Jesus: dining with outcasts dismantled purity lines → direct condemnation of caste and untouchability.
  • Ch 14 — Antigreed and Antipride: tribal values foundational to Jesus's ethics.
  • Ch 15 — Class in the Bible: the biblical "poor" = a socially/economically oppressed class; God's salvation is linked to their liberation.

3. Volume 2 — A Biblical Theology for India (full volume)

Sixteen chapters in three parts. Part I: Biblical Methods, Old Testament, Non-Christian Scriptures. Part II: Theological Portraits of Jesus. Part III: Reading the Bible from Indian Perspectives.

Chapter theses

Part I - Ch 1 — The Historical Critical Method: HCM inadequate for India; integrated "religious" + "social" reading proposed (detailed below). - Ch 2 — The Word of God and the Forms of Literature: form criticism "recovers the 'spokenness' of God's Word" — the text becomes a direct, urgent address summoning personal encounter, not a dead book. - Ch 3 — Socio-Cultural Analysis in Prophetic Theologizing: the biblical prophet as paradigm: social analysis of contemporary events driven by a God-given "alternative vision," in language that "breaks down the structures of the dominant society and empowers the dominated to structure an alternative community." - Ch 4 — The Temple of Jerusalem: built for political legitimation, the Temple domesticated Yahweh; Solomon's project "effectively reverses the movement of the Mosaic revolution," replacing an economics of equality and a politics of justice with affluence, forced labor, imperial oppression. - Ch 5 — The Inspiration of the OT and Non-Christian Scriptures: the OT is inspired "not in itself but inasmuch as it is illumined by the New"; if Christ is the Word enlightening everyone, salvation history encompasses the universe — "the inspiration of non-Christian scriptures is a distinct possibility."

Part II - Ch 6 — Are the Gospels Historical?: the Gospels are "history interpreted through faith," a "mosaic" of traditions revealing religious significance, not chronological biography. - Ch 7 — Jesus and the Spirit in the Synoptics: the Spirit grounds Jesus's sonship (infancy), installs him messianically (baptism), empowers exorcism and evangelization (ministry) — marked not by ecstatic enthusiasm but by "the authority of his teaching, and the power of his healings and exorcisms." "Sonship (the experience of God as abba, Father) and Spirit (the experience of the eschatological power of God working in and through him) were in fact the twin poles of Jesus' experience of God." - Ch 8 — Jesus the Teacher: liberative pedagogy — dialogical methods and parables conscientizing marginalized audiences toward a new fraternal world. - Ch 9 — Jesus in Matthew: a majestic, exalted Jesus who "stands above the stress of events," "almost an avatar"; the "Teacher of Righteousness" and divine Son authoritatively interpreting God's will. - Ch 10 — Mary in Luke's Annunciation: Luke fuses an OT call-narrative with a birth oracle ("a birth oracle replaces the commissioning"); Mary as "eschatological Daughter of Sion" personifying the faithful remnant. - Ch 11 — The Man Born Blind: physical sight vs spiritual insight; for India, a call to "radical openness" to a Christ who "fits no formula, who breaks through the restraints of our comfortably constructed systems."

Part III - Ch 12 — The Sacred in the Secular (Johannine Sutra, Jn 1:14): three implications — christological: "decisively excludes any sort of epiphanic or avatara type of Christianity"; anthropological: God met by serving neighbor in the secular world; cosmic: the Incarnation demands respect for matter — "the sacred interpenetrates the secular (as the soul interpenetrates the body), and is accessible only through it." - Ch 13 — Christian Priesthood in India Today: against a purely cultic, sacralized priesthood; the priest enters the Kingdom movement that "continually subverts a world structured... by relationships of oppression." - Ch 14 — 'And There Was a Great Calm' (dhvani reading of Mk 4:35–41): the worked model of the dhvani method (below). - Ch 15 — Good News to the Poor: Jesus's message has a "strongly social thrust" aimed "to set free the oppressed"; Luke deliberately modified Isaiah 61 to block spiritualizing readings of "Blessed are you poor." - Ch 16 — Laughing at Idols (Isa 44:9–20): the biblical anti-idol satire is a "damaging and therefore sinful misrepresentation of a people's religion and culture" — idolaters worship the divine that "dwells" in the image, as "bread and wine in the Christian Eucharist mediate the 'real presence' of Jesus." The "fanatical iconoclasm of the Bible" is the "dark side of its monotheism," historically issuing in "devastating destruction of peoples and cultures."

The dhvani method worked (Mk 4:35–41)

Takes the narrative as it stands (against source-dissection) and reads three oppositions: great storm vs great calm (precariousness of life on the edge of chaos); sleeping Jesus vs panicking disciples (faith vs fear); passive passenger vs commanding Lord. Yield: "It is this experience of ultimate stability behind the turmoil of our agitated and threatened existence that this story of the Stilling of the Storm evokes."

Critique of the historical-critical method

  • "The pretended neutrality of Western exegesis and its historical critical method is thus... an illusion." The method is "ideologically loaded."
  • Functions as "legitimisation of the capitalistic technocracy" — lets interpreters ignore the Gospel's challenge to wealth and power.
  • Western scholarship = "production for profit — for academic kudos if not for money."
  • "No such thing as an autonomous, impartial, academic theology floating free above the realm of human options and biases."

What he retains

  • "Sound historical criticism... will in fact bring out the objective dimension of its meaning" — reveals the text's original "intentionality," prevents "far-fetched flights of fancy." HCM = safeguard and control.

The Integral Indian Reading

Two complementary readings that must converge:

  1. Religious reading — transposes the Gospel into India's religious traditions. Two steps: "first I have to assimilate my own cultural and religious past by a reading of the Indian scriptures; then I will re-read the Gospel in the light of this new experience." Uses Indian hermeneutics: dhvani = "the resonating effect of a word through which it evokes in the hearer deep meanings."
  2. Social reading — interprets the Gospels "in the light of a liberating praxis among the socially oppressed." Targets institutional structures causing mass poverty and illiteracy; also personal liberation from greed and aggression.

Convergence: the halves correct and enrich each other, revealing "liberation announced by Jesus in its totality" — "both the liberation from social oppression... as well as the freedom from personal bondage (moksa)."

The interpreter's double identity

  • Must assimilate own religious heritage before re-reading the Gospel; requires "radical self-emptying."
  • Indian theologians alienated from their roots by "long years of Western indoctrination" in Westernized seminaries.
  • The task: "To a critical consciousness derived from Western modernization, he must bring a profound and sympathetic understanding of ancient Indian tradition; to a pluriform religious experience he must join a deep and active concern for social issues."

4. Volume 3 — Biblical Spirituality of Liberative Action

Central claim: genuine spirituality is contextualized; Jesus's Abba-rooted spirituality spills into political action, solidarity with the oppressed, struggle against unjust structures.

Structure

  1. Jesus's Foundational Experience and its Expression (ch 1–9) — the "Dharma of Jesus."
  2. Dynamics of Christian Spirituality — salvation = social + cosmic transformation, not individual rescue.
  3. Spirituality of Jesus's Professional Followers — religious life, priesthood, vows as prophetic commitment.

Key chapter theses

  • Miracles (ch 2–4): "signs of the Kingdom," not proofs — "announce and actualize (make present) the saving action of God"; subvert oppressive power structures.
  • 'As We Forgive' (ch 6): human forgiveness = result and paradigm of experiencing God's unlimited forgiveness, not a way to earn it.
  • Love Commandment (ch 7): loving God ≡ loving neighbor; active concern for others = core of spiritual life.
  • Jesus and Conflict (ch 11): root of conflict = God's unconditional love prioritizing people over the Law.
  • Social Stance (ch 14): Jesus sided with the poor/outcast, confronted the socio-religious establishment.
  • Unprejudiced Jesus, Prejudiced Church (ch 16): boundary-breaking love vs Church discrimination.
  • Priesthood as Call in the OT (ch 18): Christian priesthood models charismatic prophets, not cultic OT priesthood.
  • Christian Purusharthas (ch 22): Hindu life-goals reinterpreted; individual liberation inseparable from community liberation.

The Abba experience and the Dharma of Jesus

  • Dharma of Jesus = "dharma of unconditional and therefore of absolutely universal love."
  • Abba = "loving Parent"; experience of "unconditional love," "radically liberating."
  • God as parent → all people brothers/sisters → "empowers him to identify with the poor and the outcast and confront the powerful and the rich."
  • Mysticism and politics intertwined (via Metz): following Christ "has a mystical element and one that is situational, one that is practical and political." Genuine mysticism "pushes" one into history.
  • Prayer → praxis: the Lord's Prayer is "wholly a prayer for the Kingdom"; praying for forgiveness commits us to practicing it.
  • The Cross: "no arbitrary intrusion into the life of Jesus. It is the natural outcome of a life of solidarity with the poor and the outcast and of confrontation with the powerful who oppress them."

Vows

  • "We are freed from all things, in order that we might make ourselves slaves of all through love." Communitarian practices freeing for radical action, not private asceticism.

5. Volume 4 — Theology of Liberation: An Indian Biblical Perspective

Central claim: a biblical theology of liberation through Indian eyes — holistic liberation from poverty, caste, cultural alienation.

Chapter theses

  • Ch 1 — Interpreting the Bible in India Today: beyond Western HCM via the "Indian mind."
  • Ch 2 — The Prophet as Theologian: historically rooted critique against religious idolatry and social injustice.
  • Ch 3 — Commitment and Conversion: radical commitment to the poor + adoption of the Indian worldview.
  • Ch 4 — Two Mission Commands: Mt 28 vs Buddhist Mahāvagga; mission = liberation + compassion, not domination.
  • Ch 5 — The Bible as Magna Carta: human rights grounded in the sacredness of the person + responsibility for the marginalized.
  • Ch 6 — Class in the Bible: the "poor" = oppressed sociological group championed by God.
  • Ch 7 — The Synoptic Love-Commandment: agapē requires concrete action and struggle for societal justice.
  • Ch 8 — The NT Church: radical sharing and social protest = principles for economic liberation.
  • Ch 9 — Radical Beginnings: the Jesus movement = radically free, egalitarian, serving community; archetype for the Church.
  • Ch 10 — The Dharma of Jesus: the Sermon on the Mount as dharma, not legal code.
  • Ch 11 — Jesus and the Poor: poor = destitute + marginalized + illiterate + afflicted; end social poverty, call to spiritual poverty (freedom from mammon).
  • Ch 12 — The Christian Response to the Indian Situation: historical, incarnational, "integral."
  • Ch 13 — A Dalit Reading of the Decalogue: the Ten Commandments = absolute equality before the law; contrast with the Laws of Manu.
  • Ch 14 — John 1:1–18, an Asian Perspective: inculturated Prologue reading; Īśāvāsya Upanishad vs consumerism.
  • Ch 15 — The Kingdom of God: Jesus's Vision of a New Society: freedom + fellowship + justice.
  • Ch 16 — Jesus the Teacher: "liberative pedagogy" — dialogical, parabolic, consciousness-raising.
  • Ch 17 — The Jesus of Faith: Third World Christology from encounter with the historical Jesus, not Hellenistic formulas.

The Indian mind hermeneutic

  • "Context-sensitive rather than context-free"; reality as interconnected whole.
  • "Holistic and inclusive"; "logic of complementarity" (both/and) vs Aristotelian "logic of exclusion" (either/or).
  • Worldview: "inclusive, cosmocentric, symbolic, and practical."
  • "Because of its passion for wholeness the Indian mind is prepared to risk the chance of error rather than the loss of any part of truth."
  • Interpreter's two-fold conversion: (1) "radical commitment to the poor"; (2) conversion to the Indian worldview.

The prophet-as-theologian

  • Theologize like the prophets: rooted in concrete history, not abstract exegesis.
  • Two-fold protest: religious critique (condemns idolatry — absolutization of money, state, institutions) + social critique ("concrete expressions of exploitation and oppression").
  • Theology begins with social analysis and leads to social change.

Dharma of Jesus / Sermon on the Mount

  • Dharma (Indian sense): "all comprehensive" — religious observance, righteousness, justice, conformity to law and custom, duty.
  • Dharma of Jesus: "the complex of religious insight and ethical concern (of experience, world-view and value) which determines the life-style that Jesus proclaimed and practised."
  • As juridical law the Sermon = "thoroughly utopian law." As dharma: "The dharma of the Sermon on the Mount then proclaims freedom from the burden of the law, since it is grounded on an experience of God as abba who loves us his children with an unconditional love."

The Kingdom as New Society

  • "A new society is realized whenever humans become free internally and externally, when there is fellowship of concern among humans and when they strive for a just society."
  • Three dimensions: personal freedom (internal + external), communitarian fellowship (mutual concern, radical equality), structural justice.
  • These are "parameters by which the arrival or the delay of God's reign is to be gauged."

Human rights

  • The Bible grounds rights via: (1) sacredness of every person (imago Dei); (2) responsibility for the powerless (widow, orphan, refugee). The neighbor = locus of encountering God.
  • "In an unjust society agapē inevitably becomes a struggle for justice: it strives 'to set free the oppressed'."

Two mission commands

  • Mt 28 vs Mahāvagga: similar tripartite structure. The Buddhist command stresses the missionary's own enlightenment and unconditional compassion; Matthew's is heavily Christological. An Asian reading recovers the missionary's inner liberation: "The Christian mission, for all its christological grounding, also presupposes the 'enlightenment' of those who are sent."

Jesus of Faith christology

  • "To be a disciple of Jesus... means to experience God the way that Jesus experienced God."
  • Rooted in the abba experience → radical freedom, love, solidarity with the poor → conflict → cross.

6. The Unified Interpretive Pipeline

  1. Commitment & pre-understanding — conscious commitment to the Indian context (poverty, pluriform religiosity, caste). No neutral standpoint.
  2. Historical-critical exegesis — recover the original "author meaning"; historical base and control against eisegesis.
  3. Social analysis — structures of the biblical world and contemporary India; all theology is socially conditioned.
  4. Indian hermeneutic (dual reading) — religious reading (dhvani, symbolic depth) + social reading (liberating praxis).
  5. Praxis — total liberation: from societal oppression and personal bondage (moksha).

Worked example: Table Fellowship

  • Pre-understanding: caste/untouchability.
  • HCM: Jesus habitually dined with "tax collectors and sinners."
  • Social analysis: a shared meal = religious affirmation of belonging; subverted purity laws and elitism.
  • Dual reading: socially — confronts caste; religiously — God as loving parent rejecting ritual purity as barrier.
  • Praxis: eradicate caste discrimination in the Church; build an egalitarian community.

7. Key Concept Definitions (his own words)

  • Kingdom of God: "the decisive salvific action through which God, finally 'liberating' creation, reveals God's self as King" (Mk 1:14–15). Three dimensions: personal freedom, communitarian fellowship, societal justice.
  • The Poor (anawim): from a root meaning "bent, bowed down, afflicted" — "all those who are in any way, and not just economically, deprived of the means or the dignity they need to lead a fully human existence" (Lk 6:20). Defined by sociological powerlessness; privileged beneficiaries of God's action.
  • Inculturation: "the passage of a religious tradition from one cultural situation to another, in a movement that resembles the conversion of a person from a situation of sin to a situation of salvation"; "throwing off an imposed alien and alienating system of doctrine and worship, in order to allow Indian experiences of Jesus to find their unforced expression."
  • Dhvani: "the resonating effect of a word through which it evokes in the hearer deep meanings"; applied intertextually it "elicits deeper meaning in the hearer which otherwise would not have been perceived at all."
  • Liberative pedagogy: "pedagogy of the oppressed with a strong commitment to societal liberation"; "nonélitist and dialogical, based on the equality of all before God."
  • Communalism: life perceived "in terms of religious communities, each with a distinct identity of its own, competing with other religious groups for survival and growth"; countered by the "anticommunal Jesus" (Mk 7:1–23).
  • Table fellowship: "acted parable, through which he brings home to listeners his experience of God as Abba the loving parent" (Mk 2:15ff).
  • Antigreed: tribal value; rejection of consumerism (Mk 10:17–27).
  • Antipride: "not self-abasement but fearless and active service" (Mk 10:35–45).
  • Dharma of Jesus: "the complex of religious insight and ethical concern... which determines the life-style that Jesus proclaimed and practised"; a "dharma of unconditional and therefore of absolutely universal love."

8. Polemical Positions

Target Critique Sharpest quotes
Western academic exegesis Ideologically loaded, capitalist-conditioned, socially irrelevant "ruinous heap of hypothetical possibilities"; exegetes "fiddle while Rome burns"; seminary training = "a trained incapacity to deal with the real problems of actual living persons in their daily lives"
Latin American liberation theology Respected, but ignores Asian religiosity theology that "focuses almost exclusively on societal change, will not therefore satisfy Asian aspirations"; must include "liberation from personal bondage (moksha)"
Institutional Indian Church Colonial relic, complicit in caste "in effect a wholly owned and controlled subsidiary of a Rome-based company"; caste in Church makes the Eucharist "a sacrilege" and "parody"; Christian dalits "a sign of how little Christian we are"
Ashram / brahmanical spirituality Elitist, other-worldly, socially indifferent "a brahmanical spirituality, the spirituality of an affluent, privileged class"; "a mockery for the five hundred millions of our people who subsist below, on, or just above the poverty line"

9. Voice and Style

  • Architecture: thematic headings; deep biblical foundation first, then Indian application; essays open with broad statement of context/purpose, close with appeals for paradigm shift.
  • Rhythm: balanced, flowing sentences that build to passionate, rhetorically charged statements; exclamation points at climaxes.
  • Citations: extensive footnotes; synthesizes and critiques Western scholars (Bultmann, Jeremias) alongside Indian thinkers (Gandhi, Samuel Rayan, Ramanujan); draws on Segundo, Pieris, Metz.
  • Scripture: heavy inline citation used to subvert traditional Western readings, not proof-text.
  • Devices: sharp contrasts (mission not "conquest" but "light"; "context-sensitive" vs "context-free"; "culture of silence" vs "tinsel facade"), rhetorical questions, vivid metaphors ("two-eyed vision," "elliptical" truth).
  • Register: described by his editors as the "careful and precise activity of a committed and gifted scribe" — scholarly, analytical, prophetic.

Signature quotes

  1. "Faith endures; but no theology is perennial!"
  2. "To do theology means to contextualize one's faith."
  3. "An Indian exegesis will be greatly concerned about relevance and so will strenuously avoid the academic barrenness which afflicts 'scientific' exegesis today."
  4. "Mission is therefore concerned not with the power, security or growth of the missionizing Churches, but with the welfare of the missionized world."
  5. "Any genuine spirituality... is a contextualized spirituality, a way of life based on certain convictions and values (a dharma) which interacts creatively and appropriately with its historical context."
  6. "To experience God as Abba is therefore to experience the 'wholly other' in the give and take of human history."
  7. "In an unjust society agapē inevitably becomes a struggle for justice: it strives 'to set free the oppressed'."
  8. "To be a disciple of Jesus... means to experience God the way that Jesus experienced God."

10. Vocabulary Bank

  • Signature pairings: alienation → inculturation; social vs religious reading; contrast community; context-sensitive vs context-free.
  • Favorite texts: Mt 28:16–20; Mt 5–7; Mt 5:13–16; Mk 1:14–15; Mk 2:15ff; Mk 7:1–23; Mk 10:17–27; Mk 10:35–45; Lk 6:20; Jn 1:1–18.
  • Indian terms: dharma, moksha, dhvani, vyañjana, dalit, purusharthas, asramas.
  • Interlocutors: approving — Segundo, Pieris, Ramanujan, Rayan, Gandhi, Metz; critical — Bultmann, Osho Rajneesh (imposes advaitic pre-understanding, "drowns" the text).

A Research Glossary of Terms and Concepts, with His Own Definitions

Compiled from the Collected Writings, Vols 1–4 (NotebookLM primary-source queries, 20 July 2026)

I. Foundational Concepts

Abba experience — Jesus's foundational experience of God as "unconditional love" and a "loving Parent." It is "radically liberating" because it fulfills the basic human need to be loved, freeing a person from finding fulfillment through possessing things or clinging to attachments. Rather than an abstract, all-pervading Absolute, Abba is the unconditionally loving Parent who gifts Himself to humankind. This experience destroys religious legalism and purity boundaries. Everything else in his theology derives from it.

Dharma — A "way of life"; a "complex blend of worldview and values of belief and prescription" that holds a community together. Traditionally defining caste obligation and social duty, he deliberately redefines it for the dharma of Jesus: "the complex of religious insight and ethical concern (of experience, world-view and value) which determines the life-style that Jesus proclaimed and practised" — a "dharma of unconditional and therefore of absolutely universal love."

Spirituality — "A way of life based on certain convictions and values (a dharma) which interacts creatively and appropriately with its historical context." Hence any genuine spirituality is a contextualized spirituality; mysticism and politics are inseparable.

Kingdom of God (basileia tou theou) — "God's definitive liberative intervention in human and cosmic history"; "the decisive salvific action through which God, finally 'liberating' creation, reveals God's self as King" (Mk 1:14–15). Stripped of other-worldly connotations: not heaven-after-death, not the Church. It creates a new society measured by three dimensions — personal freedom, communitarian fellowship, structural justice — the "parameters by which the arrival or the delay of God's reign is to be gauged."

Salvation — "Integral liberation": "eschatological but not other-worldly"; it comes from God but "is actualized in and through the struggles of the poor," freeing people from social, economic, and societal oppression as well as personal bondage.

Liberation — In the Indian context: "liberation from poverty arising out of material want and liberation from oppression and social ostracism" — always paired with inner liberation (see moksha). Total liberation = both, never one.

Contextual theology — "An intentional and thought-out effort to do theology in and for a given context" by those who belong to it. "To do theology means to contextualize one's faith." "Faith endures; but no theology is perennial!"

II. The Poor and Social Analysis

The poor / anawim ('anî / 'anāw) / ptochoi — From a Hebrew root meaning "bent, bowed down, afflicted." He fiercely rejects spiritualizing the poor: they are the "sociologically poor" — "the economically destitute and the socially outcast," "all those who are in any way, and not just economically, deprived of the means or the dignity they need to lead a fully human existence" (Lk 6:20).

Class (biblical) — Against Marxist reduction, the biblical poor are defined by three propositions: a sociological group (defined by deprived social situation), a dialectical group (oppressed by antagonistic groups), and a dynamic group (through whom God shapes history).

Option for the poor — The defining element of biblical spirituality: the poor are "those on whose side God stands, and from whom God's salvation comes."

Culture of silence — An "alienated society" silenced and treated as the "mere object" of a dominant or colonizing power (adapted from Freire).

Tinsel facade — The "glittering but tinsel facade of Westernization" imposed by a privileged elite, hiding the overwhelming poverty of the "real India."

Idolatry — "The absolutization of things like money, kingship and temple or the reduction of God to an idol"; turning God into "the legitimizing principle of absolutized values like money power... or of absolutized institutions like the Temple or the state." The prime target of prophetic religious critique.

Communalism — The "turning in of religious communities upon themselves to form tightly knit defensive groups maintaining a hostile attitude" toward rival groups, fueled by insecurity; life perceived as competing religious communities. Countered by the "anticommunal Jesus" who abolished purity boundaries (Mk 7:1–23).

III. Jesus: Life, Teaching, Praxis

Jesus of faith — Against both the "Jesus of history" of academic reconstruction and the "Christ of dogma" of Hellenistic formulas: "the Jesus (not the Christ) of faith (not of history)" — "the real Jesus who lived in Palestine... as he was encountered and experienced by his first followers." The starting point of Third World Christology.

Discipleship — "To be a disciple of Jesus means to experience God the way that Jesus experienced God." Adopting Jesus's worldview, not rule-following or ritual.

Love commandment / agapē — Not affection but "effective love," a "love of concern": "to do good to someone." "To love God means, concretely, to love neighbour." "In an unjust society agapē inevitably becomes a struggle for justice: it strives 'to set free the oppressed'."

Miracle — Not "compelling 'proofs'" of divinity but "'signs', indications perceptible to those disposed to receive them"; "a proclamation in action of the 'good news'"; signifying "the subversion of a whole oppressive power structure."

Table fellowship — Jesus's habit of eating with outcasts: an "acted parable, through which he brings home to listeners his experience of God as Abba the loving parent" (Mk 2:15ff). Enacts the Kingdom as community of grace against ritual purity — his direct weapon against caste.

Conflict — "Not a secondary dispensable element in the ministry of Jesus; it is of its essence." The inevitable result of exercising love in an unjust world.

The Cross — "No arbitrary intrusion into the life of Jesus. It is the natural outcome of a life of solidarity with the poor and the outcast and of confrontation with the powerful who oppress them."

Forgiveness — Paired with "a refusal to condemn"; a "necessary precondition for effective prayer"; "only the spiral of active forgiveness can break the spiral of violence that is tearing our world apart." Human forgiveness is the result and paradigm of experiencing God's unlimited forgiveness, never a way to earn it.

Prayer — Flows from the Abba experience: "Because the Christian experiences God as a loving Parent and relates to God as a trusting child, Christian prayer will be a child's prayer." The Lord's Prayer is "wholly a prayer for the Kingdom" — prayer commits to praxis.

Metanoia — Radical dislocation of familiar patterns of perception and behavior; a total turning of the human being toward God and neighbor.

Liberative pedagogy — Jesus's teaching style: "pedagogy of the oppressed with a strong commitment to societal liberation"; "nonélitist and dialogical, based on the equality of all before God"; involves conscientization — liberating people "from the manipulative myths which legitimized their oppressive and alienating society" and "making them conscious of their worth."

Sermon on the Mount as dharma — Read as juridical law it becomes "thoroughly utopian law" with impossible demands. As dharma: "proclaims freedom from the burden of the law, since it is grounded on an experience of God as abba who loves us his children with an unconditional love."

IV. Mission and Church

Mission — "There is no uniform, unchanging, universal understanding of mission." It means "making God's love present in whatever way it can" to build God's Kingdom — never Church growth. "Mission is therefore concerned not with the power, security or growth of the missionizing Churches, but with the welfare of the missionized world."

Witness — The most crucial aspect of mission in India: mission is "not so much doing as being; not so much noisy proclamation as infectious witness."

Proclamation / evangelization — Proclamation is the verbal "announcing of the good news"; verbal evangelization is a "derivative part" of mission — an offering of love, not "conquest" or "sale."

Conversion — Personally: an "active commitment," an ongoing response to a new situation. Also his model for inculturation (below).

Church-as-mission — The Church exists not for itself but as "the symbol and the servant of God's Reign"; mission is the Church serving the world, not expanding itself.

Colonial Christianity — An "aggressive mission carried out under the patronage of the avaricious and ruthless colonial powers," treating people "as objects to be converted."
