As a prisoner of war in Scotland and England he encountered the crucified Christ's cry of dereliction ("My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?") and it became the seed of his entire theology of a God who enters, rather than stands above, human suffering. He studied at Göttingen and became Professor of Systematic Theology at Tübingen (1967–1994). Where classical theism pictures an impassible, all-powerful monarch-God, Moltmann's crucified God freely suffers with creation, and the Trinity itself becomes the pattern for non-hierarchical human and ecological community.

Example

Moltmann's theology of the "crucified God" and his ecological doctrine of creation as the Spirit's home directly informed the 1980s-90s World Council of Churches emphasis on "Justice, Peace, and the Integrity of Creation" — showing how his academic Trinitarian theology translated into concrete ecumenical social and environmental advocacy.

Illustration

Most classical pictures of God are like a king watching a battle safely from a hilltop, directing but untouched. Moltmann's crucified God is more like a parent who runs into a burning building after their child — not remaining safely outside the disaster, but taking the full cost of it into their own body.

Key Terms

  • Social Trinity: God as a non-hierarchical community of equal divine persons in mutual indwelling (perichoresis), offered as the pattern for human relationships of freedom and equality.
  • Perichoresis (Greek) — "mutual indwelling": The dynamic, reciprocal interpenetration of the three trinitarian persons — for Moltmann, a social and political, not just metaphysical, model.
  • Trinitarian Panentheism: The eschatological hope that God will ultimately mutually indwell the whole of creation, drawing it into the trinitarian life.
  • Christologia Viae (Latin) — "Christology of the way": A dynamic, unfinished Christology of Jesus still "on the way" toward a promised messianic future, rather than a completed, static dogma.

Connections

Initially followed Barth, later broke with him to stress lived experience of the Spirit over Barth's tightly bounded revelation. Colleague of Pannenberg at Wuppertal; retrieved Bonhoeffer's social ethics; drew on the Marxist philosopher Ernst Bloch's "philosophy of hope." Criticised by von Balthasar for risking the collapse of eternal, inner-trinitarian suffering into mere temporal world-process. Strongly influenced the Church of England's social theology in the 1970s-80s, though Rowan Williams later worried it risked "sacralizing" the present social order.

See also: Jürgen Moltmann (person note)

Ch. 09 — T. F. Torrance

Chapter author: Daniel W. Hardy

Core Idea

Torrance built a "scientific theology" treating the self-revealed, triune God as the objective reality theology investigates, arguing theology must conform its concepts to that reality exactly as physics conforms its theories to the actual, contingent order of the physical universe.

Detailed Explanation

Born in West China to missionary parents, Torrance studied classics and philosophy at Edinburgh before completing a doctoral thesis on the Apostolic Fathers under Karl Barth in Basel. After a spell as a parish minister in Aberdeen, he held the chairs of Church History and then Christian Dogmatics at Edinburgh (1952-1979). His central move is an analogy with the philosophy of science: just as a physicist must let the nature of light or gravity determine the right method for studying it (rather than imposing a method in advance), so theology must let the self-revealing, triune God determine theological method — an approach that made him an unusually confident conversation partner with working scientists.

Example

Torrance's sustained dialogue with Einsteinian relativity and with the physicist-philosopher Michael Polanyi's account of scientific discovery (the "heuristic leap" of insight) gave him real standing in science-and-religion conferences where most theologians of his generation could not follow the technical physics — a concrete instance of theology disciplining itself to a rigor borrowed from the natural sciences.

Illustration

You would not study a whale using the methods of geology, or a mountain range using the methods of marine biology — each object of study dictates its own appropriate method. Torrance's "scientific theology" insists God likewise dictates God's own appropriate method of study; theology goes wrong whenever it borrows a method built for studying something else (human religious feeling, say, or abstract philosophical categories) instead of letting the living God set the terms.

Key Terms

  • Scientific Theology: Theology conducted in rigorous conformity to the nature of its actual object — the self-revealing, triune God — rather than to a borrowed, external method.
  • Cataphatic / Apophatic Spiral (Greek roots) — "positive / negative": A spiralling method in which positive claims about God (cataphatic) and acknowledgment of God's transcendent mystery (apophatic) continually correct and enrich each other.
  • Heuristic Leap: Borrowed from Michael Polanyi: the mental leap by which the mind fuses scattered clues of experience into one unified insight.
  • Contingent Order: The universe's real, rational order, which is not self-explanatory but depends entirely on the free, loving will of God.

Connections

A devoted student of Barth and the principal English translator of the Church Dogmatics, Torrance stayed within Barth's basic dogmatic frame but extended it, as Barth himself never did, into sustained dialogue with the natural sciences. Close colleague of Colin Gunton (Part II.D), though Gunton eventually departed from Torrance's residual Augustinianism.

See also: T. F. Torrance (person note)

Ch. 10 — Anglican Theology

Chapter author: Peter Sedgwick

Core Idea

Twentieth-century English Anglican theology cultivated a "wisdom theology" — prayer, liturgy, and patristic retrieval over rigid system-building — rooted in the incarnational, kenotic legacy of Lux Mundi (1891), later radically challenged by a sharper critique of the secular social order.

Detailed Explanation

Anglican theology began the century holding an established, culturally privileged position in a rapidly secularizing and class-divided nation, shaped by Bishop Charles Gore, William Temple, and later Michael Ramsey's socially engaged "incarnational" theology. Mid-century brought a radical liberalizing turn — John A. T. Robinson's bestselling Honest to God (1963) and Don Cupitt's later "non-realist" theology — followed by a more rigorous philosophical and historical retrieval led by Donald MacKinnon, Stephen Sykes, Daniel Hardy, and Rowan Williams, who pushed Anglican theology to reclaim the tragic, conflictual dimensions of Jesus's story against a too-comfortable establishment self-image. Stephen Sykes's The Identity of Christianity is the sharpest internal critique: Anglican "comprehensiveness" (holding Anglo-Catholic, Evangelical, and Liberal wings together) risks becoming, he argued, a polite cover for simple incoherence.

Example

John A. T. Robinson's Honest to God (1963) — a bishop's paperback that became an unexpected national bestseller — is the clearest real-world instance of this chapter's story: it popularised Bonhoeffer's "religionless Christianity" and Tillich's "ground of being" for ordinary British readers, provoking a public debate about God-language that went far beyond academic theology.

Illustration

Anglican "comprehensiveness" is like a large extended family gathered at one table who disagree sharply about politics and religion but still insist on eating dinner together every week rather than splitting into separate households. Sykes's critique is the question every such family eventually faces: is staying at one table a genuine, hard-won unity, or just an unwillingness to admit the disagreements are serious?

Key Terms

  • Wisdom Theology: A style of theology oriented to finding the right path for a national church culture, working through essays and liturgy rather than comprehensive dogmatic systems.
  • Anglican Comprehensiveness: Holding Anglo-Catholic, Evangelical, and Liberal traditions together within one church body; criticised by Stephen Sykes as sometimes covering for a lack of theological definition.
  • Kenotic Identification (Greek root: kenosis, self-emptying): God's self-emptying solidarity with human tragedy and historical suffering, authorising the Church's active social and political engagement.
  • Acoluthetic Reason (Greek root: akolouthein, to follow): Reason understood as "following after" and being shaped by the contingent, tragic pattern of Jesus's actual life, rather than reasoning independently of it.

Connections

Stephen Sykes urged Anglicans toward Barth's intellectual rigour and self-definition; Donald MacKinnon and Daniel Hardy (also the author of the Barth and Torrance chapters) engaged deeply with Barth. Moltmann's "solidarity of God with suffering" strongly shaped 1970s-80s Anglican social theology, though Rowan Williams worried it risked sacralizing the status quo. Robinson's Honest to God fused Bonhoeffer and Tillich (both Part I) and drew on Martin Buber's I-Thou philosophy (the Buber companion volume).

Ch. 11 — H. Richard Niebuhr

Chapter author: Stanley Hauerwas

Core Idea

H. Richard Niebuhr's "radical monotheism" centres faith on God's absolute sovereignty alone, condemning "Christomonism" — the defensive absolutizing of any finite thing, even Christ, the church, or a nation — as idolatry, and reframes moral life as the "responsible self" discerning the historically "fitting" response to God's ongoing action.

Detailed Explanation

Younger brother of Reinhold Niebuhr, H. Richard studied at Yale under the pragmatist social psychology of G. H. Mead and wrote his dissertation on Ernst Troeltsch's response to historical relativism — a lifelong theme. Rather than resolving relativism by appeal to a fixed, external authority, he located an answer in radical monotheism itself: because God alone is absolute, every finite human perspective (including the Church's own) is properly relative and provisional, held humbly rather than defended absolutely. He taught at Yale Divinity School from 1931 until his death in 1962, and famously debated his brother Reinhold publicly in 1931 over how Christians should respond to the Manchurian crisis.

Example

Niebuhr's own typology in Christ and Culture (his best-known book) — Christ against culture, Christ of culture, Christ above culture, Christ and culture in paradox, Christ the transformer of culture — became one of the most widely taught frameworks in American theological education for classifying how churches relate to their surrounding society, still assigned in seminaries worldwide.

Illustration

"Christomonism," for Niebuhr, is like insisting a single instrument (however beautiful) is the entire orchestra — isolating Christ from the wider trinitarian symphony of Creator and Sustainer risks turning devotion to Christ into a defensive, idolatrous absolutizing of one part standing in for the whole.

Key Terms

  • Radical Monotheism: Centring loyalty strictly on the one transcendent source of all being, refusing to absolutize any finite value, nation, or even a Christological claim taken in isolation.
  • Theocentric Relativism: The view that all human knowledge, being historically and communally situated, is properly relative — a finitude validated, not threatened, by God's own absolute sovereignty.
  • The Responsible Self: Niebuhr's model of moral agency: not pursuing an abstract good or obeying fixed rules, but responding fittingly to God's action as read within an ongoing historical narrative.
  • The Fitting: The moral criterion of the historically appropriate, responsive action, rather than conformity to a predetermined abstract code.

Connections

Challenges Barth's Christological objectivism (Part I) as risking "Christomonism." His account of historical relativity directly anticipated Hans Frei's narrative theology and the whole postliberal "Yale school" (Part II.D). Engaged in a lifelong dialogical debate with his brother Reinhold Niebuhr (next chapter). Later sharply criticised by John Howard Yoder for implicitly ranking "Christ the transformer of culture" above the concrete nonviolent ethics of Jesus.

See also: H. Richard Niebuhr (person note)

Ch. 12 — Reinhold Niebuhr

Chapter author: William Werpehowski

Core Idea

Reinhold Niebuhr's "Christian Realism" rejects both liberal sentimentalism (believing love alone resolves political conflict) and dogmatic insularity, insisting that because sinful self-interest inevitably taints even collective moral action, justice requires the realistic, sober use of power, coercion, and resistance — even though sacrificial love (agape) remains history's ultimate, if humanly "impossible," norm.

Detailed Explanation

Raised in the German Evangelical Synod, Niebuhr's thirteen years as a pastor in industrial Detroit (1915-28), amid the harsh realities of Henry Ford's factories, convinced him his earlier "simple little moral homilies" were useless against real structural injustice — an experience he chronicled in Leaves from the Notebook of a Tamed Cynic. He taught at Union Theological Seminary, New York (1928-60), and in the 1930s broke publicly with the sentimental optimism of the Social Gospel movement. His central diagnosis: human beings stand at the anxious intersection of finitude and freedom, and that anxiety tempts every person and, especially, every nation or social group toward prideful self-assertion cloaked in self-righteous, universalizing rhetoric.

Example

Niebuhr's Christian Realism directly shaped mid-century American foreign policy thinking — statesmen including George Kennan explicitly drew on his argument that national self-interest must be checked by countervailing power and honest self-suspicion rather than either naive moralism or cynical amorality, making him arguably the most politically influential American theologian of the twentieth century.

Illustration

Sentimental liberalism, for Niebuhr, is like negotiating a hostage situation by simply asking the captor to love their neighbour — sincere, but dangerously naive about how power and self-interest actually operate at scale. Christian Realism instead insists you still need a negotiator, leverage, and a plan — while never forgetting that love, not power, remains the true measure of what a just outcome should look like.

Key Terms

  • Christian Realism: A framework insisting justice requires realistic engagement with power and coercion, since sin and self-interest persist even in collective, well-intentioned political action.
  • Anxiety: The inevitable human condition at the meeting-point of finitude and freedom — not itself sin, but the permanent temptation toward prideful self-assertion instead of trust in God.
  • Impossible Possibility: Niebuhr's description of sacrificial love (agape): the ultimate norm judging and inspiring all history, yet never fully achievable within history's actual power-struggles.
  • Ideological Taint: The self-deceiving tendency of social groups and nations to dress up self-interested claims to power in self-righteous, universal moral language.

Connections

Shares Tillich's method of correlating biblical symbols with existential human analysis (Part I). Engaged in a lifelong public debate with his brother H. Richard Niebuhr (previous chapter). Paul Lehmann criticised his Christology as too cross-focused and under-pneumatological. Fiercely opposed by pacifists John Howard Yoder and Stanley Hauerwas (also this volume's chapter author for H. Richard Niebuhr) for sacralizing state violence and compromising the Church's distinct, nonviolent witness.

See also: Reinhold Niebuhr (person note)

Ch. 13 — Revisionists and Liberals

Chapter author: James J. Buckley

Core Idea

American revisionist and liberal theologians (Edward Farley, Gordon Kaufman, Schubert Ogden, David Tracy, and the process theology movement) reject dogmatic "externalism," reconstructing Christian doctrine — often picturing God as changing, responsive, even suffering — using modern philosophy, evolutionary science, and historical consciousness, in order to make theology's truth-claims publicly, rationally accessible.

Detailed Explanation

Rooted in Friedrich Schleiermacher's nineteenth-century liberal turn and Alfred North Whitehead's philosophical "naturalism," this North American lineage includes Edward Farley's critique of the "house of authority" (the traditional package of inerrancy and ecclesial infallibility treated as finished, unquestionable propositions); Gordon Kaufman's Kantian reconstruction of humans as "biohistorical" evolutionary beings and God as a constructed symbol of serendipitous creativity; Schubert Ogden's process-philosophical case (via Whitehead and Hartshorne) for God as a genuinely responsive companion; and David Tracy's "method of correlation," placing Christian tradition and the modern situation into sustained, mutually critical dialogue. Process theology's "dipolar" God — an eternal, potential nature alongside a temporal, changing nature that genuinely suffers with the world — is the movement's most distinctive metaphysical proposal.

Example

Process theology's claim that God is the "fellow-sufferer who understands" (Whitehead's phrase) gave process-influenced pastoral counselling and hospital chaplaincy a theological alternative to a strictly impassible, unmoved God — a God who is affected by and genuinely grieves human suffering alongside the sufferer, not merely observing it from untouched eternity.

Illustration

A "dipolar" God is like a musician who has both a fixed, unchanging mastery of music theory (the primordial nature) and a live, improvised performance that genuinely responds in real time to what the audience and the other musicians do (the consequent nature) — the theory never changes, but the actual music played is always new, responsive, and never fully predetermined in advance.

Key Terms

  • House of Authority: Edward Farley's term for the traditional dogmatic package (inerrancy, ecclesial infallibility) treating revelation as a finished, unquestionable set of propositions.
  • Biohistorical Beings: Gordon Kaufman's account of humans as evolutionary, self-reflexive organisms shaped by language, culture, and nature rather than as possessors of a static metaphysical soul.
  • Dipolar Theism: The process-theological model of God as having both an eternal, potential nature and a temporal, changing nature that genuinely suffers with the actual world.
  • Mutual Immanence: The reciprocal relationship in process metaphysics whereby the world acts upon God and God indwells the world as its responsive "fellow-sufferer."

Connections

Schleiermacher is this whole movement's acknowledged "grandfather." All four figures adapt and extend Tillich's method of correlation (Part I) with different modern tools — phenomenology (Farley), linguistic analysis and Bultmann (Ogden), Kant (Kaufman), Lonergan and Ricoeur (Tracy). Barth (Part I) is their sharpest critic, rejecting any external cultural "context" as arbiter of Christ's meaning. Ronald Thiemann and Alasdair MacIntyre mount non-foundationalist and tradition-based critiques from directions closer to postliberalism (Part II.D).

Ch. 14 — Postliberal Theology

Chapter author: James Fodor

Core Idea

Postliberal theology (the "Yale school") is a "postcritical," non-foundationalist movement treating Christian doctrines as second-order grammatical rules governing a community's discourse and practice, and Scripture as a text so powerful it "absorbs the world" into its own narrative rather than being translated into external, secular categories.

Detailed Explanation

Inaugurated by George Lindbeck's The Nature of Doctrine (1984) and Hans Frei's biblical-narrative studies, postliberalism responded to the collapse of the mid-century neo-orthodox consensus by rejecting both the "cognitive-propositional" model (doctrines as timeless factual claims) and the "experiential-expressivist" model (doctrines as expressions of a universal inner religious feeling, associated with liberal theology since Schleiermacher). Instead, Lindbeck's "cultural-linguistic" model treats a religion like a language and culture: you learn to live and speak within it, and doctrines are the community's own grammatical rules for speaking correctly, not free-standing propositions to be proved to outsiders. The movement pictures the Church, in a post-Christendom "diaspora" situation, as needing to learn faithful minority survival from Judaism's own long historical experience of exile (galut).

Example

Stanley Hauerwas's application of Frei's narrative Christology into Christian ethics — insisting Christians are formed as a distinct, counter-cultural community of virtue and character by immersion in the biblical story, rather than by appeal to supposedly universal, culture-neutral moral reasoning — is postliberalism's clearest practical, real-world extension beyond academic doctrine into everyday Christian formation.

Illustration

Learning Christian doctrine, on this view, is less like memorizing a set of universal facts ("water boils at 100°C") and more like learning to speak a living language fluently — you do not "prove" French is correct to an outsider, you learn to live inside it, and its grammar only makes full sense from within the practice of speaking it.

Key Terms

  • Intratextuality: The interpretive practice of letting Scripture "absorb the world" — redescribing all of reality within the Bible's own narrative and linguistic framework, rather than translating Scripture into external categories.
  • Cultural-Linguistic Model: Lindbeck's account of religion as a comprehensive, narratively embodied culture/language, with doctrines functioning as communally authoritative grammatical rules.
  • Realistic Narrative: Hans Frei's category for biblical history: meaning is carried directly by the interplay of character and action in the story itself, prioritizing Jesus's concrete narrative identity over speculative theories about his "presence."
  • Galut (Hebrew) — "exile": The postliberal image of the Church's post-Christendom minority status, requiring Christians to learn from Judaism's long experience of faithful, non-dominant survival.

Connections

Deeply indebted to Barth's Christocentrism (Part I) and to renewed engagement with Aquinas. John Milbank, Catherine Pickstock, and Graham Ward's Radical Orthodoxy (next chapter) share its non-foundationalism but criticise its "sectarian" tendencies. Stanley Hauerwas (who also authors the H. Richard Niebuhr chapter) extends Frei's narrative Christology into virtue ethics. Peter Ochs, David Ford, and Daniel Hardy connect postliberalism to interfaith Scriptural Reasoning (Part VII).

Ch. 15 — Systematic Theology after Barth: Jüngel, Jenson, and Gunton

Chapter author: John Webster

Core Idea

Writing in the shadow of Barth's death (1968), Eberhard Jüngel, Robert Jenson, and Colin Gunton each construct a distinctively Christian, trinitarian ontology in which God's being is not a static substance but is dynamically realized in God's historical, relational self-gift in Christ.

Detailed Explanation

Jüngel, raised in the Stalinist East Germany and formed by Bultmann's existential-hermeneutical school, coined the axiom Gottes Sein ist im Werden ("God's being is in becoming") — God's identity is not fixed in advance but is realized in God's coming-to-speech and suffering on the cross. Jenson, an American Lutheran shaped by direct debate with Barth, radicalizes Barth's "actualism" (Part I) by identifying God's very triune being with the concrete temporal history of Jesus, embodied sacramentally in the Church. Gunton, an English Reformed theologian at King's College London who died suddenly during this volume's compilation, builds a relational, "perichoretic" metaphysics of the "one and the many" to protect creaturely particularity against both individualism and totalizing system.

Example

Jenson's insistence that God's triune identity is inseparable from the concrete history of Israel and Jesus, rather than a timeless metaphysical fact behind history, shapes his controversial claim that the Church's own sacramental life (baptism, Eucharist) is where that triune identity continues to be enacted in time — a claim with direct, practical consequences for how his Lutheran tradition understands sacramental real presence.

Illustration

Classical philosophical theology often pictures God like a perfect, unchanging marble statue — complete, static, admired from outside. Jüngel's "God's being is in becoming" pictures God more like a river: genuinely, identifiably the same river at every point, yet only actually existing as a living, moving, historical happening, never as a frozen block.

Key Terms

  • Entsprechungen (German) — "correspondences": Jüngel's term for the analogical correspondence between God's active, justifying grace and the human being's responsive moral action.
  • Gottes Sein ist im Werden (German) — "God's being is in becoming": Jüngel's axiom: God's being is not static substance but is dynamically realized in God's historical self-revelation and suffering.
  • Triune Identity: Jenson's radicalization of Barth's actualism: God's very being is identified with the concrete, temporal history of Jesus and its sacramental continuation in the Church.
  • Perichoretic Unity (Greek root: perichoresis, mutual indwelling): Gunton's relational, communion-based metaphysic holding together "the one and the many" without collapsing creaturely particularity into a totalizing system.

Connections

All three remain, in Webster's own framing, "theologians of revelation" continuing Barth's family of Protestant theological realism (Part I). Jenson and Gunton both reject what they see as Barth's residual Augustinianism on election. Gunton's relational ontology allies systematically with T. F. Torrance's dogmatic frame (Part II.B).

Ch. 16 — Roman Catholic Theology after Vatican II

Chapter author: Paul D. Murray

Core Idea

Vatican II (1962–65) shifted Catholic theology from a deductive, static Neo-Scholasticism into a diverse, historically conscious discipline in creative tension between revisionist/progressive correlation (the journal Concilium) and postliberal/confessional tradition-retrieval (the journal Communio).

Detailed Explanation

The Council transformed Catholicism into a genuine "world church," carrying forward the pre-conciliar nouvelle théologie (de Lubac, Part I) and transcendental Thomism (Rahner, Part I) into a newly pluriform landscape. Edward Schillebeeckx (Belgian Dominican) developed a "negative contrast experience" of suffering and injustice as a boundary-condition pointing implicitly toward God's redemptive grace, correlating tradition with contemporary social experience. Hans Küng's radical critique of papal infallibility (Infallible? An Enquiry) led Rome to revoke his teaching license in 1979 — with Rahner himself publicly criticising Küng for abandoning the Catholic "rule of faith." Nicholas Lash developed a postliberal, "grammatical" critique of church practice as a discipline of self-correcting idolatry-critique. Karol Wojtyła (Pope John Paul II), shaped by surviving Nazi occupation and Soviet repression, brought a personalist phenomenology into papal teaching against what he called the secular "culture of death."

Example

The 1979 revocation of Hans Küng's canonical mandate to teach as a Catholic theologian — following his sustained public challenge to the dogma of papal infallibility — is the clearest concrete instance in this chapter of how post-conciliar Catholic theology's new pluralism still met firm institutional limits.

Illustration

Concilium and Communio can be pictured as two siblings who grew up in the same house (pre-conciliar nouvelle théologie) but, once grown, furnish their own homes very differently: one (Concilium) keeps knocking down walls to let the neighbourhood in, the other (Communio) keeps restoring the original architecture — both insist they are being faithful to the family's true character.

Key Terms

  • Aggiornamento (Italian) — "bringing up to date": Vatican II's programmatic opening of the Church to modern values, historical-critical method, and human rights.
  • Negative Contrast Experience: Schillebeeckx's term for an experience of severe suffering or injustice that provokes immediate moral protest and implicitly points toward God's redemptive grace.
  • Koinonia (Greek) — "communion / fellowship": Vatican II's central ecclesiological paradigm (elaborated by Yves Congar), shifting the Church's self-understanding from monarchical hierarchy to sacramental communion of local churches.
  • Preferential Option for the Poor: The lens, drawn from Latin American liberation theology, adopted by much post-conciliar Catholic theology for judging economic structures and inspiring concrete acts of justice.

Connections

Rooted directly in de Lubac, Rahner, and von Balthasar (Part I). The Concilium/Communio split mirrors the wider Protestant division between Tracy's correlation and Lindbeck's postliberalism (previous chapter). Johann-Baptist Metz's "political theology," retrieving the memory of Auschwitz, directly shaped Gustavo Gutiérrez and Latin American liberation theology (Part V).

Ch. 17 — Biblical Interpretation

Chapter author: Anthony C. Thiselton

Core Idea

Thiselton traces biblical hermeneutics from Enlightenment "value-neutral" historical exegesis toward self-involving, existential, and canonical models of reading, defending a "textual realism" in which Scripture has genuine, objective, life-shaping power rather than being reducible to the reader's own projection.

Detailed Explanation

The post-Enlightenment split between historical-critical exegesis (treating the canon as a purely human, historically contingent product) and dogmatic theology suffered a crisis of confidence in WWI, prompting Barth's break with his liberal teachers (Part I) and his fresh, dialectical re-reading of Scripture "as though he had never read it before." The twentieth century then absorbed existentialism (Bultmann's use of Heidegger), the linguistic and narrative turns (Ricoeur, Wittgenstein), and Brevard Childs's "canonical" movement, which redirects attention from a text's speculative pre-history back to its final, received shape and its ongoing history of effects (Wirkungsgeschichte).

Example

James Barr's critique of "illegitimate totality transfer" — the common preacher's error of reading every historical meaning a Greek or Hebrew word ever carried, across many different passages, back into one single verse — remains a standard caution taught in seminary exegesis courses, directly traceable to this chapter's concerns about disciplined, historically responsible interpretation.

Illustration

Reading a text with real "pre-understanding" (Vorverständnis) is like tuning a radio: you cannot receive any signal at all with the dial at pure static, but you also cannot hear the actual broadcast if your own preset assumptions drown it out. Good interpretation, on this model, keeps adjusting the dial — bringing real questions to the text, but staying genuinely open to what the text itself is broadcasting back.

Key Terms

  • Vorverständnis (German) — "pre-understanding": The inevitable framework of questions and interests a reader always brings to a text — for Bultmann, the necessary starting condition for any understanding at all.
  • Canonical Context: Brevard Childs's approach directing attention to a text's final, received canonical shape and its history of effects, rather than its speculative reconstructed pre-history.
  • Logic of Self-Involvement: The view, drawn from language philosophy, that certain speech-acts and biblical texts do not merely inform but actively commit and transform the reader who receives them.
  • Illegitimate Totality Transfer: James Barr's term for the exegetical error of reading a word's whole cumulative range of historical meanings back into one specific, single occurrence.

Connections

Barth and Bultmann (Part I) represent the two great twentieth-century "theologians of the Word": Barth treats the Bible's authority as an objective "free power," Bultmann demythologizes it toward the reader's existential self-understanding. Draws heavily on Paul Ricoeur's hermeneutic of "suspicion and retrieval" and on Hans-Georg Gadamer's fusion of historical horizons, which also underlies Childs's canonical method.

Ch. 18 — Philosophical Theology

Chapter author: Ingolf U. Dalferth

Core Idea

Dalferth reframes philosophical theology as a diverse family of activities using philosophical analysis to clarify conceptual puzzles about belief in God, tracing the collapse of decontextualized natural theology under Hume's and Kant's critiques and its replacement by "recontextualized" programs grounded in the actual grammar of lived religious practice.

Detailed Explanation

Philosophical theology arose alongside seventeenth-century mechanistic science, seeking a rational theistic consensus independent of Europe's bloody post-Reformation confessional conflicts. This decontextualized "philosophical theism" collapsed under David Hume's empiricist skepticism and Immanuel Kant's refutation of speculative metaphysics in the late eighteenth century. Twentieth-century philosophical theology then had to answer logical positivism's dismissal of religious language as cognitively meaningless, increasingly giving way to a "philosophy of religion" that starts from concrete religious practice rather than abstract proofs of an abstract God.

Example

Kant's move from trying to prove God's existence to treating belief in God as a necessary postulate of practical (moral) reason — we must act as if a just, moral order underwrites reality, even though we cannot prove it theoretically — still structures how many introductory philosophy-of-religion courses frame the difference between "knowing" and "reasonably trusting" that God exists.

Illustration

Old-style natural theology tried to prove God the way a lawyer proves a case in court: marshal evidence, construct an airtight argument, force a verdict. After Hume and Kant showed the "evidence" could never be airtight, philosophical theology shifted to something more like learning a language fluently within a community that already speaks it — you come to trust and understand God-talk by living inside a tradition's practice, not by winning a courtroom argument from outside it.

Key Terms

  • Philosophical Theism: The decontextualized natural-theology project attempting to prove an abstract, omnipotent, omniscient, benevolent God using universal reason alone.
  • Critical Philosophical Theology: Kant's alternative: belief in God evaluated not as theoretical knowledge but as a necessary postulate of practical, moral reason.
  • Transcendental Theism: The idealist approach evaluating God as the necessary transcendental condition making human knowing and believing possible at all.
  • Speculative Philosophical Theology: A realist reaction to transcendental idealism treating God as the living, absolute Subject who actively integrates finite history into Godself (process/panentheist thought).

Connections

Hume and Kant supply the foundational "crisis" every subsequent philosophical theologian must navigate. Schleiermacher converted Kant's critical turn into the foundations of modern "fundamental theology." Charles Hartshorne and Whitehead's process theism (also central to the Revisionists and Liberals chapter, Part II.C) supplies the leading "speculative" alternative. Wittgenstein's linguistic philosophy underlies the modern "philosophy of religion" school (D. Z. Phillips), reading God-talk as a rule-governed practice within a language-game.

Ch. 19 — Postmodern Theology

Chapter author: Graham Ward

Core Idea

Ward distinguishes "liberal" postmodern theologies, which dissolve transcendence into a secular, nihilistic play of language, from "conservative" postmodern theologies (including his own Radical Orthodoxy), which use postmodern critique itself to retrieve premodern, liturgical, and patristic accounts of a transcendent, triune God encountered in "distance" and "alterity."

Detailed Explanation

Developed amid globalized consumer capitalism and the French "linguistic turn" (Derrida, Foucault, Lyotard), postmodern theology takes shape against the Holocaust's and Hiroshima's shattering of modernity's confidence in linear progress and rational mastery. Ward — who co-founded the British Radical Orthodoxy movement with John Milbank and Catherine Pickstock — argues postmodern deconstruction, rightly used, need not erase God but can instead open a genuinely non-foundationalist space for contemplating divine transcendence precisely through absence and distance, rather than through modernity's confident, totalizing God-concepts.

Example

Mark C. Taylor's "a/theology," celebrating the postmodern "death of God" as the final erasure of any transcendent anchor for meaning, and Radical Orthodoxy's opposite move — using the very same postmodern critique of secular reason's pretensions to re-assert a liturgical, participatory, eucharistic account of all reality — are the volume's two starkest real-world uses of identical philosophical tools toward opposite theological ends.

Illustration

Postmodern critique is like a set of tools that can be used either to demolish a house or to strip it back to sound foundations for renovation. "Liberal" postmodern theology (Taylor, Altizer) uses deconstruction to demolish transcendence altogether; "conservative" postmodern theology (Ward, Milbank, Marion) uses the very same tools to strip away modernity's own overconfident additions and rebuild on older, patristic foundations.

Key Terms

  • Rhizome: Gilles Deleuze's botanical image, adopted by Ward, for postmodern knowledge as a root-stock growing in many directions with no single centre or origin.
  • A/theology: Mark C. Taylor's radical, secularized postmodern discourse celebrating the "death of God" as erasing any transcendent anchor of meaning.
  • The Icon vs. The Idol: Jean-Luc Marion's phenomenological distinction: the idol reflects only human conceptualization back to the viewer, while the icon offers a "gift of the invisible," drawing the viewer into encounter with divine distance and kenotic love.
  • Radical Orthodoxy: The movement (Milbank, Pickstock, Ward) combining Augustinian theology, postmodern critique, and radical politics to read all creation as liturgical participation in the triune God.

Connections

Taylor, Altizer, and Winquist radicalize Tillich's and Bultmann's existentialism (Part I) into secularized "death of God" theology. Shares Lindbeck's cultural-linguistic non-foundationalism and Barth's Christological realism (Part I, Part II.D), which conservative postmodernists expand with explicit liturgical and metaphysical commitment. Jean-Luc Marion and Michel de Certeau retrieve the Greek Fathers to think a God "without Being." John Milbank and Catherine Pickstock are Ward's direct collaborators in Radical Orthodoxy, itself building on Henri de Lubac's nature-grace critique (Part I).

Ch. 20 — Theology and the Physical Sciences

Chapter author: Philip Clayton

Core Idea

Clayton argues the late-twentieth-century collapse of Newtonian reductionism (relativity, quantum uncertainty, Gödel, chaos theory) freed theology from its defensive retreat into private feeling, enabling a constructive "theology of nature" where divine action works as a transcendent, "top-down" influence in, with, and through physical processes — not as a rule-breaking intervention.

Detailed Explanation

The historical divorce of theology from natural philosophy began with the Reformers' sola scriptura and sola fides, which anchored theological certainty in the immediate human-divine relationship and effectively ceded the physical world to a secular, mechanistic account (Hobbes's "matter in motion"). Twentieth-century physics itself then dismantled deterministic reductionism from within: Einstein's relativity, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, Gödel's incompleteness theorem, and chaos theory together showed the universe is not the closed, fully-predictable machine classical physics assumed — reopening genuine conceptual space for a theology of nature.

Example

Clayton's use of Arthur Peacocke's "top-down" model — God influencing the world's overall pattern the way a mind influences a brain's neurons without violating any single neuron's own physics — has shaped how contemporary science-and-religion dialogue explains prayer and providence without requiring God to "break" a law of physics at any specific point.

Illustration

Old-style "God of the gaps" arguments treated divine action like a repairman called in only when a machine broke down — needed only where science's explanation ran out. Clayton's "top-down" panentheism instead pictures divine action more like a composer's overall shaping of a symphony's meaning and direction, present in every note without needing to override the physics of how any single instrument makes its sound.

Key Terms

  • Lumen Naturale (Latin) — "natural light": Calvin's term for reason's innate capacity to perceive God in the physical world — downgraded in Reformed theology as insufficient without the Spirit's direct salvific work.
  • Panentheism: The model in which the physical world exists "within" God while God remains eternally "more than" the world — used to explain divine action without violating physical law.
  • Emergence: The view that higher-level complex realities (life, mind, culture) have genuinely new, irreducible explanatory principles not fully captured by their lower-level physical components.
  • Decoherence: The quantum-physical theory that scale alone collapses the wave function into the single macroscopic world we observe — undercutting earlier theologies that anchored divine action directly in observer-dependent quantum collapse.

Connections

Aligns with T. F. Torrance's "scientific theology" and Pannenberg's "hypothetical realism" (Part II.A, II.B) in treating scientific rigor as a model for theological method. Draws on Arthur Peacocke's "top-down" divine action and intersects with Moltmann's ecological doctrine of creation and the Spirit (Part II.A).

Ch. 21 — Theology and the Biological Sciences

Chapter author: Celia Deane-Drummond

Core Idea

Deane-Drummond critiques the deterministic "gene myth" that reduces humanity to its genetic blueprint, proposing instead a "wisdom-based" theological ethic in which humans are relational, caring stewards in kinship with creation, not its dominating exploiters.

Detailed Explanation

Darwin's Origin of Species (1859) first challenged static natural theology by showing species emerge through natural selection and that humans are biologically continuous with other hominids; Watson and Crick's 1953 discovery of DNA's structure then triggered the modern genetic revolution — the Human Genome Project, cloning, biotechnology — forcing theology to confront urgent new pastoral, ethical, and ecological questions. Central flashpoints include animal ethics (are animals owed "theo-rights" as vulnerable creatures God entrusted to human care?), the challenge of a 98% genetic overlap with primates to traditional readings of the imago Dei, and rival visions of the earth as a single, self-regulating system (James Lovelock's "Gaia").

Example

The sharp public debate between Richard Dawkins's genetic reductionism in The Selfish Gene (humans as "survival machines" for self-replicating genes) and theologian Keith Ward's defence of purposive divine intelligence behind evolution (God, Chance and Necessity) played out in bestselling books and public lectures throughout the 1990s-2000s, making this one of the volume's most publicly visible science-theology confrontations.

Illustration

The "gene myth" treats a human being like a pre-written computer program simply executing its code. Deane-Drummond's wisdom-based alternative treats a human being more like a jazz musician who has real, given musical training (genetics) but still improvises a genuinely new, responsible performance in relationship with the other musicians (the rest of creation) — biology sets real constraints without dictating the whole performance.

Key Terms

  • Theo-rights: Andrew Linzey's concept: because God created animals vulnerable to human domestication and exploitation, they deserve moral and structural protection analogous to that owed to children.
  • Speciesism: The (originally secular) charge of giving humans automatic moral priority over other species — pressed by Peter Singer, and requiring theologians to re-examine the imago Dei in light of close human-primate genetic kinship.
  • Gaia Hypothesis: James Lovelock's model of Earth as a single, self-regulating organic system — retrieved by ecofeminists as an image of divine immanence, though its most radical form risks casting humanity as an unwanted "parasite."
  • Omega Point: Pierre Teilhard de Chardin's eschatological term for evolution's ultimate convergence point, where the cosmos's rising complexity reaches final union with God.

Connections

Engages Teilhard de Chardin's evolutionary "cosmic Christ" synthesis; Ian Barbour and John Haught's process-influenced models of creation (linked to Part II.C's Revisionists and Liberals); Moltmann's ecological Christology and John Zizioulas's Orthodox model of humanity as "priest of creation" (Part II.A, Part VI); and ecofeminists Rosemary Radford Ruether and Sallie McFague, who link patriarchal and ecological domination (paralleling the Feminism, Gender, and Theology chapter, Part V).

Ch. 22 — Theology and the Social Sciences

Chapter author: Richard H. Roberts

Core Idea

Roberts traces sociology's rise as theology's ambitious "aspirant successor" as queen of the sciences, critiques theology's defensive, self-isolating survival strategies, and proposes a "somatic" (embodied) theology reconnecting the Gospel to the real, global-local conditions of late modernity.

Detailed Explanation

Marx, Weber, and Durkheim's modern social science was built on the assumption that religion was a premodern residue to be critically explained away as humanity matured — a marginalization physically enacted when Wilhelm von Humboldt and Schleiermacher structurally separated the theology faculty from the humanities at the founding University of Berlin. Roberts situates his own proposal within the wider "crisis" of the late-twentieth-century human sciences (Husserl's Krisis, Foucault's archaeology of the "death of God and man") and a "detraditionalized" postmodern condition, arguing theology too often responds by retreating into institutionally self-protective isolation rather than genuine engagement.

Example

Roberts's sustained critique of John Milbank's Radical Orthodoxy — which he calls "postmodern quasi-fundamentalism" for entirely repudiating secular social theory as "heresy" rather than engaging real ethnographic and sociological evidence about actual human suffering — is the chapter's sharpest concrete case study in what Roberts considers theology's temptation to defensive self-isolation.

Illustration

Roberts's "somatic theology" is like insisting a doctor examine the actual patient's body rather than only consulting an old textbook diagram of an idealized body. Where much modern theology retreated into abstract, self-protecting argument (the textbook), Roberts wants theology to get back into direct, embodied contact with the real, suffering, socially-embedded human beings modern sociology actually studies.

Key Terms

  • Geisteswissenschaften (German) — "human/spiritual sciences": Wilhelm Dilthey's early-20th-century configuration of the human sciences, which Roberts notes structurally repeated theology's exclusion from the secular academic humanities.
  • Somatic Theology: Roberts's proposal for a theology of committed physical embodiment, connecting with humanity's shared, globally distributed processes of socialization rather than abstract linguistic system-building.
  • Mauvaise Foi (French) — "bad faith / false consciousness": Existentialist term Roberts applies to a theology that keeps a safe, self-protective distance from the real conflicts of the modern world purely to preserve its own institutional survival.
  • Ecclesial Supersession: Roberts's critical label for Milbank's Radical Orthodoxy: a strategy of "out-narrating" secular reason that Roberts judges a sectarian evasion of real ethnography and lived suffering.

Connections

Reviews Troeltsch and Weber's classic "church-sect" typology; treats Bonhoeffer's Sanctorum Communio and H. Richard Niebuhr's Social Sources of Denominationalism (Part I, Part II.C) as exemplary non-reductive dialogues between theology and sociology. Sharply critiques John Milbank's Radical Orthodoxy (Part II.E) and retrieves Moltmann's "dialectic of the real" (Part II.A) against theology's self-isolation.

Ch. 23 — Theology and Spirituality

Chapter author: Mark A. McIntosh

Core Idea

McIntosh addresses the modern, artificial split between theology and spirituality — for most of Christian history one indissoluble unity — arguing true theology is a sharing in God's own wisdom through contemplation, realized only through lived moral and spiritual formation, not through procedural "method" that brackets out the investigator's own person.

Detailed Explanation

British scholar Evelyn Underhill's early-twentieth-century writings first challenged William James's reduction of spiritual experience to a neutral, pre-thematic "interiority" stripped of theological content. Anselm Stolz's landmark Theology of Mysticism (Theologie der Mystik, 1937) then critiqued early-modern neoscholasticism's own separation of dogmatic theology from spiritual practice, retrieving a trinitarian dynamism in which grace is not an external scholastic cause but active participation in the Spirit's work of conforming the believer to the Son and leading them to the Father. Simone Weil's contemplative, non-possessive attentiveness and von Balthasar's Ignatian-formed "kneeling theology" (Part I) supply the movement's mature constructive expressions.

Example

Sarah Coakley's and Rowan Williams's contemporary work — showing how doctrines like the Trinity and Christology actually took shape historically within the praying, liturgical life of the early Church, not first as abstract philosophical propositions later applied to worship — puts McIntosh's whole argument into concrete historical-theological practice.

Illustration

Studying spirituality with modern "method" alone is like trying to understand what it feels like to fall in love purely by reading a chemistry textbook on hormones — you can gather real, accurate data while missing the actual thing entirely, because the phenomenon only fully discloses itself to someone personally involved in it, not to a detached outside observer.

Key Terms

  • Contemplatio (Latin) — "contemplation": A sharing in God's own wisdom, realized only within an intentional apprenticeship of moral and spiritual formation, not by detached observation.
  • Formatio (Latin) — "formation": The ancient/medieval pedagogical practice of exposing the whole of human existence to God, contrasted with modern "method," which brackets out the investigator's own subjectivity.
  • Theologia Mystica (Latin) — "mystical theology": The classical, premodern integration of prayer, liturgy, and doctrine as one single existential knowledge taught directly by God.
  • Trinitarian Dynamism: Stolz's model of grace as active participation in the unfolding trinitarian life, rather than an externally applied scholastic cause.

Connections

Takes von Balthasar's Ignatian-formed "kneeling theology" (Part I) as its primary modern exemplar. Henri de Lubac (Part I) is a fellow nouvelle théologie figure retrieving patristic resources against neoscholastic nature-grace dualism. William James's Varieties of Religious Experience serves as the chapter's negative contrast-case.

Ch. 24 — Pastoral and Practical Theology

Chapter author: Stephen Pattison and Gordon Lynch

Core Idea

Since WWII, practical theology has moved from an "applicationist" model (passing down ministerial hints and tips) to a rigorous three-way critical conversation between lived contemporary experience, theological tradition, and other academic disciplines — treating lived experience as real data able to challenge and revise received doctrine, not merely receive it.

Detailed Explanation

Anton Boisen, a mental-health chaplain whose own psychological crises led him to found the Clinical Pastoral Education movement, first urged ministers to read "living human documents" — actual lived experience treated as seriously as historic written texts. Seward Hiltner and Don Browning at Chicago then gave the field its liberal-rational academic structure: Hiltner's distinction between "operation-centered" disciplines (conclusions drawn a posteriori from practice) and "logic-centered" disciplines (systematic theology's textual/theoretical starting point), and Browning's four-stage "revised correlational method" (descriptive, historical, systematic, strategic) seeking a genuine "fusion of horizons" between practice and normative text.

Example

James Poling's and Edward Wimberly's "radical-liberationist" practical theology — incorporating power, race, and disability directly into pastoral method, rather than assuming a supposedly neutral liberal-rational starting point — shows practical theology's most concrete recent turn: pastoral care itself becomes a site of critical, not just comforting, theological work.

Illustration

The older "applicationist" model of pastoral theology worked like a cooking show: here is the finished, tested recipe (doctrine), now here is how to plate and serve it in a hospital room or a funeral home. Boisen's "living human documents" approach flips the kitchen around: the actual, specific ingredients in front of you (a real person's suffering, in all its mess) get to change the recipe itself, not just how it is served.

Key Terms

  • Living Human Documents: Boisen's category treating actual lived human experience, especially in distress, as a text as theologically rich as historic written Christian sources.
  • Operation-Centered Disciplines: Hiltner's term for theological fields (like pastoral theology) whose conclusions emerge from reflection on acts and practice, contrasted with "logic-centered" systematic theology.
  • Phronesis (Greek) — "practical wisdom": The neo-Aristotelian goal (via MacIntyre) Browning retrieves for practical theology: constructive, moral living over abstract technical or dogmatic certainty.
  • Revised Correlational Method: Browning's four-stage method (descriptive, historical, systematic, strategic) seeking a fusion of horizons between contemporary practice and normative Christian texts.

Connections

Critiques Schleiermacher's older, deductive "applicationist" model. Hiltner's and Browning's method draws directly on Tillich's correlation and David Tracy's revised correlation (Part I, Part II.C). Henri Nouwen and Thomas Oden represent a "neo-traditional confessional" reaction retrieving patristic pastoral wisdom. Moltmann's and Metz's political theology (Part II.A, II.D) directly shaped later liberationist practical theology.

Ch. 25 — Feminism, Gender, and Theology

Chapter author: Rachel Muers

Core Idea

Feminist theology exposes and disrupts the structural sin of patriarchy and the idolatry of an exclusively male God-image, insisting theology is always done from a situated, accountable standpoint — never from a neutral, ungendered viewpoint — and works to reconstruct the divine-human relation around mutuality rather than domination.

Detailed Explanation

Feminist theology grew alongside "second-wave" feminism as women gained wider access to theological education and ordained ministry in Europe and North America. It was then decisively expanded and challenged by women theologians from Africa, Asia, and Latin America, who criticised the white, middle-class bias of early Western feminist theology and insisted theological method be accountable to concrete struggles against colonial, economic, and patriarchal oppression together, not gender oppression alone. The field spans from critical retrieval of biblical and patristic resources to root-and-branch reconstruction of doctrine — the body, embodiment, and even ecology becoming central theological loci rather than marginal concerns.

Example

Mary Daly's trajectory from The Church and the Second Sex (1968), a reform-minded critique of Catholic patriarchal structures, to Beyond God the Father (1975), a full "post-Christian" rejection of the male "Sky-Patriarch-Punisher" God, is the volume's clearest real-world case of how feminist critique can move from internal reform to a decisive parting of ways with institutional Christianity altogether.

Illustration

Imagine a family photograph album where, for generations, only the fathers and sons were ever allowed to be photographed holding the family Bible — the mothers and daughters cooked the meal being blessed, but never appeared in the picture of blessing itself. Feminist theology's basic move is to ask: who has been left out of the photograph of God-language and church authority, and what happens to the picture once they are put back in?

Key Terms

  • Kyriarchy (Greek root: kyrios, lord/master): Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza's term for the interlocking system of lordship — patriarchal, colonial, and class-based domination together — showing gender is never the only axis of structured inequality.
  • Han-puri (Korean: 한풀이) — "purging of han (unresolved grief/resentment)": A Korean shamanistic ritual of telling histories of unjust, unavenged suffering, retrieved by Chung Hyun Kyung to describe the Spirit's liberating, healing work among oppressed Asian women.
  • Sensible Transcendental (French: transcendantal sensible): Luce Irigaray's concept of transcendence achieved through, not despite, concrete sexed embodiment — connected to theologies of the Incarnation.
  • Eros / Erotic Power: Carter Heyward's reclamation of the erotic as God's own creative, relational work in human relationships, against a patriarchal tradition that marginalized desire.

Connections

Critically engages Barth's and Lindbeck's Christocentric, patriarchal dogmatic frameworks (Part I, Part II.D). Critiques de Lubac's and von Balthasar's "Marian" (passive, receptive) model of the Church for relying on static gender archetypes (Part I). Sarah Coakley, Tina Beattie, and Janet Martin Soskice retrieve patristic and medieval women's piety in dialogue with Irigaray.

Ch. 26 — Black Theology of Liberation

Chapter author: Dwight N. Hopkins

Core Idea

Black theology treats faithful action in the struggle for black humanity as the first step and doctrinal reflection as a self-critical second step, locating its sources in West African heritage, the trauma of slavery, and the ongoing fight against white supremacy, and re-reading the Exodus and the Incarnation as messages of concrete liberation.

Detailed Explanation

Contemporary black theology dates programmatically to 31 July 1966, when Northern African American clergy published a "black power" statement in the New York Times validating the "black power" chant Stokely Carmichael had launched during the Meredith March. Its founding generation (James H. Cone, J. Deotis Roberts, Albert Cleage, Cecil Cone) fought a real "academic apartheid" in North American seminaries and white-controlled church structures. Since the late 1970s, later generations have pushed the field further: womanist theology (Jacqueline Grant, Delores S. Williams) named the "double" or even "multiple jeopardy" black women face across race, gender, and class simultaneously; Black Roman Catholic theologians (M. Shawn Copeland, Diana L. Hayes) have challenged both white Catholic dominance and Protestant dominance within black theology itself.

Example

James H. Cone's adaptation of Barth's Christological realism and Tillich's "ultimate concern" (both Part I) to the concrete historical experience of black oppression — arguing God is, in a real and not merely metaphorical sense, "black" because God is unconditionally on the side of the oppressed — is the discipline's founding and most contested theological move.

Illustration

Ontological blackness, as Victor Anderson criticises it, is like a single stage costume every black character in a play is required to wear regardless of who they actually are underneath — Anderson's push for a non-essentialist black identity is the demand to let each actor's own face show through, rather than requiring one fixed mask to represent an entire community.

Key Terms

  • Ontological Blackness: The essentialized, overdetermined concept of black identity constructed by white supremacy — criticised by Victor Anderson, who argues for a non-essentialist, internally diverse black identity.
  • Hoodoo / Sacred Africanity: The syncretic blend of West African traditional religion and Christian forms forged by enslaved Africans, read by Cecil Cone and Will Coleman as an authentic spiritual undercurrent of black faith.
  • Xodus: Garth Kasimu Baker-Fletcher's framework for reconstructing African American manhood beyond internalized white supremacy, in ecological, non-sexist partnership with womanist theology.
  • Dark Salutations: Riggins R. Earl Jr.'s term for stylized greetings of recognition within the black community (e.g. "brotherman," "soul sister") as a lived linguistic ethics of dignity.

Connections

Draws directly on Barth's Christological realism and Tillich's "ultimate concern" (Part I). Delores Williams and Jacqueline Grant's womanist critique parallels the broader feminist theology chapter (previous entry). Charles H. Long criticises Cone for painting "black" onto an inherited European dogmatic structure rather than starting from non-Christian African sources.

Ch. 27 — Latin American Liberation Theology

Chapter author: Rebecca S. Chopp and Ethna Regan

Core Idea

Liberation theology reconstructs the doctrines of God, sin, redemption, and church around the historical, political liberation of the poor — recognised as the active subjects, not passive objects, of history — worked out through grassroots Base Ecclesial Communities and a "preferential option for the poor."

Detailed Explanation

Emerging in the late 1960s against a backdrop of colonial economic dependency and brutal military dictatorships, the movement was catalysed by the 1968 Medellín conference of Latin American bishops, which officially committed the Catholic Church to the preferential option for the poor, and by Gustavo Gutiérrez's programmatic A Theology of Liberation (1973). It reads "liberation" as a tensive theological metaphor reframing salvation as historical and social, not merely private and spiritual, and uses Paulo Freire's conscientización (consciousness-raising pedagogy) to help the poor recognise themselves as history's active subjects rather than its passive victims. The movement paid a severe institutional and human cost: Leonardo Boff was silenced for ten months by the CDF (led by Joseph Ratzinger) in 1985, and Archbishop Óscar Romero and Jon Sobrino's fellow Jesuits were martyred in El Salvador.

Example

Leonardo Boff's account of Base Ecclesial Communities (CEBs) as a genuine "reinvention of the church" — small, lay-led, scripture-reading communities of the poor functioning with minimal clerical hierarchy — gives liberation theology's abstract claim about "the poor as subjects of history" a concrete, replicable institutional form still active across Latin America today.

Illustration

Traditional charity is like handing a hungry person a fish through a fence — the giver stays safely on one side. Liberation theology's preferential option for the poor is more like climbing over the fence and helping rebuild the pond together — it insists God's own solidarity with the poor requires structural, not just charitable, transformation.

Key Terms

  • Opción Preferencial por los Pobres (Spanish) — "preferential option for the poor": The foundational principle that God freely chooses to reveal Godself among the poor, requiring the Church's own structures and witness to align with them.
  • Conscientización (Spanish/Portuguese, from Paulo Freire) — "conscientization / consciousness-raising": The pedagogical process by which the poor critically analyse their own socio-political situation and come to see themselves as active agents of history.
  • Comunidades Eclesiais de Base (Portuguese (CEBs)) — "Base Ecclesial Communities": Small grassroots Christian communities of the poor practising contextual, lay-led faith — Boff's "ecclesiogenesis," the Church reinventing itself from below.
  • Pueblo Crucificado (Spanish) — "crucified people": Jon Sobrino's category naming Latin America's exploited and murdered poor as those who, historically, continue to bear Jesus's own passion.

Connections

Shares West German political theology's critique of the ahistorical bourgeois subject with Moltmann and Metz (Part II.A, Part II.D), though liberationists prioritise concrete praxis over academic fundamental theology. Adapts Rahner's transcendental theology of grace and "anonymous Christianity" (Part I) toward ecumenical openness to non-Christian liberation struggles. Criticised from outside by Schubert Ogden and disciplined institutionally by Joseph Ratzinger's CDF (also central to the Roman Catholic Theology after Vatican II chapter, Part II.D).

Ch. 28 — African Theology

Chapter author: Tinyiko Sam Maluleke

Core Idea

African theology is an enacted, oral, and performed practice — danced, sung, prayed — that serves local Christian communities directly rather than academic debate, seeking to free the African church from "prefabricated" Western dogma and become truly indigenous.

Detailed Explanation

Written African theology emerged through ecumenical consultations in the 1950s, historically split between "African theology" (cultural inculturation, chiefly north of the Limpopo) and "South African black theology" (political-economic liberation under apartheid) — agendas that have since increasingly converged. The Kairos Document (1985), a prophetic theological challenge to apartheid-era church silence, and the post-Cold War rise of "theology of reconstruction" (moving from reactive critique toward constructive engagement with democracy and nation-building) mark two major turning points. Throughout, the underlying communal ethic ubuntu — "I am because we are" — supplies much of the discipline's philosophical grammar.

Example

The Kairos Document (1985), signed by South African theologians during the apartheid state of emergency, publicly named "state theology" and even much "church theology" as complicit with injustice, and called instead for a "prophetic theology" of direct resistance — a concrete instance of African theology functioning as urgent, enacted political intervention rather than academic reflection.

Illustration

Prefabricated housing looks like a real house from outside but was designed elsewhere, for a different climate and family, then simply shipped in and assembled. Maluleke's complaint about "prefabricated" Western dogma is exactly this: a theology designed for Europe's questions and climate, assembled in Africa without being grown from African soil — African theology's task is to grow a house that actually fits the ground it stands on.

Key Terms

  • Translation Theologies: Lamin Sanneh and Kwame Bediako's thesis that African Christianity's explosive growth is explained by the Gospel's translatability into vernacular languages, letting it speak in its own right rather than through a colonial tongue.
  • Theology of Reconstruction: A post-Cold War paradigm (Jesse Mugambi, Charles Villa-Vicencio) urging proactive engagement with democracy, human rights, and nation-building, beyond reactive inculturation or liberation.
  • Ubuntu (Zulu/Xhosa) — "communal personhood": "I am because we are": the traditional communal ethic underlying much contemporary African and South African theological reflection.
  • Enacted / Narrative Theology: The conviction that oral, performed theology — prayer, drumbeat, lived grassroots witness — is theology in its own right, not merely raw material awaiting academic systematization.

Connections

Challenges Barth's sharp faith/religion polarity (Part I), insisting African traditional religions be treated as genuine theological interlocutors. Engages John Mbiti in a foundational debate over what "African theology" even means. Intersects with the feminist Circle of Concerned African Women Theologians (Mercy Amba Oduyoye) and adapts James Cone's black-power hermeneutics (previous chapter) to the South African context.

Ch. 29 — Theologies of South Asia

Chapter author: Felix Wilfred

Core Idea

South Asian theology is a contextual, interreligious discipline privileging space (the concrete social and cultural context) over abstract linear history, developing through active "core-to-core" dialogue with Hindu, Buddhist, and Islamic traditions and through Dalit theology's confrontation with caste hegemony.

Detailed Explanation

Christians are a small minority across South Asia's vast multi-religious landscape. The Church of South India's 1947 union of Anglican, Methodist, Congregationalist, and Presbyterian traditions offered an early ecumenical model responding to national independence movements; Sri Lanka's 1971 youth revolt briefly united Christians, Buddhists, and Marxists in common struggle; ongoing persecution (Pakistan's blasphemy laws, Bishop John Joseph's 1998 protest suicide) and the martyrdom of Michael Rodrigo for grassroots interreligious work mark the discipline's real costs. Dalit theology, developed against caste discrimination, deliberately reads the suffering of Jesus through the historical experience of India's "crushed" outcastes, rejecting theologies adapted from classical, caste-structured Hinduism.

Example

Aloysius Pieris's "core-to-core dialogue" — going beyond comparing religious concepts to seeking an actual, mutually transforming meeting between Christian agape (self-giving love) and Buddhist gnosis (liberating wisdom) — has shaped concrete interreligious monastic and ashram communities across South and Southeast Asia that practice, not just theorize, this encounter.

Illustration

Comparing religions at the level of doctrine alone is like comparing two rivers only by looking at maps of where they are drawn — you learn their shape but never get wet. "Core-to-core dialogue" insists on actually stepping into both rivers, letting each tradition's deepest current — Christian love, Buddhist wisdom — genuinely touch and change the other, not just be mapped side by side.

Key Terms

  • Cosmotheandric Vision: Raimon Panikkar's holistic framework integrating the cosmic, divine, and human dimensions of reality as radically interrelated, not separable.
  • Dalit Theology (Sanskrit/Marathi: dalit) — "crushed / broken": A contextual theology reading the Gospel and Christ's suffering through the historical experience of caste-oppressed "outcastes," rejecting theologies borrowed from caste Hinduism.
  • Core-to-Core Dialogue: Aloysius Pieris's method of interreligious engagement seeking mutual, symbiotic transformation between traditions, not merely conceptual comparison.
  • Dialogue of Everyday Life: A theology of religions starting from concrete daily relationships among ordinary believers of different faiths, rather than from abstract doctrinal deduction.

Connections

Sebastian Kappen, Samuel Rayan, and M. M. Thomas combine socialist commitment to the poor with critique of both caste hegemony and institutional Christianity. Adapts and criticises Tillich's correlation and Tracy's revised correlation (Part I, Part II.C) as too Western in scope. Jacques Dupuis adapted Rahner's transcendental openness (Part I) into a pluralistic theology of religions that provoked controversy in Rome — directly continuing the Roman Catholic Theology after Vatican II chapter's themes (Part II.D).

Ch. 30 — Contextual Theology in East Asia

Chapter author: Archie Chi Chung Lee

Core Idea

East Asian theology develops a "cross-textual hermeneutics," reading East Asian cultural, literary, and religious texts alongside the Bible as equally active sources, rejecting Western binary and "Germanic captive" modes of thought in favour of frameworks rooted in Confucian, Buddhist, and shamanistic heritage.

Detailed Explanation

Formed through severe twentieth-century crises — the Opium Wars' humiliation, Japanese colonization of Korea (1910-45) and Taiwan (1895-1945), Korea's division, China's 1949 communist takeover and Cultural Revolution (1966-76), and Hong Kong's 1997 handover — East Asian theology channels historical trauma directly into theological method. Korean minjung ("the people") theology centres the collective, unjust suffering (han) of history's exploited masses, while Kazoh Kitamori's Theology of the Pain of God (1946) uses the Japanese Buddhist-influenced concept of tsurasa (redemptive pain born of love) to describe how God's love overcomes divine wrath at the cross.

Example

Wang Weifan's "life-birthing God" (sheng sheng), drawn from the ancient Chinese Yijing (Book of Change), pictures God not as a static, distant substance but as an ever-generating life-force continuously giving birth to, sustaining, and protecting creation — offering Chinese Christians a genuinely indigenous doctrine of God rather than a translated Western one.

Illustration

Cross-textual hermeneutics works like a bilingual conversation between two equally fluent speakers rather than a translator quietly converting everything into just one language. The Bible speaks, and the Asian cultural text (a Confucian classic, a shamanistic ritual, the Yijing) speaks back as an equal partner — neither is simply reduced to explaining or confirming the other.

Key Terms

  • Cross-Textual Hermeneutics: Archie Lee's method of reading an Asian cultural/literary text and the biblical text in active, mutually critical dialogue, generating new postcolonial meaning.
  • Han (Korean: 한/恨): Deep-seated collective grief and indignation from unjust suffering — the central category of Korean minjung theology.
  • Sheng Sheng (Chinese: 生生) — "ever-generating / life-birthing": Wang Weifan's model of God, drawn from the Yijing, as an unceasing life-force rather than a static substance.
  • Minjung (Korean: 민중/民衆) — "the people / the masses": The oppressed, marginalized subjects of history whose collective social biography is the locus of Korean minjung theology.
  • Tsurasa (Japanese: つらさ/辛さ) — "pain / hardship": Kazoh Kitamori's Buddhist-influenced concept of redemptive pain born of love, explaining how God's love overcomes wrath at the cross.

Connections

Minjung theologians reject Barth's Pauline Christ-kerygma in favour of the historical Jesus and the people's own social biography (Part I). C. S. Song and Kosuke Koyama adapt Tillich's correlation (Part I) using local "buffalo-eye" stories rather than Western philosophical categories. John B. Cobb's process theology (drawing on Mahayana Buddhist sunyata and anatman) is a key Western dialogue partner.

Ch. 31 — Postcolonial Biblical Interpretation

Chapter author: R. S. Sugirtharajah

Core Idea

Postcolonial biblical interpretation places colonialism and globalization at the centre of biblical studies, exposing how supposedly neutral historical-critical scholarship and Bible translation were historically mobilized in service of imperial and missionary expansion, and recovering suppressed subaltern voices and readings.

Detailed Explanation

Sugirtharajah, a Sri Lankan scholar at the University of Birmingham, introduced postcolonial criticism into biblical studies in a landmark 1996 article, drawing on postcolonial literary theorists (Edward Said, Gayatri Spivak, Homi Bhabha) and passing through heritagist, liberationist, and dissentient phases shaped by geopolitical partition and decolonization (the 1947 founding of Israel, the 1967 war, African and Australian colonization). Its central move is refusing the claim that historical-critical exegesis is neutral or value-free, showing instead how it has often quietly served imperial interests.

Example

Sugirtharajah's critique of Joachim Jeremias's classic study of Jesus's parables — showing how its scholarly apparatus imports "Orientalist" assumptions about a static, exotic Middle East — demonstrates postcolonial method concretely: even celebrated, mainstream biblical scholarship can carry unexamined imperial assumptions.

Illustration

Reading a colonial-era map of Africa that names rivers and mountains only after European explorers, as though no one had ever lived there or named them before, hides an entire history under a single layer of paint. Postcolonial biblical interpretation does the same work on the biblical text and its scholarship: scraping back the "explorer's" layer of names and assumptions to recover who and what was already there.

Key Terms

  • Orientalism: Edward Said's term for a Western discourse of power that flattens the "Other" into fixed, exotic stereotypes in order to dominate and control it.
  • Hybridity / Mimicry: Homi Bhabha's terms for the unstable, creative in-between spaces where colonizer and colonized cultures interact, destabilizing simple binary oppositions.
  • Subaltern (from Latin/English: of lower rank): The colonized or marginalized "Other" whose voice has been silenced or spoken for by others — postcolonial reading works to recover it directly.
  • Nativism: The strategy of reclaiming indigenous, pre-colonial traditions (e.g. Setswana ancestral Badimo) to resist and subvert colonial translations and categories.

Connections

Shares Lindbeck's non-foundationalist interest in the biblical text (Part II.D) but radically challenges his "intratextual" confidence, insisting the text itself carries imperial and patriarchal violence needing critique, not just inhabiting. Musa Dube extends postcolonial feminist interpretation from Botswana. Challenges John Hick's pluralism and Gavin D'Costa's theology of religions (Part VII) as too abstract, ignoring real political and economic power.

Ch. 32 — Ecumenical Theology

Chapter author: Mary Tanner

Core Idea

Ecumenical theology moved from comparing denominational differences to a "consensus/convergence" method retrieving shared biblical and patristic heritage, discovering churches already share a "real though imperfect communion" grounded in the Trinity's own relational life.

Detailed Explanation

Rooted in early-twentieth-century missionary cooperation (Edinburgh 1910), the movement split into Faith and Order (doctrinal unity, Lausanne 1927) and Life and Work (practical social action, Stockholm 1925), merging into the World Council of Churches in 1948. Roman Catholic participation intensified after Vatican II's Unitatis Redintegratio (1964, Part V's Ecclesiology material). Landmark convergence texts include Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (BEM, 1982) and the Lutheran-Catholic Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999). The Santiago Conference (1993) made koinonia (communion) the central biblical paradigm, grounding church unity directly in the Trinity's relational life rather than in institutional uniformity.

Example
