The 1999 Lutheran-Catholic Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification formally resolved a doctrinal dispute dating to the sixteenth-century Reformation, declaring the two traditions' historic condemnations of each other on justification no longer applied — the clearest concrete achievement of the whole consensus method this chapter describes.

Illustration

The old "comparative method" was like two families each insisting their own family recipe for a dish was the only correct one. The "consensus/convergence method" is like both families going back together to find the original grandmother's recipe both versions actually descended from — discovering a shared root deeper than their more recent differences.

Key Terms

  • Anamnesis (Greek: ἀνάμνησις) — "memorial": The biblical concept used in BEM to resolve eucharistic disputes: the Eucharist is not a repetition of Christ's sacrifice but a dynamic, present realization of its benefits.
  • Koinonia (Greek: κοινωνία) — "communion": The central paradigm (Santiago 1993) grounding church unity in the relational, triune life of God rather than hierarchical or competitive structures.
  • Reconciled Diversity: A model of unity where denominations achieve full visible communion while remaining distinct, recognizable bodies — plural fellowship over structural merger.
  • Oikoumene (Greek: οἰκουμένη) — "the whole inhabited world": Konrad Raiser's term shifting ecumenical theology's starting point from narrow church history to the whole "household of life" God sustains.

Connections

Barth participated directly in the WCC's founding (Amsterdam 1948, Part I). John Zizioulas's Orthodox trinitarian pneumatology (next chapter) shaped the Canberra (1991) and Santiago (1993) turns to koinonia. Moltmann's and Boff's "social Trinity" (Part II.A, Part V) underpinned the WCC's trinitarian panentheism. Chung Hyun Kyung's controversial 1991 Canberra presentation (Part V) dramatized the tension between patristic tradition and radical contextual hermeneutics within the ecumenical movement itself.

Ch. 33 — Eastern Orthodox Theology

Chapter author: Rowan Williams

Core Idea

Twentieth-century Orthodox theology recovers the patristic and Byzantine heritage — apophaticism, relational ontology, eucharistic ecclesiology — presenting God's being as a relational communion of love and true knowledge of God as contemplative participation (theosis) in the divine energies, not rationalistic mastery.

Detailed Explanation

The 1917 Russian Revolution's expulsion of intellectuals made Paris, and specifically the Institut Saint-Serge (founded 1925), the centre of Orthodox theological revival. Émigré theologians split into two camps: Sergei Bulgakov's "Sophianic" school, pursuing a speculative, romantic-idealist metaphysics of divine wisdom, and Vladimir Lossky's and Georges Florovsky's "Neopatristic synthesis," seeking a rigorous return to the Greek Fathers and Gregory Palamas's essence-energies distinction. Rowan Williams, a leading Western scholar of this tradition (and later Archbishop of Canterbury), traces how it moved Orthodox theology from abstract school-theology toward presenting the Church itself as the living, sacramental image of the Trinity.

Example

Vladimir Lossky's insistence that theology is completed not in a system of correct propositions but in ekstasis — the contemplative "shock" of encountering the unmasterable living God — concretely shapes Orthodox liturgical practice, where icons and apophatic (negative) theological language deliberately resist offering a fully graspable, controllable picture of God.

Illustration

Western scholastic theology often works like assembling a complete, correctly-labelled model of God from available parts. Lossky's apophatic Orthodoxy works more like standing before a brilliant light so bright you cannot look directly at it — you know something real and overwhelming is there precisely because ordinary sight fails, not despite it.

Key Terms

  • Sobornost (Russian: соборность) — "conciliarity / organic unity-in-diversity": The communal unity by which the Church, through the Spirit's eucharistic gathering, becomes the living image of the Trinity, overcoming individualist isolation.
  • Bogochelovechestvo (Russian: богочеловечество) — "divine humanity / Godmanhood": Soloviev's and Bulgakov's term for the cosmic process by which the Incarnation reconciles and deifies human personality and the material cosmos.
  • Ekstasis (Greek: ἔκστασις) — "ecstasy / stepping-out": In Lossky's apophatic theology, the contemplative self-transcendence by which the believer is "shocked" past conceptual control into encounter with the living God.
  • Podvig (Russian: подвиг) — "ascetic struggle / achievement": Florovsky's category for Christ's history as a concrete, free ascetic triumph over mortality and sin, not a static metaphysical state.

Connections

Florovsky's 1931 debate with Barth (Part I) sharpened his insistence on revelation's historical priority. Lossky maintained close ties with de Lubac and the nouvelle théologie (Part I). Von Balthasar (Part I) is the closest Western analogue to Bulgakov's dramatic, kenotic trinitarian theology. Moltmann (Part II.A) explicitly incorporated the Cappadocian "social trinitarianism" John Zizioulas synthesized from this tradition.

Ch. 34 — Pentecostal and Charismatic Theology

Chapter author: Allan Anderson

Core Idea

Pentecostal/Charismatic theology centres on a direct, personal encounter with the Holy Spirit, expressed as "narrative and oral" theology of praise and healing rather than scholastic dogma, expecting the New Testament's apostolic gifts (tongues, prophecy, healing) to be present realities today ("restorationism").

Detailed Explanation

Pentecostalism began with the Azusa Street Revival (1906-08) in Los Angeles, led by African American preacher William J. Seymour, emerging from nineteenth-century Holiness/Sanctification movements. Three historical phases followed: Classical Pentecostalism (1901-1920s, e.g. Assemblies of God), the Charismatic Movement entering mainline Protestant and Catholic churches from 1960, and the "Third Wave" of independent, non-denominational megachurches since 1975 — now Christianity's fastest-growing global sector. Theologically, salvation is organized around the "fivefold gospel": Jesus as Saviour, Sanctifier, Baptizer in the Spirit, Healer, and soon-Coming King.

Example

David Yonggi Cho's Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul — the world's single largest congregation, built on a "theology of prosperity" and small home-cell groups — is the clearest concrete instance of Pentecostalism's explosive, indigenized global growth outside its North American origins.

Illustration

If much academic systematic theology reads like a carefully argued written brief, Pentecostal theology is closer to a live musical performance: the "text" is as much sung, prayed, and enacted in the moment as it is argued on a page, and its truth is confirmed by what happens (healing, tongues, transformed lives) as much as by what is logically demonstrated.

Key Terms

  • Baptism in the Holy Spirit: The distinct, post-conversion experience of spiritual empowerment, linked by classical Pentecostals to speaking in tongues as initial evidence.
  • Fivefold Gospel: Pentecostalism's core Christology: Jesus as Saviour, Sanctifier, Baptizer in the Spirit, Healer, and Coming King.
  • Restorationism: The conviction that the contemporary Church should "restore" the apostolic purity and charismatic power of the first-century Church.
  • Moya (Shona/Zulu) — "spirit / breath": African contextual pneumatology integrating the Holy Spirit with traditional concepts of vital force and ancestral healing.

Connections

Pentecostal scholars like Gordon Fee engage Barth's neo-orthodoxy (Part I) directly through Luke-Acts exegesis to defend Spirit-baptism as distinct from conversion. Walter Hollenweger's sociological research mapped Pentecostalism's non-Western, oral roots against Eurocentric academic norms. Chung Hyun Kyung's Canberra pneumatology (Part V, Part VI's Ecumenical chapter) intersected with, and was debated within, global Charismatic circles.

Ch. 35 — Evangelical Theology

Chapter author: David F. Wells

Core Idea

Evangelical theology is organized around sola scriptura (Scripture as reality's normative interpretive framework) and solus Christus (atonement as penal substitution), asserting the transcendent God has objectively revealed Godself in history and requires personal conversion and active global evangelization, against both liberal relativism and sacramental clericalism.

Detailed Explanation

Emerging from the early-twentieth-century fundamentalist-modernist controversy, post-WWII "neo-evangelicalism" built serious scholarly infrastructure (Tyndale House, Cambridge) and multi-volume systematic theologies (Carl F. H. Henry, Millard Erickson). The movement organized itself globally and non-hierarchically through the 1974 Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization, producing the Lausanne Covenant (drafted by John Stott) to coordinate theology, social responsibility, and mission across denominations and nations. The 1978 Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy, co-led by J. I. Packer, gave the movement's commitment to Scripture's total truthfulness its classic formal statement.

Example

David Wells's own trilogy (No Place for Truth, 1993; God in the Wasteland, 1994; Above All Earthly Pow'rs, 2004) argues that consumerism and therapeutic psychology, not liberal theology alone, have quietly eroded Evangelicalism's confidence in objective truth from within — a sustained cultural diagnosis that shaped Evangelical seminary curricula across North America.

Illustration

If liberal revisionist theology (Part II.C) treats modern culture as a genuine conversation partner reshaping the tradition, classical Evangelical theology treats Scripture more like a fixed, load-bearing wall in a house: culture can renovate many rooms, but this wall itself is never up for structural renegotiation.

Key Terms

  • Penal Substitution: The atonement model in which Christ voluntarily bears the divine wrath and penalty due to human sin, satisfying God's holy justice on the cross.
  • Biblical Inerrancy: The conviction, formalized in the 1978 Chicago Statement, that Scripture is wholly truthful and without error in all it affirms.
  • Wesleyan Quadrilateral: A method coordinating Scripture, tradition, reason, and experience, with Scripture retained as the primary norm — associated with Evangelicalism's Wesleyan wing.
  • Evangelization: The urgent task of proclaiming the Gospel to prompt personal conversion, distinguished by classical Evangelicals from purely secular humanitarian development.

Connections

Carl Henry and G. C. Berkouwer engaged Barth (Part I) for decades, praising his Christocentrism while rejecting his refusal to simply identify the biblical text with the objective Word of God. John Hick's turn from Evangelical faith to religious pluralism (Part VII) served as Evangelicalism's key negative contrast-case. Thomas Oden's patristic retrieval parallels the neo-traditional reaction in Pastoral and Practical Theology (Part IV).

Ch. 36 — Theology of Religions

Chapter author: Gavin D'Costa

Core Idea

D'Costa maps the classic pluralism/inclusivism/exclusivism typology for Christian responses to religious diversity, argues all three are ultimately variants of a single underlying exclusivism, and proposes a return to explicitly trinitarian theology of religions that holds difference and commonality together without dissolving either into an abstract, secularized pluralism.

Detailed Explanation

Pluralism (all religions are equally valid paths to "the Real"; Christ is one relative revelation among many), inclusivism (Christ is the definitive revelation, but grace works causally within other religions too), and exclusivism (salvation requires explicit faith in Christ, mediated through gospel and baptism) organized most twentieth-century Christian thinking about other faiths. D'Costa, an Indian Roman Catholic theologian and consultant to the Pontifical Commission for Interreligious Dialogue, controversially argues pluralism is not neutral at all but its own kind of "exclusivist secular agnosticism" — an intolerant ideology that quietly controls the public sphere by reducing every religion to equivalent private opinion.

Example

D'Costa's critique that John Hick's pluralism functions as a hidden new orthodoxy — requiring every religion to accept, in advance, that its own most particular and exclusive truth-claims are merely mythical — plays out concretely whenever interfaith dialogue events implicitly require participants to bracket exactly the convictions (like the unique divinity of Christ) that matter most to them.

Illustration

Pluralism presents itself like a referee who claims to be entirely neutral between all the teams on the field — but D'Costa's point is that a referee who insists no team is allowed to actually win, or that every goal must count exactly the same regardless of the game each team thinks it's playing, has already imposed a very particular (and disputable) rule of its own.

Key Terms

  • Pluralism: The view that all religions are equally valid paths to one divine Reality, with Christ as one relative revelation among many.
  • Inclusivism: Christ as the normative, definitive revelation, while grace is nonetheless causally active within other religions.
  • Exclusivism: Salvation tied strictly to explicit faith in Christ, mediated through hearing the Gospel and baptism.
  • Exclusivist Secular Agnosticism: D'Costa's critical label for pluralism itself, which he argues functions as its own intolerant orthodoxy despite claiming neutrality.

Connections

Rahner's inclusivist "anonymous Christianity" (Part I) is D'Costa's primary dialogue partner, though he seeks a more explicitly trinitarian alternative. John Hick is his chief target of critique. Aloysius Pieris (Part V) represents a liberationist, socially engaged approach prioritizing justice over doctrine. George Lindbeck's postliberalism (Part II.D) informs D'Costa's stress on Christianity's irreducible particularity.

Ch. 37 — Judaism and Christian Theology

Chapter author: Peter Ochs

Core Idea

Ochs maps the post-Shoah recovery of Christian theology's relationship to Judaism, promoting "non-supersessionism" — the conviction that God's covenant with Israel remains permanent and unrevoked — and "scriptural reasoning," a tripartite reading practice linking any Christian doctrine back to its grounding in Israel's own story.

Detailed Explanation

The catastrophe of the Shoah drove Jewish and Christian theologians alike to repent of centuries of Christian anti-Judaic theology, including the traditional "supersessionist" claim that the Church simply replaced Israel in God's plan. Ochs co-authored the landmark 2001 Jewish statement on Christianity, Dabru Emet ("speak the truth"), and champions "scriptural reasoning" — reading a doctrine simultaneously through an Old Testament text, a Gospel text, and a community's own lived situation — as a method that keeps Christology rooted in Israel's ongoing story rather than floating free of it.

Example

Robert Jenson's argument that the risen Christ remains, permanently, "the risen Jew" — so that Christ's own concrete Jewish identity is not incidental but theologically load-bearing — gives non-supersessionism a sharply concrete Christological form rather than leaving it as an abstract ethical commitment about tolerance.

Illustration

Supersessionism pictured Israel's covenant like an old, cancelled contract, fully replaced by a new one. Non-supersessionism insists it is more like an original, still-valid contract that a second, related agreement (the New Covenant) has joined and extended, not torn up — both remain binding and real, read together rather than one erasing the other.

Key Terms

  • Non-Supersessionism: The conviction that God's covenant with Israel is permanent and enduring, rejecting the traditional claim that the Church has replaced Israel in salvation history.
  • Tripartite Reading: A postliberal hermeneutical practice reading any doctrine through an Old Testament text, a Gospel text, and a community's lived context together.
  • Jeremianic Turn: John Howard Yoder's category for early rabbinic Judaism's shift (modeled on Jeremiah 29) toward pacifist, landless exilic existence, taken as a model for Anabaptist ecclesiology.
  • Shalom: Kendall Soulen's eschatological model: God's final redemption does not erase the difference between Israel and the nations but brings them into mutual, interdependent blessing.

Connections

Barth's Christocentrism (Part I) once called the synagogue "idolatrous," yet his own scriptural obedience forced him to affirm Israel's enduring election — a "Barthian-yet-post-Barthian" foundation later German non-supersessionists built on. George Lindbeck (Part II.D) links healing the Jewish-Christian schism to Catholic-Protestant reconciliation itself. John Milbank (Part II.E) rejects tripartite reading as anachronistic, which postliberals read as a return to supersessionism.

Ch. 38 — Islam and Christian Theology

Chapter author: Ataullah Siddiqui

Core Idea

Siddiqui traces Christian theology's engagement with Islam from confrontational missiology toward collaborative dialogue, arguing a genuine theology of religions must be grounded in the postcolonial reality of Christians and Muslims as literal neighbours, not an academic abstraction.

Detailed Explanation

Large-scale postcolonial migration created genuinely multi-religious European neighbourhoods, turning Christian-Muslim dialogue from an academic luxury into an urgent pastoral and political necessity. Karl Rahner's description of Islam as a "concrete monotheism" — a real, valid adoration of the one God, though lacking trinitarian differentiation — helped open Vatican II's own more positive posture in Nostra Aetate and Lumen Gentium toward Islamic monotheism, Mary, and the shared hope of the Day of Judgement. Kenneth Cragg's The Event of the Quran reshaped Christian scholarship by treating the Quran as a literary-historical event and taking Muhammad's character and achievement seriously on its own terms rather than through inherited polemic.

Example

The 1954 Bhamdoun Consultation in Lebanon, where Muslims and Christians first formally organized to resist the joint expulsion of religion and moral values from modern public life, is the chapter's clearest concrete instance of interfaith cooperation moving from private theological reflection into organized public action.

Illustration

Keith Ward's proposal that Christians who already accept the Hebrew Bible as divinely inspired (theopneustos, "God-breathed") should logically be open to recognizing a comparable inspired status for the Quran works like extending a courtesy you already extend to one older sibling's writing to a younger sibling's writing on the same grounds — consistency, not compromise, is the argument's own logic.

Key Terms

  • Concrete Monotheism: Rahner's term for Islamic monotheism: a real, valid adoration of the one God, though without trinitarian differentiation.
  • Cragg's Corner: Siddiqui's term for the conceptual meeting-place Kenneth Cragg established by treating the Quran as a literary-historical event worthy of serious Christian engagement.
  • Theopneustos (Greek) — "God-breathed / divinely inspired": Keith Ward's category, applied by extension to the Quran given Christians already grant it to the Hebrew Bible.
  • Bhamdoun Consultation: The 1954 Lebanon gathering where Muslims and Christians first organized jointly to resist religion's expulsion from public life.

Connections

Barth and Emil Brunner (Part I) represent early neo-orthodox resistance, rejecting Islamic monotheism as a merely human "religion." Hans Küng's "global ethics" project (Part II.D) became a major dialogical bridge. Rahner's transcendental inclusivism (Part I) directly underpinned Nostra Aetate and Lumen Gentium's positive posture toward Islam. Keith Ward and John Hick (this Part, previous chapter) represent the pluralist transition Siddiqui situates this dialogue against.

Ch. 39 — Buddhism and Christian Theology

Chapter author: Paul O. Ingram

Core Idea

Ingram traces Christian-Buddhist engagement from competing claims to salvation toward "mutual creative transformation," in which conceptual, socially engaged, and contemplative "interior" dialogue reshape Christian understandings of selfhood, ultimate reality, and even the Trinity, revealing wisdom and love as interdependent practices of liberation in both traditions.

Detailed Explanation

Catalyzed by the 1980 East-West Religions in Encounter conference in Hawaii and the founding of the Society for Buddhist-Christian Studies, the dialogue runs on several tracks at once: John B. Cobb's process-theological "creative transformation" (Christians temporarily indwelling Buddhist concepts before returning home changed); Lynn de Silva's retrieval of Buddhist "non-self" (anatta/anatman) to show the biblical self, too, is an interdependent psychophysical unity rather than a static Greek-style immortal soul; and Raimon Panikkar's contemplative "interior dialogue," seeking ultimate reality beyond either tradition's conceptual boundaries altogether.

Example

Thomas Merton's and Paul Knitter's "socially engaged dialogue," grounding Buddhist-Christian encounter directly in the preferential option for the poor (Part V), shows Buddhist wisdom (prajna) and Christian love (agape) converging in shared practical action, not just shared philosophical concepts — most visibly in Merton's own late-life monastic dialogue with Buddhist teachers before his death in Thailand in 1968.

Illustration

"Creative transformation" works like a musician who spends real time immersed in an entirely different musical tradition — not merely borrowing a few exotic notes, but coming home changed, playing their own tradition's music with a genuinely new depth they could not have reached by staying only within their original training.

Key Terms

  • Creative Transformation: John B. Cobb's process-theological method: Christians indwell Buddhist concepts and return "creatively transformed," with Christ as the ultimate image of this relational process.
  • Anatta / Anatman (Pali / Sanskrit) — "non-self": The Buddhist doctrine of the shifting, non-substantial self, used by Lynn de Silva to argue the biblical self is likewise an interdependent psychophysical unity, not a static soul.
  • Interior Dialogue: Raimon Panikkar's contemplative, monastic method of seeking ultimate reality beyond either tradition's own conceptual and dogmatic boundaries.
  • Sunyata (Sanskrit) — "emptiness": The Mahayana Buddhist concept of ultimate reality as absolute emptiness, used by John P. Keenan to construct a Mahayana-Buddhist reading of Mark's Gospel.

Connections

Tillich (Part I) held a landmark dialogue with Zen master Shin'ichi Hisamatsu; Moltmann (Part II.A) integrated Buddhist-influenced ecological and co-suffering themes into his creation theology. Rahner's "anonymous Christianity" and Küng's view of Buddhism as an "extraordinary way of salvation" (Part I, Part II.D) are respected but criticised here for treating Buddhism as mere preparation for the Gospel rather than a valid path in its own right.

Ch. 40 — Theology and the Visual Arts

Chapter author: John W. de Gruchy

Core Idea

De Gruchy argues the visual arts are intrinsic to theology itself, not peripheral illustration, uniquely able to awaken human sensibility to reality's "tragic ugliness and transforming beauty" and to expand understanding of the Incarnation, representation, and social transformation.

Detailed Explanation

Shaped by South Africa's anti-apartheid struggle, de Gruchy traces a growing twentieth-century dialogue: from P. T. Forsyth's early lectures on the Pre-Raphaelites, through Bishop George Bell's wartime partnership with secular artists and Paul Tillich's major influence on American art academies, to the late-century rise of postcolonial, feminist, and liberationist art. He grounds visual art theologically in the eighth-century Iconoclastic Controversy's resolution: because the Incarnation is real (God genuinely took visible, material flesh), producing physical images of Christ is not idolatry but a legitimate theological consequence of what Christians actually believe happened.

Example

Rahner's argument that theology remains incomplete until it treats the non-verbal arts as an "intrinsic moment" of its own life directly inspired de Gruchy's whole thesis — a concrete instance of one chapter's theologian (Part I) supplying the theoretical foundation for another discipline's method decades later.

Illustration

Treating visual art as mere "illustration" of theology already settled in words is like treating a wedding photograph as just a decoration for a marriage certificate — it misses that the image itself can capture and communicate something true about the event that the legal document alone cannot.

Key Terms

  • Icon (Greek: eikōn) — "image": A sacred image whose theological legitimacy the iconophiles grounded directly in the Incarnation: because God took visible flesh, physical images of Christ are theologically warranted, not idolatrous.
  • Kitsch: Banal, sentimentalized art lacking real aesthetic and spiritual integrity, contrasted by de Gruchy with genuine "good art."
  • Embodiment: The material, physical manifestation of an artist's vision, read as a theological analogue for the Incarnation and the sacramental character of physical reality.
  • Aesthetic Judgment: The collaborative, cross-cultural practice of evaluating beauty and taste across diverse postcolonial encounters, rather than treating art merely as a pedagogical tool.

Connections

Directly inspired by Rahner's claim that theology needs the non-verbal arts (Part I). Barth and Bonhoeffer's Reformed image-suspicion (Part I) is shown to hold latent resources for visual art despite itself. Von Balthasar's Glory of the Lord (Part I) put theological aesthetics on the academic map, though de Gruchy criticises him for fitting art too rigidly into Catholic dogmatic categories.

Ch. 41 — Theology and Music

Chapter author: Jeremy S. Begbie

Core Idea

Begbie proposes "theology through music": treating musical practice itself as a medium of genuine theological discovery, grounded in creation out of nothing and the Incarnation, where music's own "sonic order" lets physical reality voice its own praise, and musical patterns of tension, waiting, and simultaneous harmony offer real conceptual models for eschatology and Trinity.

Detailed Explanation

Despite deep historical roots in Augustine, Luther, and Calvin, music had been conspicuously excluded from modern systematic theology in favour of literature and the visual arts — an absence Begbie's "Theology Through the Arts" project at Cambridge sought to correct. He retrieves Albert Blackwell's typology of "Pythagorean" (intellectual-mathematical) and "Incarnational" (sensed, material) musical traditions, and studies Barth's and Bonhoeffer's own deeply personal musical lives as unexpectedly rich theological resources.

Example

Bonhoeffer's own prison letters retrieve the musical technique of cantus firmus (a fixed, foundational melody) and counterpoint to explain how ordinary "this-worldly" human relationships and suffering can be woven, as genuinely distinct melodic lines, into the single sovereign love of God — turning a technical musical concept into pastoral theology written from a Nazi prison cell.

Illustration

Polyphony — several independent melodic lines sounding together, each remaining fully itself while genuinely harmonizing with the others — gives Begbie a working model for the Trinity that a single, static visual image (like a triangle) cannot: three persons, each fully and distinctly themselves, in real time, in real relationship, without competing for the same musical "space."

Key Terms

  • Sonic Order: The physical, mathematical integrity of natural sound embedded in creation, eliciting "perceptive trust" in the cosmic order of the Logos.
  • Cantus Firmus (Latin) — "fixed song": The foundational, eternal melody of God's love that grounds human existence, to which life's other "melodies" act as counterpoint.
  • Patience / Waiting: The theological and musical schooling of hope in the "meantime" between promise and fulfilment, where musical tension and delayed resolution train steadfastness.
  • Polyphony: Multiple distinct melodic lines sounding simultaneously — retrieved by Begbie to challenge static, visual-spatial models of Christology and Trinity.

Connections

Explores Barth's lifelong love of Mozart, whose music Barth called "parables of the kingdom" (Part I) without treating it as independent natural revelation. Examines how Bonhoeffer's prison writings (Part I) use cantus firmus and counterpoint theologically. Colin Gunton (Part II.D), Begbie's own mentor, shares his interest in "performance" hermeneutics.

Ch. 42 — Theology and Film

Chapter author: Jolyon Mitchell

Core Idea

Mitchell traces film's theological reception from censorious suspicion to a resource that can provoke ethical questioning, illustrate doctrine, and even catalyse prayer, arguing directors function as "visual storytellers" crafting genuine cinematic theologies through image and sound, not merely words on a screen.

Detailed Explanation

Cinema's rapid twentieth-century rise was initially met with severe ecclesiastical hostility and moral censorship — the Catholic "Legion of Decency" and Pope Pius XI's 1936 encyclical Vigilanti Cura policed film content directly. From the 1960s-70s, North American scholars (Hurley, Wall, May) began serious exploratory theological engagement with film, culminating in a late-century academic boom and film's integration into liturgical worship itself. Mitchell insists theologians must develop genuine visual sensitivity and engage actual film theory, not merely treat movies as illustrated sermons.

Example

Larry Kreitzer's "reversing the hermeneutical flow" — deliberately using a film adaptation to shed fresh light back onto the biblical text it is based on, rather than only using the Bible to judge the film — has become a concrete, widely-used classroom method in theology-and-film courses.

Illustration

Early Christian suspicion of cinema treated it like a stranger at the door to be screened and often turned away. Contemporary theological film criticism treats it more like a foreign-language conversation partner: you have to actually learn the grammar of camera angle, edit, and sound before you can hear what it is really saying, rather than assuming it is only saying, badly, what a sermon could say better.

Key Terms

  • Auteur Theory: The film-criticism framework privileging the director's personal, overarching vision as a film's primary organizing "author."
  • Reversing the Hermeneutical Flow: Larry Kreitzer's method of bringing a biblical text, a literary work, and its film adaptation into dialogue, letting the film illuminate the Scripture.
  • Interpretive Arch: Robert Jewett's two-way exegetical method moving between a film's world and the biblical text's world, treating both with equal exegetical seriousness.
  • Transcendental Style: Paul Schrader's term for a sparse, non-manipulative filmic style (Ozu, Bresson, Dreyer) that rejects Hollywood convention to facilitate direct encounter with the sacred.

Connections

Tillich's method of correlation (Part I) is the methodological baseline early cinematic theologians used to correlate film with Christian symbols. Lindbeck's "intratextual" world (Part II.D) is challenged by critics who see film as a culture's own "thermometer." Graham Ward (Part II.E) uses popular cinema constructively in his own urban dogmatics. Shares de Gruchy's (previous chapter) concern about images' potential to dehumanize the Other.

Unit 1 — Biblical Foundations I — Repentance and the Forgiveness of Sins

The Old Testament Matrix

The Hebrew vocabulary shapes everything that follows. The governing term is teshuvah — literally "turning/returning," not "feeling sorry." Repentance in the Old Testament is a change of direction, a coming back to covenant, and only derivatively a state of emotion. This is why the prophetic call is always "Return to me" (Joel 2:12; Hos 14:1) rather than "regret your actions."

The sacrificial system provided for sin in two categories — the hattat (purification/sin offering) and the asham (reparation/guilt offering, Lev 4-5) — with the annual Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur, Lev 16) as the comprehensive rite: two goats, one sacrificed, one — the scapegoat (azazel) — laden with the people's sins and driven into the wilderness. Note the two distinct mechanisms already present: expiation by blood and removal by transfer.

Psalm 51 (the Miserere) is the tradition's central penitential text, and its theology is sophisticated: it asks for interior renewal ("create in me a clean heart"), locates sin primarily against God ("against you, you alone, have I sinned"), and relativises sacrifice itself — "the sacrifice acceptable to God is a broken spirit." The Church prays it every Friday at Morning Prayer for precisely this reason.

The prophetic and narrative deepening. Nathan's confrontation of David (2 Sam 12) supplies the pattern of accusation, acknowledgement, forgiveness, and remaining consequence — David is forgiven ("the LORD has put away your sin") yet the child dies. Any adequate theology of penance must account for this structure, which is the seed of the later distinction between guilt and temporal punishment.

Jesus and the Forgiveness of Sins

The programmatic announcement. "The kingdom of God is at hand; repent (μετανοεῖτε) and believe in the gospel" (Mk 1:15). Metanoia — literally a change of nous, of mind and outlook — is the Greek rendering of teshuvah and carries the same directional force.

The decisive controversy: the paralytic (Mk 2:1-12). Jesus says "your sins are forgiven"; the scribes object, "who can forgive sins but God alone?"; Jesus heals the man "so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins." Three points a BTh student must draw out:

  1. The scribes' premise is correct — only God forgives sin.
  2. Jesus does not deny it; he claims the prerogative.
  3. The phrase "on earth" is doing deliberate work. Forgiveness is not deferred to a heavenly tribunal; it is exercised visibly, in history, by a man. This is the christological foundation of any sacramental — that is, visible and ecclesial — ministry of forgiveness.

The parables and encounters. The sinful woman (Lk 7:36-50 — "her many sins are forgiven, for she loved much"), Zacchaeus (Lk 19:1-10, where conversion issues immediately in restitution), and above all Luke 15 — the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the prodigal son. The last is the tradition's controlling image: the father runs, the confession is interrupted before it finishes, the robe and ring precede any probation. Grace outruns the penitent's script.

Illustration. Notice what the prodigal never gets to do. He rehearses a speech — "treat me as one of your hired servants" — and the father cuts him off mid-sentence. Any theology of penance that makes the penitent's performance the cause of the forgiveness has inverted the parable. The confession matters, but it is a response to a father already running, not a fee paid at a gate.

Unit 2 — Biblical Foundations II — The Power of the Keys and Apostolic Practice

The Three Foundational Texts

Text Recipient Words
Matthew 16:19 Peter "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven..."
Matthew 18:18 The disciples / community "Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven" — set in the context of fraternal correction (18:15-17)
John 20:22-23 The apostles, Easter evening "He breathed on them and said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained'"

Exegetical observations that matter for the doctrine:

  • "Binding and loosing" is a rabbinic technical pair covering both doctrinal decision (declaring something permitted or forbidden) and disciplinary action (excommunicating or restoring to fellowship). The Church's later reading — the authority to forgive or withhold forgiveness — falls squarely within the second sense.
  • Matthew 18 sets the power in a communal, procedural context: private correction, then two or three witnesses, then the assembly, then treating the unrepentant "as a Gentile and a tax collector." This is the New Testament's clearest picture of ecclesial discipline, and it is the direct ancestor of canonical penance (Unit 3).
  • John 20:22 deliberately echoes Genesis 2:7 — God breathing life into Adam — and Ezekiel 37. The forgiveness of sins is presented as an act of new creation, and it is bound to the gift of the Spirit.
  • "If you retain" is the crucial half for the later doctrine. The authority is discretionary, which presupposes some means of knowing what is to be forgiven or retained — the exegetical basis Trent will use for the necessity of confessing sins (Unit 9).

Apostolic Practice in the Epistles

  • 2 Cor 5:18-20 — God "gave us the ministry of reconciliation (diakonian tēs katallagēs)... we are ambassadors for Christ." Reconciliation is entrusted to a ministry, not left to private transaction.
  • 1 Cor 5:1-5 and 2 Cor 2:5-11 — the single clearest apostolic case: Paul orders a grave sinner excluded from the community, and later urges that he be forgiven and restored lest he "be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow." Exclusion, repentance, readmission — the shape of canonical penance is already visible.
  • James 5:14-16 — "confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed," set immediately alongside the anointing of the sick by the presbyters, whose effect includes "if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven."
  • 1 John 1:9 — "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us"; and 1 Jn 5:16-17, the puzzling distinction between "sin unto death" and sin "not unto death," which foreshadows the later mortal/venial distinction without settling it.

Teaching point. The New Testament does not give a rite. What it gives is: the authority to forgive and retain, entrusted to a ministry; a communal disciplinary procedure; and the practice of confession. Every later form of the sacrament — canonical, tariffed, scholastic, modern — is an attempt to house those three elements in a workable pastoral structure. Understanding this saves you from the two opposite errors of claiming the confessional box is apostolic and of claiming the sacrament was invented in the Middle Ages.

Unit 10 — Casuistry, Jansenism, and Alphonsus Liguori

The post-Tridentine period produced a distinctive and often-caricatured body of work: the moral manuals, written to train confessors in judging concrete cases (casus). The genuine question underlying the whole enterprise was: when a moral obligation is doubtful, how free is the penitent?

The Systems

System Principle Tendency
Rigorism / Tutiorism One must always follow the safer opinion favouring the law Condemned as excessive (Alexander VIII, 1690)
Probabiliorism One may follow the opinion favouring liberty only if it is more probable than the opinion favouring the law Dominican tendency
Equiprobabilism Where the opinions are equally probable, liberty may be followed Alphonsus Liguori
Probabilism Any solidly probable opinion favouring liberty may be followed, even if the contrary is more probable Jesuit tendency
Laxism A slenderly probable opinion suffices Condemned (Innocent XI, 1679)

The caricature and the reality. Pascal's Provincial Letters (1656-57) made "casuistry" a byword for moral evasion, and the laxist excesses were real enough to be condemned by Rome itself. But the underlying project — the disciplined application of principle to concrete circumstance, with attention to the penitent's actual freedom, knowledge, and constraints — is indispensable to any real pastoral practice. The modern equivalent is clinical ethics.

Jansenism

Antoine Arnauld's De la fréquente communion (1643) argued for a return to patristic severity: penitents should be tested by long delays before absolution, and communion should be approached only rarely and after prolonged preparation.

The pastoral effect was chilling in the exact sense: absolution deferred, communion avoided, a generation formed in scrupulosity and fear. Jansenist rigorism is the single largest factor behind the sombre reputation of Catholic penitential practice in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and its influence long outlasted its formal condemnation.

Alphonsus Liguori (1696-1787)

The decisive corrective figure, and patron of confessors and moral theologians. His Theologia Moralis charted the equiprobabilist middle course between laxism and rigorism, and — more importantly for practice — his pastoral counsel insisted that the confessor is father and physician before he is judge, that absolution should not be needlessly deferred, and that scrupulous penitents must be treated with gentleness rather than severity.

Teaching point. Liguori is the pivot between the Tridentine juridical emphasis and the modern pastoral one. Pius X's encouragement of frequent communion (1905) and the 1973 Rite's language of healing both stand in his line. A good essay on the modern reform traces the continuity back through him rather than presenting Vatican II as a rupture.

Unit 5 — Celtic Tariffed Penance and the Great Transition

This is the largest single structural change in the history of any sacrament, and it came not from a council but from Irish monks.

The Irish System

Irish Christianity developed outside the Roman civic structure, in a monastic and tribal setting where the anmchara ("soul friend") was a normal spiritual institution. From this grew a radically different penitential practice:

Canonical penance Tariffed (Celtic) penance
Repeatable? Once in a lifetime Repeatable without limit
Public or private? Public state (ordo paenitentium) Entirely private
Minister The bishop Any priest, often a monk
Penance determined by The bishop's judgement A fixed tariff in a written handbook
Sequence Confession, penance, then absolution Confession, absolution, then satisfaction
Lifelong disabilities? Yes No

The Penitentials

Handbooks listing sins with their assigned penances, sometimes with startling specificity. The major ones: Finnian (6th c.), Columbanus (c. 600), Cummean (7th c.), and Theodore of Canterbury (late 7th c.), whose Penitential was the most influential in England.

Their governing principle is medicinal and is stated explicitly by Columbanus: contraria contrariis sanantur — "contraries are cured by contraries." The talkative are given silence, the greedy fasting, the violent restraint. The confessor is a physician of souls prescribing a remedy, not merely a judge imposing a fine.

Commutation and its abuses. Because tariffs could run to years of fasting, systems of commutation (arreum) developed, allowing substitution — so many psalms recited, so many alms given, so many days on bread and water — in place of longer periods. Genuine pastoral flexibility shaded easily into a market in penances, and the eventual monetisation of that logic is one root of the indulgence controversy (Unit 7).

The Transition on the Continent

Columbanus and the Irish missionaries brought the practice to Gaul and beyond around 600. The reaction was initially hostile: the Third Council of Toledo (589) actually condemned the practice of repeated confession and absolution as an "abomination" and a departure from canonical tradition.

Yet within two centuries the argument was over — not because it was won theologically, but because the new system worked and the old one had ceased to function. The Council of Chalon-sur-Saône (813) recognised both forms as legitimate, and the private, repeatable form steadily became universal.

Two Consequential Shifts

1. Absolution moves before satisfaction. In canonical penance, reconciliation followed completed penance. In the tariffed system, the priest absolved and the penitent then performed the assigned satisfaction. This reordering is what makes possible the scholastic account in which satisfaction remedies the temporal punishment remaining after the guilt is forgiven (Unit 6) — and therefore, downstream, the whole theology of indulgences.

2. The formula changes from deprecatory to indicative. Early formulas were prayers: "May God absolve you," Absolutionem et remissionem tribuat tibi omnipotens Deus. From roughly the twelfth century the West adopts the indicative: "Ego te absolvo a peccatis tuis" — "I absolve you." Aquinas defends the indicative form as expressing that the priest acts as an instrumental cause in Christ's person, not merely as an intercessor. The Eastern churches retain deprecatory forms to this day, and this remains a genuine difference of theological accent.

Illustration. Think of the shift as the difference between a court that sentences you and a clinic that treats you. Canonical penance was juridical and one-shot: you were tried, sentenced, and readmitted, once. The Irish system was medical and ongoing: you came back whenever you were ill, and the physician had a manual of prescriptions. The Church never formally chose between these models — it ended up carrying both, which is why the sacrament still speaks simultaneously of a tribunal and of a hospital.

Unit 13 — Contemporary Debates and Pastoral Application

Live Debates

1. The seal versus mandatory reporting. The most serious contemporary conflict. Several jurisdictions — following child-protection inquiries, notably Australia's Royal Commission — have legislated or proposed to legislate that clergy must report abuse disclosed in confession. The Church's position is that the seal admits no exception and that a priest must accept civil penalty rather than violate it. The counter-argument is that the protection of children must override any professional privilege.

A fair treatment should note what Catholic practice actually permits, which is often missed in public debate: the confessor may — and pastorally should — make absolution's fruitfulness depend on the penitent's genuine purpose of amendment, which can include requiring that the penitent self-report or take protective steps; and he may urge the penitent to repeat the disclosure outside confession, where the seal does not bind. What he may not do is himself disclose.

2. Fundamental option. Developed by Josef Fuchs and others: mortal sin is not adequately described as a single grave act, but as a fundamental reorientation of the person away from God, which individual acts may or may not express. Veritatis Splendor §§65-70 accepts that there is a fundamental orientation of freedom but rejects the separation of that orientation from concrete choices, insisting that gravely disordered acts freely chosen with full knowledge can themselves constitute the rejection of God.

3. Frequency and the "crisis of confession." Whether the remedy is better catechesis on sin, more availability, better ars celebrandi of the sacrament, wider use of Rite II, or something more fundamental about the culture's relation to guilt.

4. General absolution. Whether the restrictions of Misericordia Dei are pastorally sustainable in mission territories and situations of severe priest shortage.

5. Confession and psychotherapy. They must be distinguished: the confessor is not a therapist, absolution is not catharsis, and grace is not insight. But they are not opposed, and a competent confessor recognises when a penitent's difficulty is a matter for referral rather than penance — most obviously with scrupulosity, which the tradition has long identified as a spiritual affliction requiring gentleness and firm direction rather than more confession.

The Indian and Asian Context

  • Shame and honour. In cultures organised around honour and shame rather than guilt and innocence, the disclosure of sin carries social weight that Western pastoral manuals often fail to anticipate. Anonymity may matter far more; face-to-face celebration may be experienced as exposure rather than encounter.
  • Community and reconciliation. Indigenous and village practices of communal reconciliation — the resolution of disputes before elders, with restitution and restored relationship — offer a genuine point of contact with the ecclesial dimension recovered by LG 11, and with Rite II in particular.
  • Caste. As with baptism and the Eucharist, the theological question is unavoidable: reconciliation with the Church that one has wounded by sin is hollow where caste division within that same Church remains unaddressed. Social sin (Reconciliatio et Paenitentia 16) supplies the vocabulary for naming this in the confessional and in preaching.
  • Inculturation. Michael Amaladoss's methodological caution applies: adaptation must proceed from actual living symbols of reconciliation in the culture, not from a designer's scheme.

Practical Notes for the Confessor

Point Guidance
The confessor's fourfold role Judge, physician, teacher, and father — the tradition insists on all four, and the modern rite emphasises the last three
Deferral of absolution Rare and requires genuine absence of contrition or purpose of amendment; Liguori's counsel against needless deferral remains normative
The scrupulous penitent Do not permit repeated confession of the same forgiven material; give a clear, simple rule of obedience
Doubtful matter Where the penitent's culpability is genuinely uncertain, the tradition's moral systems (Unit 10) exist precisely to protect freedom
Danger of death Any priest may absolve any sin and lift any censure (c. 976) — the Novatian settlement in canonical form
Anonymity The penitent's right; the confessional grille must remain available (Misericordia Dei)

Unit 14 — Examination Preparation

Likely Essay Questions

  1. "The history of penance is the history of a single sacrament housed in three incompatible structures." Discuss with reference to canonical, tariffed, and modern practice.
  2. Why did canonical penance collapse, and what does its collapse reveal about the relation between doctrine and pastoral viability?
  3. Assess the significance of the Novatian schism for the Church's understanding of its own power to forgive, comparing it with the Donatist controversy.
  4. "Thesis 1 of the Ninety-Five Theses, not the abuses of Tetzel, is the real origin of the Reformation dispute over penance." Evaluate.
  5. Explain and assess Trent's teaching that absolution is a judicial act, and show how the requirement of integral confession follows from it.
  6. Trace the contrition/attrition debate from Abelard to Trent, and assess its pastoral consequences.
  7. "The 1973 Rite recovered an ecclesial dimension that scholastic theology had always taught but practice had obscured." Discuss with reference to LG 11 and the res et sacramentum.
  8. How should the Church respond to legislation requiring the breach of the seal of confession?
  9. Account for the collapse in the practice of confession since the 1960s, and assess the proposed remedies.

Ten-Second Recall Anchors

  • Teshuvah / metanoia = turning, not feeling.
  • "Hermas: one plank, once." — the single post-baptismal repentance.
  • "Sacrificati, thurificati, libellatici" — the categories of the lapsed.
  • "Novatian says no, the Church says yes" — no sin beyond forgiveness (CCC 982).
  • "Irish monks changed everything" — private, repeatable, tariffed.
  • Contraria contrariis sanantur — the penitentials' medicinal principle.
  • "1215: once a year, and the seal" — Omnis utriusque sexus.
  • "Guilt versus temporal punishment" — the distinction indulgences presuppose.
  • "Attrition suffices with the sacrament" — Trent's pastoral settlement.
  • "Judicial act, therefore integral confession" — Trent Session XIV.
  • "Borromeo built the box in the 1560s" — younger than the Reformation.
  • "Reconciled with God and with the Church" — LG 11.

Comparative Analysis Exercises

  • Tabulate canonical penance against tariffed penance across minister, repeatability, publicity, and sequence.
  • Compare Tertullian's De Paenitentia with his De Pudicitia and account for the change.
  • Set the four Reformation objections beside Trent Session XIV's canons and assess how directly each is met.
  • Compare the medieval Ego te absolvo with the 1973 formula and list what the revision recovers.
  • Compare Novatianism and Donatism as the same instinct applied to different sacraments.

Further Reading

Primary: Shepherd of Hermas, Vision II / Mandate IV · Tertullian, De Paenitentia and De Pudicitia · Cyprian, De Lapsis · the Irish Penitentials (Finnian, Columbanus, Cummean, Theodore) · Lateran IV c. 21 · Aquinas, ST III q.84-90 and Suppl. · Luther, Ninety-Five Theses · Calvin, Institutes III.4 · Trent Session XIV · Ordo Paenitentiae (1973) · Reconciliatio et Paenitentia

Modern: Bernhard Poschmann, Penance and the Anointing of the Sick · Karl Rahner, Theological Investigations XV (penance essays) · James Dallen, The Reconciling Community · John Mahoney, The Making of Moral Theology · Monika Hellwig, Sign of Reconciliation and Conversion

Unit 7 — Indulgences and the Late Medieval Crisis

Indulgences cannot be understood, or fairly criticised, without the distinctions the tradition drew. Getting these right is essential for the Reformation unit.

The Underlying Distinction

The tradition distinguishes:

  • The guilt of sin (culpa) — remitted by absolution in the sacrament.
  • The temporal punishment due to sin (poena temporalis) — the residual disorder and debt, which may remain after the guilt is forgiven, and is expiated either in this life (by satisfaction, penance, works of charity) or in purgatory.

The biblical warrant offered is precisely the Nathan-David episode (Unit 1): the sin is forgiven, yet a consequence remains.

An indulgence is the remission of that temporal punishment, not the forgiveness of sin. An indulgence presupposes that the sin has already been forgiven in confession. This distinction was routinely obscured in popular preaching, which is a large part of why the system detonated.

The Treasury of Merits

The theological basis was formalised by Clement VI in the bull Unigenitus Dei Filius (1343): the infinite merits of Christ, together with those of Mary and the saints, constitute a treasury (thesaurus) which the Church, exercising the power of the keys, may apply to individual members.

How It Went Wrong

  • Indulgences originated in commutation — the Celtic practice of substituting a lighter work for a heavier penance (Unit 5). The logic was already in place; only the scale changed.
  • The Crusade indulgences (from Urban II, 1095) established the plenary indulgence attached to a costly work.
  • Extension to the dead by way of suffrage (15th c.) transformed the pastoral dynamics entirely, since one could now purchase relief for deceased relatives.
  • Financial association — almsgiving as the qualifying work, with the alms directed to a specific project — produced, in practice, a market.
  • The immediate trigger: the St Peter's Basilica indulgence preached in Germany by the Dominican Johann Tetzel, with its notorious jingle (attributed by Luther): "As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs."

Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (31 October 1517)

Read the Theses carefully and you find a document that is not, at this stage, a rejection of the sacrament or even of indulgences as such, but a protest against their misuse:

  • Thesis 1 is the theological heart: "When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said 'Repent' (poenitentiam agite), he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance." Luther is exploiting a translation point — the Vulgate's poenitentiam agite ("do penance") renders the Greek metanoeite ("repent, be converted"), and Luther, following Erasmus's Greek text, argues the Latin had narrowed an interior lifelong conversion into a discrete ritual act.
  • Thesis 36: "Any truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt, even without indulgence letters."
  • Thesis 82 is the sharp pastoral question: if the pope can release souls from purgatory, "why does he not empty purgatory for the sake of holy love... rather than for the sake of miserable money?"

Teaching point. Thesis 1 is the hinge of the whole Reformation on this sacrament. Everything downstream — the rejection of enumerated confession, of satisfaction, of the priestly tribunal — flows from the claim that repentance is the whole shape of the Christian life rather than a repeatable transaction. A good essay begins here rather than with Tetzel.

The Catholic Correction

The Church's own reform was real, if late: Trent Session XXI abolished the office of quaestores (indulgence-preachers) outright, and Session XXV affirmed indulgences while condemning "all evil gains" attached to them. Paul VI's Indulgentiarum Doctrina (1967) substantially reformed the system, abolishing the misleading numerical day-and-year attachments and re-grounding indulgences in the communion of saints.

Unit 4 — The Lapsi Crisis and the Novatian Schism

The single most important test case for the Church's power to forgive, and a standing example of how doctrine gets clarified under pressure.

The Decian Persecution (250-251)

The Emperor Decius required all citizens to sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate (libellus) proving they had done so. The scale of Christian compliance was catastrophic and unexpected — in Carthage, Cyprian reports, the crowds rushed to comply.

The categories of the fallen (lapsi) mattered enormously for how they were later treated:

Category What they did
Sacrificati Actually offered sacrifice — the gravest
Thurificati Burned incense before the idols
Libellatici Did not sacrifice but obtained a certificate, usually by bribery, falsely stating they had
Acta facientes Had a false declaration entered in the public records

The Crisis of the Libelli Pacis

Confessors — those who had suffered for the faith and survived — began issuing libelli pacis, "certificates of peace," to the lapsed, on the strength of their own merits, demanding their immediate readmission. Some were issued in bulk and blank.

This posed the real question sharply: is reconciliation a charism of the heroic, or an act of the Church's ordained ministry?

Cyprian's Resolution: De Lapsis (251)

Cyprian of Carthage navigated between two extremes:

  • Against the confessors' laxity — the libelli pacis cannot bypass the bishop; reconciliation belongs to the ordinary ministry of the Church, not to private spiritual authority however heroically earned.
  • Against rigorism — the lapsed can be forgiven after appropriate penance, graded by the gravity of the lapse (the libellatici more leniently than the sacrificati).
  • The practical settlement, reached at the Council of Carthage (251) and confirmed subsequently: penance proportioned to the offence, with reconciliation available — and, when a new persecution threatened under Gallus, reconciliation accelerated so that the penitents could face it fortified by the Eucharist.

The Novatian Schism

Novatian, a Roman presbyter and able theologian (his De Trinitate is substantial), took the rigorist line: the Church has no power to reconcile the lapsed, who must be left to God's mercy. When Cornelius, a moderate, was elected Bishop of Rome in 251, Novatian was set up as a rival — the first significant antipope — and the schism persisted for centuries.

Why this matters doctrinally. The Church's rejection of Novatianism established three principles that the whole later sacrament presupposes:

  1. No sin is beyond the Church's power to forgive. This is the direct ancestor of the Catechism's flat statement that "there is no offence, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive" (CCC 982).
  2. Reconciliation is ministerial, exercised through the ordained, not charismatic or self-authorising.
  3. The Church is a corpus permixtum — a mixed body of saints and sinners — not a society of the pure. This is the same argument Augustine would deploy against the Donatists over baptism a century and a half later, and the two controversies should be studied together.

Teaching point. Novatianism and Donatism are the same instinct applied to two different sacraments: the demand that the Church be visibly pure, met in both cases by the Church's insistence that holiness is Christ's gift rather than the members' achievement.

Unit 3 — The Patristic Era — Canonical Penance

The Problem: Post-Baptismal Sin

Baptism forgives all sin. What, then, of grave sin committed after baptism? The early Church had no obvious answer, and its first instinct was severe. Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-27 appeared to exclude a second repentance outright, and this rigorist reading was widely held.

The Shepherd of Hermas (c. 140)

The decisive text. Hermas reports a revelation permitting one — and only one — post-baptismal repentance. The concession is explicitly framed as an act of mercy for a Church that had discovered its members sinning gravely, and as strictly non-repeatable.

This "second plank after shipwreck" (later formalised by Trent as secunda tabula post naufragium) is the origin of the whole penitential system. Note its logic: it is a concession, granted reluctantly, and its non-repeatability is the price of granting it at all.

The Three Capital Sins and the Structure of Canonical Penance

The system addressed three grave, publicly-known sins: apostasy, murder, and adultery. Its shape:

  1. Confession to the bishop — sins were disclosed privately to the bishop, who determined the penance. (The persistent claim that patristic confession was itself public is a misconception; what was public was the penance, not usually the disclosure.)
  2. Enrolment in the ordo paenitentium, the "order of penitents" — a distinct canonical state, with its own place in the assembly, distinctive dress, sometimes shorn hair, and often prostration.
  3. The penance itself — fasting, almsgiving, prayer, sexual continence, exclusion from the Eucharist, often lasting years or decades. Nicaea's canons 11-13 legislate terms of several years for various categories.
  4. Reconciliation by the bishop's imposition of hands, ordinarily on Holy Thursday.
  5. Permanent consequences even after reconciliation: in many churches, penitents were barred for life from marriage or remarriage, from military service, from public office, and from ordination.

Exomologesis is Tertullian's term for the whole process — the public "confessing out" of one's penitent condition through this disciplined life.

Tertullian's Two Positions

A superb illustration of the tension in the early Church, since the same author argues both sides at different periods:

  • De Paenitentia (Catholic period, c. 203) — permits the "second repentance," describes exomologesis vividly, and urges sinners not to delay out of shame.
  • De Pudicitia (Montanist period, c. 217) — reverses course, denying the Church has any power to forgive adultery and fornication, and attacking a bishop (probably Callistus of Rome) for a decree extending forgiveness to sins of the flesh.

The Fatal Practical Consequence

Because canonical penance was once-only, public, severe, and carried lifelong disabilities, the entirely predictable result was mass deferral to the deathbed — the same pattern that afflicted baptism in the same period (compare the Sacraments course, Unit 2). Bishops themselves often counselled the young to wait. Augustine's blunt assessment of deathbed penance is worth quoting in essays: he says of such a person that we cannot be sure he is condemned, but neither can we praise the security of his repentance.

By the sixth century the system had effectively collapsed — not because the Church rejected it, but because almost nobody used it. This vacuum is what the Irish penitentials would fill.

Unit 8 — The Reformation

The Reformers' Objections

Four objections, which every exam answer should be able to state and which Trent will answer point by point:

  1. Enumeration is impossible and produces despair. Requiring confession of all mortal sins by species and number binds consciences to an impossible standard. Calvin is scathing: the requirement is "a torture of consciences" (Institutes III.4), since no one can number their sins any more than they can number the hairs on their head.
  2. Satisfaction impugns Christ's satisfaction. If Christ has made full satisfaction, human works of satisfaction detract from its sufficiency.
  3. Attrition is servile. Sorrow motivated by fear of punishment is not repentance at all but self-interest — Luther calls attrition the sorrow of a gallows-penitent.
  4. Priestly absolution usurps God's prerogative when construed as a judicial act rather than the declaration of a forgiveness God grants directly to faith.

The Positions

Figure Position
Luther Wavered on whether penance is a sacrament — in The Babylonian Captivity (1520) he lists it as one of three, then withdraws it for lacking a divinely instituted visible sign, leaving baptism and the Supper. But he retained private confession and absolution enthusiastically as a means of consolation, calling it a precious gift; what he rejected was compulsory enumeration, satisfaction, and the juridical framing. Absolution is the word of the gospel applied to the individual
Calvin Denies it is a sacrament (Institutes III.4, IV.19); attacks enumeration and satisfaction sharply; retains and indeed strengthens ecclesiastical discipline through the consistory, and permits voluntary private confession to a minister for the troubled conscience
Anglican The Book of Common Prayer provides a General Confession and absolution in the daily offices and Communion; auricular confession is retained as voluntary — the Exhortation invites anyone who "cannot quiet his own conscience" to seek a minister for counsel and absolution. The classic formula: "All may, none must, some should"
Anabaptists Reject sacramental penance; practise the ban and shunning as community discipline

Teaching point — note the irony parallel to the Eucharist. Luther is in some respects closer to Catholic practice than Calvin on private confession and absolution, which he wanted retained in Lutheran churches and which survived in Lutheran orders for centuries. The Reformation dispute was never simply "confession versus no confession"; it was about compulsion, enumeration, satisfaction, and the juridical character of absolution.

Unit 6 — The Scholastic Synthesis

Lateran IV (1215), Canon 21 — Omnis utriusque sexus

The single most consequential piece of penitential legislation ever enacted. It requires all the faithful who have reached the age of discretion to confess their sins to their own priest at least once a year, and to receive the Eucharist at Easter.

It also legislates the seal in the strongest terms and with a striking image: the priest is to be "discreet and cautious, so that in the manner of a skilled physician he may pour wine and oil on the wounds of the injured"; and the priest who betrays a sin revealed in confession is to be deposed and confined to a monastery for perpetual penance. The seal is thus as old as the universal obligation itself.

(Note: the same canon underlies the Easter communion obligation treated in the Eucharist course.)

The Anatomy of the Sacrament

The scholastics identified four constituent elements — three acts of the penitent and one of the priest:

Element Content
Contritio Sorrow for sin with the purpose of amendment
Confessio Disclosure of sins to the priest
Satisfactio The penance performed to repair the disorder caused by sin
Absolutio The priest's sacramental absolution

Aquinas's structural move (ST III q.84 and the Supplement): since the sacrament has no physical element like water or oil, the three acts of the penitent function as the quasi-materia, and the absolution is the form. This is the classic solution to the awkwardness of fitting penance into the matter/form scheme.

The threefold distinction applied:

Level Content
sacramentum tantum The acts of the penitent and the absolution
res et sacramentum Interior penance — and, importantly, reconciliation with the Church
res tantum The forgiveness of sins and the restoration of grace

Note that penance, unlike baptism, confirmation, and orders, imprints no character — which is precisely why it is repeatable.

Contrition versus Attrition

The central medieval controversy, and a standard exam question.

  • Contritio — sorrow arising from the love of God, from having offended one who is supremely good. Peter Abelard and the "contritionists" held that such sorrow of itself obtains forgiveness, with confession serving mainly to declare a forgiveness already received. This risks making the sacrament redundant.
  • Attritio — imperfect sorrow, arising from fear of hell, the ugliness of sin, or loss of heaven. Duns Scotus and the "attritionists" held that attrition, joined to the sacrament, suffices — the sacrament supplying what the disposition lacks.

Aquinas's position is subtler than either label: attrition disposes toward, and in the sacrament is transformed into, contrition by the grace conferred. Trent will settle the practical question in the attritionists' favour (Unit 9): attrition, which excludes the will to sin and hopes for pardon, is a sufficient disposition when joined to sacramental absolution.

Why this matters pastorally. The attritionist settlement is what makes the sacrament genuinely available to ordinary penitents. If only perfect contrition sufficed, no one could ever be sure of the sacrament's effect — the very anxiety the Reformers would later charge the system with producing.

Jurisdiction and Reserved Sins

A distinctive feature of penance among the sacraments: valid absolution requires not only orders but also jurisdiction (in modern terms, the faculty to hear confessions). Certain grave sins were reserved to the bishop or the Holy See. The modern residue is in CIC c. 1357 and the latae sententiae excommunications reserved to the Apostolic See — with the crucial exception that in danger of death any priest can absolve any sin (c. 976), a rule that expresses the Novatian settlement in canonical form.

Unit 12 — Theological Significance

1. Christological. The sacrament continues Jesus's own ministry. The scribes' question at Mark 2:7 — "who can forgive sins but God alone?" — is answered not by denying the premise but by asserting that the Son of Man forgives on earth, visibly, through a human agent. Sacramental confession is the extension of that visibility.

2. Pneumatological. John 20:22 binds the power to forgive to the gift of the Spirit, in a scene deliberately echoing the creation of Adam. Forgiveness is new creation, not merely the cancelling of a debt.

3. Ecclesial. LG 11: reconciliation with God and with the Church. Sin wounds the body; the res et sacramentum of penance is precisely reconciliatio cum Ecclesia. This is why the sacrament is celebrated with a minister of the Church rather than in private prayer alone, and why Rite II exists.

4. Anthropological and medicinal. The two governing metaphors — tribunal and hospital — both have deep roots (the juridical from canonical penance and Trent, the medicinal from the penitentials' contraria contrariis sanantur and Lateran IV's "skilled physician"). Neither alone is adequate: a purely juridical account produces scrupulosity, a purely therapeutic one dissolves the reality of guilt.

5. Eschatological. Purgatory, temporal punishment, and satisfaction locate the sacrament within a larger account of purification that does not end at death.

6. On the seal. The sigillum confessionis is, in Catholic teaching, absolute and without exception — the confessor may not reveal what he has heard for any reason whatever, and may not even use the knowledge in a way that could disadvantage the penitent. CIC c. 983 §1 declares it "inviolable"; c. 1386 §1 imposes latae sententiae excommunication reserved to the Apostolic See for direct violation. There is no provision for dispensation, and no exception for danger to life or for civil law. Its theological ground: what is said in confession is said to God, the priest hearing it not as a man but as God's minister — he genuinely does not "know" it as ordinary human knowledge.

Unit 9 — Trent and the Post-Tridentine Settlement

Session XIV (25 November 1551)

Trent treated Penance together with Extreme Unction. Its doctrine and canons answer the Reformers point by point.

Point Trent's teaching
Institution A true and proper sacrament instituted by Christ, principally in John 20:22-23
Distinct from baptism Necessary for those who fall after baptism; the secunda tabula post naufragium, "the second plank after shipwreck"
Necessity of confession Penitents must confess all mortal sins of which they are conscious after diligent examination, including hidden ones and those against the last two commandments, according to species and number and with the circumstances that change the species
Attrition Imperfect contrition, conceived from the consideration of sin's ugliness or fear of hell, is a true gift of God; though insufficient alone to justify, it disposes to grace in the sacrament
Absolution is judicial Not a bare ministry of announcing forgiveness, but a judicial act (actus iudicialis) in which the priest pronounces sentence as a judge — hence the necessity of confession, since a judge cannot judge a cause he does not know
Satisfaction Real and salutary; does not detract from Christ's merit but derives all its power from it — "we can do nothing of ourselves as of ourselves"
The minister Priests alone, requiring jurisdiction as well as orders; reservation of cases upheld

Teaching point on canon 6. Trent's insistence on the judicial character of absolution is the doctrinal hinge, because it generates the requirement of confession as a matter of internal logic: if the priest is a judge, he must know the case. Any essay on why Catholics confess to a priest should run through this argument rather than through mere positive-law appeal.

The Institutional Consequences

  • The Roman Ritual (1614) standardised the rite for the Latin Church.
  • The confessional box — a genuine innovation, introduced by Charles Borromeo in Milan in the 1560s and rapidly adopted. Its purpose was twofold: to guarantee anonymity and to prevent solicitation and scandal by physically separating confessor and penitent. It is worth stressing to students that this piece of furniture, so identified with the sacrament in the popular mind, is younger than the Reformation.
  • Seminary formation in moral theology was established to produce competent confessors — which generated the manual tradition and, with it, the controversies of the next unit.

Unit 11 — Vatican II and the 1973 Rite of Penance

The Conciliar Mandate

Sacrosanctum Concilium 72 is brief and consequential: "The rite and formulas for the sacrament of penance are to be revised so that they more clearly express both the nature and the effect of the sacrament."

Lumen Gentium 11 supplies the theological substance the revision would express — those who approach the sacrament "obtain pardon from the mercy of God for the offence committed against him and are at the same time reconciled with the Church, which they have wounded by their sins."

This is the recovery of the ecclesial dimension, and it is the interpretive key to the whole reform. The scholastic tradition had it (reconciliatio cum Ecclesia was the res et sacramentum), but centuries of private practice had obscured it in ordinary consciousness. Sin is never merely a private transaction between the individual and God; it damages the body.

The Ordo Paenitentiae (2 December 1973)

The three forms:

Rite Structure Use
Rite I Reconciliation of individual penitents The ordinary form
Rite II Communal celebration with individual confession and absolution Liturgy of the Word, communal examination, then individual confession; strongly recommended, and the clearest expression of the ecclesial dimension
Rite III Communal celebration with general confession and absolution Strictly restricted — see below

The restriction on Rite III (elaborated in CIC cc. 961-963 and tightened by John Paul II's motu proprio Misericordia Dei, 2002): general absolution requires either danger of death with insufficient time, or a grave necessity judged by the diocesan bishop — and the number of confessors being insufficient merely because of a large gathering or a great feast does not constitute grave necessity. Those absolved are obliged to confess their grave sins individually as soon as possible.

The renewed structure of Rite I deliberately restores elements long lost: welcome and a blessing, a reading from Scripture (frequently omitted in practice, but integral to the rite as revised), the confession, the penance, the act of contrition, the absolution, a proclamation of praise, and dismissal.

The new formula of absolution replaced the terse Ego te absolvo with a fully Trinitarian prayer, of which the older formula is now the conclusion:

"God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit."

Notice how much doctrine this recovers: the Father's initiative, the paschal mystery, the Spirit's mission, the ministry of the Church, and only then the indicative absolution.

Later Magisterial Documents

Document Date Content
Reconciliatio et Paenitentia 1984 John Paul II's post-synodal exhortation; important for its careful treatment of social sin (§16), which it accepts in an analogical sense while insisting that sin is always ultimately a personal act
Veritatis Splendor 1993 §§65-70 critique fundamental option theory (Unit 12)
Misericordia Dei 2002 Restates the discipline on individual confession and restricts general absolution
Misericordiae Vultus / Misericordia et Misera 2015 / 2016 Francis's Jubilee of Mercy documents; institute the Missionaries of Mercy and extend to all priests the faculty to absolve the sin of abortion

The Crisis of Practice

Any honest treatment must name it: the collapse in the frequency of confession across most of the Western Church from the late 1960s is among the most dramatic shifts in Catholic practice in modern history — in many countries from near-universal regular use to a small minority.

Diagnoses vary and are genuinely contested: the weakening of the sense of sin; the shift from a juridical to a therapeutic culture; the Humanae Vitae crisis and the resulting quiet disengagement from the confessional over contraception; loss of the mortal/venial distinction; poor experiences of the sacrament; the general decline of practice; and — a point often overlooked — that the near-universal reception of communion at every Mass, following Pius X's reforms, removed the practical link by which confession had been tied to communion.

Unit 1 — Biblical Foundations of Baptism
